content.value:
Rājamārtaṇḍa Pātañjalavṛtti of Bhoja, transcribed by Suryansu Ray from a
                    manuscript.

The manuscript from which this e-text was transcribed was written in the Devanāgarī
                script. The electronic text below is in a lossless transliteration using the Latin
                alphabet. The transliteration scheme used is the IAST (
The International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration

). IAST differs in
                small ways from ISO 15919, but is preferred by most working Sanskrit scholars.
                Conversion of this file to ISO 15919 can be achieved by performing the following
                replacements throughout the file:
ṛ -> r̥ and ṃ -> ṁ
Text division is as Devanāgarī ("ityevam" not "ity evam".)

Initial vowel elision for avagraha is reversed and marked with a + sign: e.g.,
                "prathamo+adhyāyaḥ"
Gentlemen at the Indology site:

I have typed out the Bhojavṛtti, the commentary on the yoga aphorisms of
                            Patañjali, the popular commentary of King Bhoja who ruled in the 11th
                            century. It is presented as a Word DOC file, which has been converted
                            into a PDF file. It is a 125-page Devanāgarī document.

The material was typed by me personally from traditional old manuscript
                            belonging to our family guru.

I have appended an English article at the end of the vṛitti and made a
                            separate section in which all the yoga sūtras are given in one
                            place.

I would like to donate this Bhojavṛitti e-text to your INDOLOGY website
                            for the general public. I have taken great care to ensure that there are
                            no mistakes in the commentary.
With best wishes,
Dr. Suryansu Ray
New Delhi

content.value: from Suryansu Ray suryansuray@yahoo.com
date 26 March 2010 07:19
subject Re: Sending Commentary of King Bhoja on Yoga.
Dear Dr Dominik Wujastyk,

Thank you for your interest in my Bhojavṛtti, the Commentary by King
                            Bhoja on Patañjali's Yoga aphorisms. I have attached the material
                            hereto. The description follows.

1. I am a retired professor from Zakir Husain College, Delhi
                                    University. Around the mid-fifties, when I was a young boy, the
                                    guru of my father visited our house in Calcutta for a month. He
                                    carried a palm-leaf manuscript of this Bhojavṛtti in the
                                    Devanāgarī script, which must have been very old. He reluctantly
                                    allowed me to copy it out in my notebooks, which I did in a
                                    week. He had it checked through a friend of my father. The notes
                                    remained there for 40 years, until I rediscovered them in 1995.
                                    The pages had become yellowish and brittle with age, and were in
                                    bad handwriting, because I am a Bengali and Hindi script was
                                    forieign to me those days.

In the course of 15 years, I typed out the handwritten pages and
                                    compared the material with materials in libraries in Delhi. I
                                    found many alternative expressions, some justifiable, some not.
                                    I noted down those which could be accepted. You will find them
                                    in my vṛttis inserted in square brackets with pa0, meaning
                                    pāṭhāntara. Even in some sūtras there are different readings,
                                    which I have pointed out there.

2. That my material is genuinely old can be seen from the fact
                                    that this text does not contain any European punctuation marks
                                    -- there are no commas, semicolons, quotation marks, etc. The
                                    whole vṛtti is written using only single and double vertical
                                    strokes for punctuation. Besides, joining different words
                                    together with the rules of sandhi is compulsorily done. Long
                                    continuous expressions abound, with compounds mixed with
                                    joinings, as is the case with classical commentaries. I feel
                                    that modern-day punctuation marks should not be introduced in
                                    the text, because putting hyphens may obstruct the other
                                    meanings inherent in the text.

[In response to an enquiry about copyright and distribution
                            permission:]
from Suryansu Ray suryansuray@yahoo.com
date 26 March 2010 15:31
subject Re: Sending Commentary of King Bhoja on Yoga.
Dear Dr. Dominik Wujastyk,

1. In India when we donate something, -- the exact word is daana,
                                --- we lose all rights to it. The Bhojavṛtti I sent to you is your
                                property now, and you will use it as you please.

2. In India, the tradition is that, at some time in our life, we
                                become initiated to the sprirituality through a spiritual master
                                (guru). The best gurus are mendicant sannyāsīs, who are constantly
                                moving on foot, staying at a town not more than three months. They
                                usually avoid contact with society and stay at temples, etc. They do
                                not have any address, but through his disciples scattered all over
                                India some rumour would float that he left Pune last month and his
                                whereabouts are now not known. In 1955, when I was a 15-year-old
                                boy, this much I knew: that the manuscript this Hindi-speaking sādhu
                                was carrying was something valuable. Sanskrit was taught at my
                                school and my Sanskrit Paṇḍit told me that it would be better if I
                                could keep a copy of it. The matter was in 4 volumes, each with two
                                wooden covers and two holes to bind them together. He was possibly
                                carrying it from one Gurukul (Traditional Vedic School) to another.
                                That was why HE WAS RELUCTANT to allow me to touch it because I was
                                then ignorant of the subject. Such gurus give up even their names,
                                and assume a name ending with -ānanda (bliss). They are known by the
                                succession of disciples, and people refer to them as a disciple of
                                so and so. Later, I came to Delhi for higher studies and started
                                teaching in Delhi University. I had my own guru, who is no more in
                                the body. These days such gurus are rare. They did not have any
                                property or address, walked barefoot constantly, suddenly appearing
                                where big congregations or yajñas were held, giving initiation
                                (dīkṣā) to a few unknown people, and travelling in the company of a
                                few recluse disciples. They did not have any worry for procuring
                                food. In the afternoon they would come down to the locality where
                                people would give them alms in rice, āṭā (wheat powder) and potato.
                                They would go back to their shelter, cook it with wooden fire and
                                take a few morsels without salt. Even these days millions of such
                                sādhus exist but they do not come to the locality any more. ---
                                Instead a modern sort of religious people have emerged, who are
                                making money for their speeches, have built big Ashrams and are
                                imparting wrong information. Yoga has become some sort of physical
                                exercises.

3. My origianal typing was in ITRANS in Swami Satchidananda's
                                Itranslator. Para by para I converted the matter in transliteration
                                and Devanāgarī through his software. I am sending my ITRANS code
                                with this letter.
With best wishes, Suryansu Ray, New Delhi

                                    week. He had it checked through a friend of my father. The notes
                                    remained there for 40 years, until I rediscovered them in 1995.
                                    The pages had become yellowish and brittle with age, and were in
                                    bad handwriting, because I am a Bengali and Hindi script was
                                    forieign to me those days.
                                In the course of 15 years, I typed out the handwritten pages and
                                    compared the material with materials in libraries in Delhi. I
                                    found many alternative expressions, some justifiable, some not.
                                    I noted down those which could be accepted. You will find them
                                    in my vṛttis inserted in square brackets with pa0, meaning
                                    pāṭhāntara. Even in some sūtras there are different readings,
                                    which I have pointed out there.
                            2. That my material is genuinely old can be seen from the fact
                                    that this text does not contain any European punctuation marks
                                    -- there are no commas, semicolons, quotation marks, etc. The
                                    whole vṛtti is written using only single and double vertical
                                    strokes for punctuation. Besides, joining different words
                                    together with the rules of sandhi is compulsorily done. Long
                                    continuous expressions abound, with compounds mixed with
                                    joinings, as is the case with classical commentaries. I feel
                                    that modern-day punctuation marks should not be introduced in
                                    the text, because putting hyphens may obstruct the other
                                    meanings inherent in the text.
                            3. The 9 files included in this zipped file are as follows: (1) Bhojavṛtti in Devanagari.doc. -- This is the main
                                            text, written in the Devanāgarī font callted Sanskrit
                                            2003. This powerful font was created by Swami
                                            Satchidananda of Omkarananda Ashram, Haridwar, India
                                            (www.omkarananda-ashram.org), in collaboration with
                                            Ulrich Stiehl, Heidelberg (www.sanskritweb.net). Ulrich
                                            had earlier tabulated all the consonant conjuncts
                                            actually seen in the religious and philosophical works
                                            of the classical and vedic language. The respected
                                            Swami-ji has included all these conjuncts in his font.
                                            (In fact he is better known for his Itranslator, which
                                            includes Sanskrit 2003 an the default font.) I have
                                            included the Sanskrit 2003 font into my zipped file.
                                        Ulrich has written a long technical manual on how to use
                                            this Itranslator. -- At the end of this DOC file you can
                                            find my English article titled "On the Yoga of Patanjali
                                            and King Bhoja." This article reveals to the uninitiated
                                            the secrets of spiritual practices like the Yoga through
                                            which man can break out of the horrible vortex of
                                            transmigration and return to his original
                                            fully-conscious state, never to be entangled again in
                                            the material body.
                                    (2) Bhojavṛtti in Devanagari. pdf.--- This is a pdf
                                            conversion of the above doc file.
                                    (3) Bhojavṛtti in transliteration.doc.--- Some readers
                                            may find it convenient to read this transliterated
                                            version of the above doc file. This conversion has been
                                            made through the Itranslator of Swami-ji. The font used
                                            here is called URW Palladio ITU, which is created by
                                            Ulrich and is freely available from his website. I have
                                            included 4 fonts from this package.
                                    (4) Bhojavṛtti in transliteration.pdf. --- This is the
                                            pdf version of the doc file.
                                    (5) Sanskrit2005.ttf -- the font of Swamiji in which I
                                            have typed the main doc Devanagari file.
                                    (6) Four fonts belonging to URW Palladio ITU (Regular,
                                            Bold, Italics, Bold-Italics). -- these are four ttf
                                            files.
                        In case of any doubt please feel free to talk to me. I have taken great
                            care to see that there is no mistake in the commentary. Nevertheless, to
                            err is human, and for which the Mother Earth is still in her orbit.
                        With best wishes, Suryansu Ray,
                        Dr. Suryansu Ray
                        4-B, Pocket-B Vikaspuri Extension 
 Outer Ring Road
 New Delhi - 119918,
 India.
                    [In response to an enquiry about copyright and distribution
                            permission:]
                        from Suryansu Ray suryansuray@yahoo.com
                        date 26 March 2010 15:31
                        subject Re: Sending Commentary of King Bhoja on Yoga.
                        Dear Dr. Dominik Wujastyk,
                        1. In India when we donate something, -- the exact word is daana,
                                --- we lose all rights to it. The Bhojavṛtti I sent to you is your
                                property now, and you will use it as you please.
                            2. In India, the tradition is that, at some time in our life, we
                                become initiated to the sprirituality through a spiritual master
                                (guru). The best gurus are mendicant sannyāsīs, who are constantly
                                moving on foot, staying at a town not more than three months. They
                                usually avoid contact with society and stay at temples, etc. They do
                                not have any address, but through his disciples scattered all over
                                India some rumour would float that he left Pune last month and his
                                whereabouts are now not known. In 1955, when I was a 15-year-old
                                boy, this much I knew: that the manuscript this Hindi-speaking sādhu
                                was carrying was something valuable. Sanskrit was taught at my
                                school and my Sanskrit Paṇḍit told me that it would be better if I
                                could keep a copy of it. The matter was in 4 volumes, each with two
                                wooden covers and two holes to bind them together. He was possibly
                                carrying it from one Gurukul (Traditional Vedic School) to another.
                                That was why HE WAS RELUCTANT to allow me to touch it because I was
                                then ignorant of the subject. Such gurus give up even their names,
                                and assume a name ending with -ānanda (bliss). They are known by the
                                succession of disciples, and people refer to them as a disciple of
                                so and so. Later, I came to Delhi for higher studies and started
                                teaching in Delhi University. I had my own guru, who is no more in
                                the body. These days such gurus are rare. They did not have any
                                property or address, walked barefoot constantly, suddenly appearing
                                where big congregations or yajñas were held, giving initiation
                                (dīkṣā) to a few unknown people, and travelling in the company of a
                                few recluse disciples. They did not have any worry for procuring
                                food. In the afternoon they would come down to the locality where
                                people would give them alms in rice, āṭā (wheat powder) and potato.
                                They would go back to their shelter, cook it with wooden fire and
                                take a few morsels without salt. Even these days millions of such
                                sādhus exist but they do not come to the locality any more. ---
                                Instead a modern sort of religious people have emerged, who are
                                making money for their speeches, have built big Ashrams and are
                                imparting wrong information. Yoga has become some sort of physical
                                exercises.
                            3. My origianal typing was in ITRANS in Swami Satchidananda's
                                Itranslator. Para by para I converted the matter in transliteration
                                and Devanāgarī through his software. I am sending my ITRANS code
                                with this letter.
                        With best wishes, Suryansu Ray, New Delhi

children.translated_text: Auspicious Invocation
||The <s>Yoga Sūtras</s> of <s>Patañjali</s>||
|| Accompanied by the <s>Rājamārtaṇḍa</s> commentary composed by <s>Bhojadeva</s>, Lord of <s>Dhārā</s> ||

children.text: dehārddhayogaḥ śivayoḥ sa śreyāṃsi tanotu vaḥ|
children.translated_text: May that union of <s>Śiva</s> and <s>Śakti</s> in half the body bestow blessings upon you,
by the mere remembrance of which, a person attains <s>kaivalya</s> (liberation), even though it is difficult to attain. ||1||
By the remembrance of whom even the threefold sufferings of men

children.text: prayānti sadyo vilayaṃ taṃ stumaḥ śivamavyayam ||2||
children.translated_text: immediately come to dissolution—we praise that imperishable <s>Śiva</s>. ||2||
Victorious is that unprecedented statement of the sage <s>Patañjali</s>,
by which even the separation (<s>viyoga</s>) of <s>Puruṣa</s> (spirit) and <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) is declared to be <s>Yoga</s> (union). ||3||
Victorious are the words of the Lord of Serpents (<s>Patañjali</s>), whose brilliance—like the rays of the sun dispelling the darkness of accumulated ignorance flashing within—

children.text: vibhāvyamānāḥ satataṃ manāṃsi yāḥ satāṃ sadānandamayāni kurvate||4||
children.translated_text: which, being constantly contemplated, make the minds of the virtuous always filled with bliss. ||4||
By one who composed the grammar (<s>anuśāsana</s>) of words, who produced [a commentary] on <s>Patañjali</s>'s [work],
who also extended a commentary called <s>Rājamṛgāṅka</s> on medicine,
by whom the impurity of speech, mind, and body was removed, just as by the Lord of the Hooded Ones (<s>Śeṣa</s>/<s>Patañjali</s>)—
victorious are the radiant words of that King <s>Śrī Raṇaraṅgamalla</s> (i.e., <s>Bhoja</s>). ||5||
What is exceedingly difficult to understand, that they abandon saying 'the meaning is clear';
on clear meanings, they produce excessive elaboration with useless compounds and the like;
and in the wrong place, with many useless ramblings, they create confusion
for the listeners—thus all commentators produce a distortion of subject matter. ||6||
Casting aside prolixity, removing the net of conceptual alternatives,
having ascertained the proper meanings and illuminating what is subtle,
this elucidation within <s>Patañjali</s>'s doctrine, by me,
is extended as a cause of awakening for the wise. ||7||
<s>Samādhipāda</s> (Chapter on Concentration)
Now, the chapter on <s>Samādhi</s> (concentration). ||1||
Now, the teaching of <s>Yoga</s>. ||Samādhi 1||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- anena sūtreṇa śāstrasya sambandhābhidheyaprayojanānyākhyāyante|
                        athaśabdo+adhikāradyotako maṅgalārthakaśca| yogo yuktiḥ samādhānam| yuja
                        samādhau

| anuśiṣyate vyākhyāyate
                        lakṣaṇabhedopāyaphalairyena tadanuśāsanam| yogasyānuśāsanaṃ yogānuśāsanam|
                        tadā+a+aśāstraparisamāpteradhikṛtaṃ boddhavyamityarthaḥ| tatra śāstrasya
                        vyutpādyatayā yogaḥ sasādhanaḥ saphalo+abhidheyaḥ| tadvyutpādanaṃ ca phalam|
                        vyutpāditasya yogasya kaivalyaṃ phalam| śāstrābhidheyayoḥ
                        pratipādyapratipādakabhāvalakṣaṇaḥ sambandhaḥ| abhidheyasya tatphalasya ca
                        kaivalyasya sādhyasādhanabhāvaḥ| etaduktaṃ bhavati --- vyutpādyasya yogasya
                        sādhanāni śāstreṇa pradarśyante| tatsādhanasiddho yogaḥ kaivalyākhyaṃ
                        phalamutpādayati ||1||
children.translated_text: That by which [<s>Yoga</s>] is taught and expounded through definition, classification, means, and fruit—that is the teaching (<s>anuśāsana</s>). The teaching of <s>Yoga</s> is <s>yogānuśāsana</s>. From that point, until the completion of the treatise, [the subject] should be understood as being under consideration—this is the meaning. Therein, <s>Yoga</s> together with its means and its fruit is the subject matter (<s>abhidheya</s>) to be expounded by the treatise. Its exposition is the purpose. <s>Kaivalya</s> (liberation) is the fruit of <s>Yoga</s> once expounded. The connection between the treatise and the subject matter is characterized by the relation of that which is to be demonstrated and the demonstrator. Between the subject matter and its fruit, <s>Kaivalya</s>, there is the relation of end and means. This amounts to saying: the means of <s>Yoga</s>, which is to be expounded, are shown by the treatise. <s>Yoga</s>, accomplished through those means, produces the fruit called <s>Kaivalya</s>. ||1||

Commentary: By this <s>sūtra</s>, the connection (<s>sambandha</s>), subject matter (<s>abhidheya</s>), and purpose (<s>prayojana</s>) of the treatise are declared. The word '<s>atha</s>' indicates the commencement of a topic and serves an auspicious purpose. <s>Yoga</s> means union, concentration. [The root is] '<s>yuja samādhau</s>' (yuj in the sense of concentration).
Therein, 'What is <s>Yoga</s>?'—he says:
<s>Yoga</s> is the cessation of the modifications of the mind. ||Samādhi 2||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- cittasya nirmalasattvapariṇāmarūpasya yā
                        vṛttayo+aṅgāṅgibhāvapariṇāmarūpāstāsāṃ nirodho bahirmukhatayā
                        pariṇativicchedādantarmukhatayā pratilomapariṇāmena svakāraṇe layo yoga
                        ityākhyāyate| sa ca nirodhaḥ sarvāsāṃ cittabhūmināṃ sarvaprāṇināṃ dharmaḥ
                        kadācit kasyāñcidbhūmavāvirbhavati| tāśca kṣiptaṃ mūḍhaṃ vikṣiptam ekāgraṃ
                        niruddhamiti cittasya bhūmayaścittasyāvasthāviśeṣāḥ| tatra kṣiptaṃ rajasa
                        udrekādasthiraṃ bahirmukhatayā sukhaduḥkhādiviṣayeṣu vikalpiteṣu vyavahiteṣu
                        vā rajasā preritam| tacca sadaiva daityadānavādīnām| mūḍhaṃ tamasa udrekāt
                        kṛtyākṛtyavibhāgamantareṇa krodhādibhirviruddhakṛtyeṣveva niyamitam| tacca
                        sadaiva rakṣaḥpiśācādīnām| vikṣiptaṃ tu sattvodrekādvaiśiṣṭyena parihṛtya
                        duḥkhasādhanaṃ sukhasādhaneṣveva śabdādiṣu pravṛttam| tacca sadaiva devānām|
                        etaduktaṃ bhavati --- rajasā pravṛttirūpaṃ tamasā parāpakāraniyataṃ sattvena
                        sukhamayaṃ cittaṃ bhavati| etāstisraścittāvasthāḥ samādhāvanupayoginyaḥ|
                        ekāgraniruddharūpe dve ca sattvotkarṣādyathottaramavasthitattvāt
                        samādhāvupayogaṃ bhajete| sattvādikramavyutkrame tvayamabhiprāyaḥ ---
                        dvayorapi rajastamasoratyantaheyatve+apyetadarthaṃ rajasaḥ
                        prathamamupādānam| yāvanna pravṛttirdarśitā tāvannivṛttirna śakyate
                        darśayitumiti dvayorvyatyayena pradarśanam| sattvasya tvetadarthaṃ paścāt
                        pradarśanaṃ yat tasyotkarṣeṇottare dve bhūmī yogopayoginyāviti|
                        anayordvayorekāgraniruddhayorbhūmyoryaścittasyaikāgratārūpaḥ pariṇāmaḥ sa
                        yoga ityuktaṃ bhavati| ekāgre bahirvṛttinirodhaḥ| niruddhe ca sarvāsāṃ
                        vṛttināṃ saṃskārāṇāṃ ca pravilaya ityanayoreva bhūmyoryogasya
                        sambhavaḥ||2||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The mind, whose nature is the transformation of pure <s>sattva</s> (lucidity)—its modifications (<s>vṛttis</s>), which are of the nature of transformations in the part-whole relationship—their cessation (<s>nirodha</s>), meaning the interruption of outward-directed transformation and the dissolution into its own cause through inverse transformation in an inward direction, is what is called <s>Yoga</s>. And that cessation is the property of all mental states of all living beings, though it manifests at some time in some particular state. And those [states] are: <s>kṣipta</s> (restless), <s>mūḍha</s> (stupefied), <s>vikṣipta</s> (distracted), <s>ekāgra</s> (one-pointed), and <s>niruddha</s> (restrained)—these are the states of the mind, the particular conditions of the mind. Among these, the restless (<s>kṣipta</s>) state, due to the predominance of <s>rajas</s> (passion), is unstable, directed outward by <s>rajas</s> toward objects of pleasure and pain, whether imagined or obstructed. And that is the permanent state of <s>Daityas</s> and <s>Dānavas</s> (demons). The stupefied (<s>mūḍha</s>) state, due to the predominance of <s>tamas</s> (darkness), without discrimination between what should and should not be done, is confined to wrong actions by anger and such emotions. And that is the permanent state of <s>Rākṣasas</s> and <s>Piśācas</s> (ghouls). The distracted (<s>vikṣipta</s>), however, due to the predominance of <s>sattva</s> (lucidity), having particularly avoided the means of suffering, is engaged only in the means of pleasure such as sound and other sense objects. And that is the permanent state of the <s>Devas</s> (gods). This amounts to saying: by <s>rajas</s>, the mind has the nature of activity; by <s>tamas</s>, it is confined to harming others; by <s>sattva</s>, it is blissful. These three mental states are not useful for <s>samādhi</s>. The two states of <s>ekāgra</s> (one-pointed) and <s>niruddha</s> (restrained), due to the excellence of <s>sattva</s>, being established in successively higher levels, become useful for <s>samādhi</s>. Regarding the order and reversal of <s>sattva</s> and the others, this is the intention: although both <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s> are absolutely to be abandoned, for this purpose <s>rajas</s> is taken up first, because until activity is shown, cessation cannot be shown—hence the reversed presentation of the two. But <s>sattva</s> is presented afterward for this purpose: that through its excellence, the two higher states become useful for <s>Yoga</s>. Of these two states, <s>ekāgra</s> and <s>niruddha</s>, the transformation of the mind that has the nature of one-pointedness—that is said to be <s>Yoga</s>. In the one-pointed state, there is cessation of outward modifications. In the restrained state, there is the complete dissolution of all modifications and their latent impressions—thus <s>Yoga</s> is possible only in these two states. ||2||

children.text:
idānīṃ sūtrakāraścittavṛttinirodhapadāni vyākhyātukāmaḥ prathamaṃ cittapadaṃ
                        vyācaṣṭe ---
children.translated_text: Now, the <s>sūtrakāra</s> (author of the aphorisms), wishing to explain the terms '<s>citta</s>' (mind), '<s>vṛtti</s>' (modification), and '<s>nirodha</s>' (cessation), first expounds the term '<s>citta</s>':
Then the seer abides in its own nature. ||Samādhi 3||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- draṣṭuḥ puruṣasya tasmin kāle svarūpe cinmātratāyāmavasthānaṃ
                        sthitirbhavati| ayamarthaḥ --- utpannavivekakhyāteścitsaṃkramābhāvāt
                        kartṛtvābhimānanivṛttau procchannapariṇāmāyāṃ buddhāvātmanaḥ
                        svarūpeṇāvasthānaṃ sthitirbhavati ||3||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Of the seer, that is, of <s>Puruṣa</s> (the spirit), at that time there is abiding (<s>avasthāna</s>), stable dwelling, in its own nature, which is pure consciousness (<s>cinmātratā</s>). This is the meaning: when <s>vivekakhyāti</s> (discriminative knowledge) has arisen, due to the absence of the transfer of consciousness to objects, when the false sense of agency has ceased, when the <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) has its transformations concealed—then there is the abiding of the Self in its own nature. ||3||
But in the state of emergence (<s>vyutthāna</s>), 'What is its nature?'—he says:
At other times, [there is] identification with the modifications. ||Samādhi 4||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- itaratra yogādanyasmin kāle vṛttayo yā vakṣyamāṇalakṣaṇāstābhiḥ
                        sārūpyaṃ tadrūpatvam| ayamarthaḥ --- yādṛśyo vṛttayaḥ sukhaduḥkhamohātmikāḥ
                        prādurbhavanti tādṛgrūpa eva saṃvedyate vyavahartṛbhiḥ puruṣaḥ| tadevaṃ
                        yasminnekāgratayā pariṇate citiśakteḥ svasmin rūpe pratiṣṭhānaṃ bhavati
                        yasmiṃścendriyavṛttidvāreṇa viṣayākāreṇa pariṇate puruṣastadrūpākāra iva
                        paribhāvyate| yathā jalataraṅgeṣu calatsu candraścalanniva pratibhāṣate
                        taccittam ||4||
children.translated_text: Commentary: 'At other times'—at a time other than <s>Yoga</s>, the modifications (<s>vṛttis</s>) that have the characteristics to be described—identification (<s>sārūpya</s>) with them means assuming their form. The meaning is: whatever modifications arise, consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, <s>Puruṣa</s> is perceived by experiencers as having that very form. Thus, in whichever state the mind is transformed through one-pointedness, there is the establishment of the power of consciousness in its own form; and in whichever state the mind is transformed through sense-modifications into the form of objects, <s>Puruṣa</s> is perceived as if having that form—just as the moon, when water-waves are moving, appears as if moving. That is the mind. ||4||
In order to explain the term '<s>vṛtti</s>' (modification), he says:
The modifications are fivefold, afflicted and non-afflicted. ||Samādhi 5||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- vṛttayaścittapariṇāmaviśeṣāḥ| vṛttisamudāyalakṣaṇasyā+avayavino
                        yā+avayavabhūtā vṛttayastadapekṣayā tayappratyayaḥ (aṣṭā0 5|2|42)| etaduktaṃ
                        bhavati --- pañca vṛttayaḥ kīdṛśyaḥ| kliṣṭā akliṣṭāḥ|
                        kleśairvakṣyamāṇalakṣaṇairākrāntāḥ kliṣṭāḥ| tadviparītā akliṣṭāḥ ||5||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The modifications (<s>vṛttis</s>) are particular transformations of the mind. The <s>vṛttis</s>, which are the component parts of the whole characterized as the aggregate of modifications—in relation to that, the suffix '<s>-tayaḥ</s>' [is used] (<s>Aṣṭādhyāyī</s> 5.2.42). This amounts to saying: the five <s>vṛttis</s>—of what kind? Afflicted (<s>kliṣṭa</s>) and non-afflicted (<s>akliṣṭa</s>). Those seized by the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), whose characteristics will be described, are afflicted. Those opposite to them are non-afflicted. ||5||

children.text: etā eva pañca vṛttayaḥ saṅkṣipya uddiśyante ---
children.translated_text: These very five modifications are briefly enumerated:
[They are] valid cognition (<s>pramāṇa</s>), error (<s>viparyaya</s>), conceptualization (<s>vikalpa</s>), sleep (<s>nidrā</s>), and memory (<s>smṛti</s>). ||Samādhi 6||
Commentary: He states their definitions in order:
Perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), inference (<s>anumāna</s>), and verbal testimony (<s>āgama</s>) are the valid means of knowledge. ||Samādhi 7||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- atrātiprasiddhatvāt pramāṇānāṃ śāstrakāreṇa bhedanirūpaṇenaiva
                        gatatvāllakṣaṇasya pṛthak lakṣaṇaṃ na kṛtam| pramāṇalakṣaṇantu ---
                        avisaṃvādi jñānaṃ pramāṇamiti| indriyadvāreṇa bāhyavastūparāgāccittasya
                        tadviṣayasāmānyaviśeṣātmano+arthasya viśeṣāvadhāraṇapradhānā vṛttiḥ
                        pratyakṣam| gṛhītasambandhālliṅgālliṅgini sāmānyādhyavasāyo+anumānam|
                        āptavacanamāgamaḥ ||7||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Here, since the means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇas</s>) are extremely well-known, the author of the treatise has not given a separate definition, considering that by merely describing the divisions, the definition is understood. The definition of <s>pramāṇa</s>, however, is: non-deceptive knowledge is <s>pramāṇa</s>. The modification of the mind that, through the channel of the senses, due to the coloring by external objects, has as its chief function the ascertainment of the particular of an object whose nature consists of the universal and the particular—that is direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>). The general determination of the indicated object from the indicator, both having a grasped relationship—that is inference (<s>anumāna</s>). The statement of a reliable person is verbal testimony (<s>āgama</s>). ||7||
Having thus explained the modification in the form of valid cognition, he states the modification in the form of error:
Error is false knowledge not established in the true form [of the object]. ||Samādhi 8||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- atathābhūte+arthe tathotpadyamānaṃ jñānaṃ viparyayaḥ| yathā
                        śuktikāyāṃ rajatajñānam| atadrūpapratiṣṭhamiti| tasyārthasya yadrūpaṃ tasmin
                        rūpe na pratiṣṭhati tasyārthasya yat pāramārthikaṃ rūpaṃ na tat
                        pratibhāsayatīti yāvat| saṃśayo+apyatadrūpapratiṣṭhitatvānmithyājñānam|
                        yathā sthāṇurvā puruṣo veti ||8||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Knowledge that arises as 'thus' regarding an object that is not 'thus' is error (<s>viparyaya</s>). For example, the cognition of silver in a seashell. 'Not established in the true form'—it does not reflect the true nature of that object—this is the meaning. Doubt also, since it is not established in the true form, is false knowledge. For example, 'Is it a post or a person?' ||8||
In order to explain the modification of conceptualization, he says:
<s>Vikalpa</s> (conceptualization) follows verbal knowledge and is devoid of a corresponding object. ||Samādhi 9||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- śabdajanitaṃ jñānaṃ śabdajñānaṃ| tadanupatituṃ śīlaṃ yasya saḥ
                        śabdajñānānupātī| vastunastathātvamanapekṣamāṇo yo+adhyavasāyaḥ sa vikalpa
                        ityucyate| yathā puruṣasya caitanyaṃ svarūpamiti| atra devadattasya kambala
                        iti śabdajanite jñāne ṣaṣṭhyā yo+adhyavasito bhedastamihāvidyamānamapi
                        samāropya pravartate+adhyavasāyaḥ| vastutastu caitanyameva puruṣaḥ ||9||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Knowledge born of words is 'verbal knowledge.' That which has the habit of following it is 'following verbal knowledge.' A determination that does not depend on the actual nature of an object—that is called <s>vikalpa</s>. For example, 'Consciousness is the essential nature of <s>Puruṣa</s>.' Here, in the cognition generated by the words '<s>Devadatta</s>'s blanket,' the difference implied by the genitive case—though non-existent in reality, the determination operates by superimposing it. But in reality, consciousness alone is <s>Puruṣa</s>. ||9||
In order to explain sleep, he says:
Sleep (<s>nidrā</s>) is that modification which has the cognition of absence as its support. ||Samādhi 10||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- abhāvapratyaya ālambanaṃ yasyāḥ sā tathoktā| etaduktaṃ bhavati ---
                        yā santatamudriktatvāttamasaḥ samastaviṣayaparityāgena pravartate vṛttiḥ sā
                        nidrā| tasyāśca sukhamahamasvāpsamiti smṛtidarśanāt
                        smṛteścānubhavavyatirekeṇānupapattervṛttittvam ||10||
children.translated_text: Commentary: That which has the cognition of absence (<s>abhāvapratyaya</s>) as its support (<s>ālambana</s>) is so called. This amounts to saying: the modification that operates with the complete abandonment of all objects due to the excessive predominance of <s>tamas</s> (darkness)—that is sleep. And its status as a <s>vṛtti</s> (modification) is established because the memory 'I slept happily' is observed, and because memory is impossible without prior experience. ||10||
In order to explain memory, he says:
Memory (<s>smṛti</s>) is the non-deprivation of an experienced object. ||Samādhi 11||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- pramāṇenānubhūtasya viṣayasya yo+ayamasampramoṣaḥ saṃskāradvāreṇa
                        buddhāvārohaḥ sā smṛtiḥ| tatra pramāṇaviparyayavikalpā jāgradavasthāḥ| tā
                        eva tadanubhavabalāt prakṣīyamāṇāḥ svapnaḥ

children.translated_text: Sleep, however, has no perceived object. And memory has as its cause valid cognition, error, conceptualization, and sleep. ||11||

Commentary: The non-deprivation (<s>asampramoṣa</s>) of an object experienced through a means of valid knowledge, meaning its ascent to the <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) through the channel of latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>)—that is memory. Among these, valid cognition, error, and conceptualization are waking states. Those very states, being weakened through the power of their experience, constitute dream.
Having thus explained the modifications, in order to explain cessation together with its means, he says:
Their cessation is achieved through <s>abhyāsa</s> (practice) and <s>vairāgya</s> (detachment). ||Samādhi 12||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- abhyāsavairāgye vakṣyamāṇalakṣaṇe tābhyāṃ
                        prakāśapravṛttiniyamarūpā yā vṛttayastāsāṃ nirodho bhavatītyuktaṃ bhavati|
                        tāsāṃ vinivṛttabāhyābhiniveśānāmantarmukhatayā svakāraṇa eva citte
                        śaktirūpatayā+avasthānam| tatra viṣayadoṣadarśanajena vairāgyeṇa
                        tadvaimukhyamutpādyate| abhyāsena ca sukhajanakaṃ
                        śāntapravāhapradarśanadvāreṇa dṛḍhasthairyamutpādyate| itthaṃ tābhyāṃ
                        bhavati cittavṛttinirodhaḥ ||12||
children.translated_text: Commentary: <s>Abhyāsa</s> (practice) and <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion), whose characteristics will be described, by these two, the cessation (<s>nirodha</s>) of the <s>vṛttis</s> (mental modifications), whose nature is illumination, activity, and restraint, takes place—this is what has been stated. The abiding of those [<s>vṛttis</s>], whose external attachment has ceased, turned inward, in their own cause, namely the mind, in the form of latent power—in that, through <s>vairāgya</s> born of seeing the defects of sense objects, aversion toward them is produced. Through <s>abhyāsa</s>, firm stability is produced by demonstrating the peaceful flow that generates happiness. Thus, through these two, the cessation of the mental modifications (<s>cittavṛttinirodha</s>) occurs. ||12||
To explain <s>abhyāsa</s>, he says:
Therein, the effort toward steadiness is <s>abhyāsa</s> (practice). ||Samādhi 13||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- vṛttirahitasya cittasya svarūpaniṣṭhaḥ pariṇāmaḥ sthitistasyāṃ
                        yatna utsāhaḥ punaḥpunastathātvena cetasi niveśanamabhyāsa ityucyate
                        ||13||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The transformation of the mind devoid of <s>vṛttis</s> (modifications), established in its own nature, is <s>sthiti</s> (steadiness). The effort toward that, the exertion, the repeated fixing of [the mind] in such a state in consciousness, is called <s>abhyāsa</s>. ||13||
He states the further specification of that very [<s>abhyāsa</s>]:
But that [<s>abhyāsa</s>] becomes firmly grounded when practiced for a long time, without interruption, and with devotion. ||Samādhi 14||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- bahukālaṃ nairantaryeṇādarātiśayena ca sevyamāno dṛḍhabhūmiḥ
                        sthiro bhavati| dārḍhyāya prabhavatītyarthaḥ ||14||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Being practiced for a long time, without interruption, and with great devotion, it becomes firmly grounded, stable. It becomes effective for firmness—this is the meaning. ||14||
He states the characteristic of <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion):
The consciousness of mastery in one who is free from craving for objects seen or heard about is <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion). ||Samādhi 15||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- dvividho hi viṣayo dṛṣṭa ānuśravikaśca| dṛṣṭa ihaivopalabhyamānaḥ
                        śabdādiḥ| devalokādāvānuśravikaḥ| anuśrūyate gurumukhādityanuśravo vedastata
                        āgata ānuśravikaḥ| tayordvayorapi viṣayayoḥ
                        pariṇāmavirasatvadarśanādvigatagardhasya yā vaśīkārasaṃjñā mamaite vaśyā
                        nāhameteṣāṃ vaśya iti yo+ayaṃ vimarśastadvairāgyamucyate ||15||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Objects are indeed of two kinds: seen and heard about. The 'seen' is that which is perceived here in this world, such as sound and the other [sense objects]. The 'heard about' pertains to the world of the gods and such [realms]. What is heard from the teacher's mouth is <s>anuśrava</s> (tradition), i.e., the <s>Vedas</s>; what comes from that is <s>ānuśravika</s> (based on tradition). The consciousness of mastery (<s>vaśīkārasaṃjñā</s>) of one who, seeing the insipidity in the transformation of both those kinds of objects, is free from desire—'these are under my control; I am not under their control'—this deliberation is called <s>vairāgya</s>. ||15||
He states the further specification of that very [<s>vairāgya</s>]:
The supreme [<s>vairāgya</s>] is freedom from craving for the <s>guṇas</s> (constituents of nature), arising from the discernment of <s>Puruṣa</s> (the Self). ||Samādhi 16||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tadvairāgyaṃ paraṃ prakṛṣṭaṃ prathamaṃ vairāgyaṃ viṣayaviṣayaṃ
                        dvitīyaṃ guṇaviṣayamutpannaguṇapuruṣavivekakhyātereva bhavati|
                        nirodhasamādheratyantānukūlatvāt ||16||
children.translated_text: Commentary: That <s>vairāgya</s>, the supreme, the most excellent—the first <s>vairāgya</s> pertains to [external] objects; the second pertains to the <s>guṇas</s> (constituents of nature) and arises only from the discernment (<s>khyāti</s>) of the distinction between the <s>guṇas</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>. Because it is extremely conducive to <s>nirodhasamādhi</s> (the samādhi of cessation). ||16||
Having thus stated the essential nature of <s>yoga</s>, he now describes the varieties of <s>samprajñāta</s> (cognitive samādhi):
<s>Samprajñāta</s> [samādhi] is accompanied by <s>vitarka</s> (deliberation), <s>vicāra</s> (reflection), <s>ānanda</s> (bliss), and <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness). ||Samādhi 17||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- samādhiriti śeṣaḥ| samyak saṃśayaviparyayarahitatvena prajñāyate
                        prakarṣeṇa jñāyate bhāvyasya rūpaṃ yena sa samprajñātaḥ
                        samādhirbhāvanāviśeṣaḥ| sa vitarkādibhedāccaturvidhaḥ --- savitarkaḥ
                        savicāraḥ sānandaḥ sāsmitaśca| bhāvanā bhāvyasya viṣayāntaraparihāreṇa
                        cetasi punaḥpunarniveśanam| bhāvyaṃ ca dvividham --- īśvarastattvāni ca|
                        tānyapi dvividhāni jaḍājaḍabhedāt| jaḍāni caturviṃśatiḥ| ajaḍaḥ puruṣaḥ|
                        tatra yadā mahābhūtānīndriyāṇi sthūlāni viṣayatvenādāya
                        pūrvāparānusandhānena śabdārthollekhasambhedena ca bhāvanā kriyate tadā
                        savitarkaḥ samādhiḥ| asminnevāvalambane
                        pūrvāparānusandhānaśabdollekhaśūnyatvena yadā bhāvanā pravartate tadā
                        nirvitarkaḥ| tanmātrāntaḥkaraṇalakṣaṇaṃ sūkṣmaviṣayamālambya tasya
                        deśakāladharmāvacchedena yadā bhāvanā tadā savicāraḥ| tasminnevāvalambane
                        deśakāladharmāvacchedaṃ vinā dharmimātrāvabhāsitvena bhāvanā kriyamāṇā
                        nirvicāra ityucyate| evaṃparyantaḥ samādhiḥ grāhyasamāpattiriti
                        vyapadiśyate| yadā tu rajastamoleśānuviddhamantaḥkaraṇasattvaṃ bhāvyate tadā
                        guṇabhāvāccitiśakteḥ sukhaprakāśamayasya sattvasya bhāvyamānasyodrekāt
                        sānandaḥ samādhirbhavati| tasminneva samādhau ye baddhadhṛtayastattvāntaraṃ
                        pradhānapuruṣarūpaṃ na paśyanti te vigatadehāhaṃkāratvādvidehaśabdavācyāḥ|
                        iyaṃ grahaṇasamāpattiḥ| tataḥ paraṃ
                        rajastamoleśānabhibhūtaśuddhasattvamālambanīkṛtya yā pravartate bhāvanā
                        tasyāṃ grāhyasya nyagbhāvāccitiśakterudrekāt sattāmātrāvaśeṣatvena samādhiḥ
                        sāsmita ityucyate| na cāhaṃkārāsmitayorabhedaḥ śaṅkanīyaḥ| yato
                        yatrāntaḥkaraṇamahamiti ullekhena viṣayān vedayate so+ahaṃkāraḥ|
                        yatrāntarmukhatayā pratilomapariṇāme prakṛtilīne cetasi sattāmātramavabhāti
                        sā+asmitā| asminneva samādhau ye kṛtaparitoṣāḥ paraṃ paramātmānaṃ puruṣaṃ na
                        paśyanti teṣāṃ cetasi svakāraṇe layamupāgate prakṛtilayā ityucyante| ye
                        paraṃ puruṣaṃ jñātvā bhāvanāyāṃ pravartante teṣāmiyaṃ
                        vivekakhyātirgrahītṛsamāpattirityucyate| tatra samprajñāte samādhau
                        catasro+avasthāḥ śaktirūpatayā+avatiṣṭhante| tatraikaikasyāstyāga
                        uttarottareti caturavastho+ayaṃ samprajñātaḥ samādhiḥ ||17||
                        asamprajñātamāha ---

children.translated_text: The other [<s>samādhi</s>] is preceded by the practice of the cause of cessation,
and only <s>saṃskāras</s> (latent impressions) remain. ||Samādhi 18||

Commentary: '<s>Samādhi</s>' is to be supplied. That by which the form of the object of meditation is correctly known, free from doubt and error, with excellence—that is <s>samprajñāta samādhi</s>, a special type of meditation. It is fourfold according to the distinction of <s>vitarka</s> (deliberation) and the rest: <s>savitarka</s> (with deliberation), <s>savicāra</s> (with reflection), <s>sānanda</s> (with bliss), and <s>sāsmita</s> (with I-am-ness). Meditation (<s>bhāvanā</s>) is the repeated focusing of the mind on the object of meditation to the exclusion of other objects. The object of meditation is of two kinds: <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord) and the <s>tattvas</s> (principles). These too are of two kinds, according to the distinction between insentient and sentient. The insentient are twenty-four. The sentient is <s>Puruṣa</s>. When meditation is performed by taking the gross elements and sense organs as the object, with the connection of prior and subsequent reasoning and with the mingling of word and meaning, that is <s>savitarka samādhi</s>. When meditation proceeds on this same support but without the connection of prior and subsequent reasoning and without verbal elaboration, that is <s>nirvitarka</s>. When meditation is performed taking the subtle object characterized by the <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements) and the inner instrument (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>) as its support, with delimitation by space, time, and attribute, that is <s>savicāra</s>. When meditation is performed on this same support without delimitation by space, time, and attribute, appearing as the bare <s>dharmin</s> (substance) alone, it is called <s>nirvicāra</s>. <s>Samādhi</s> up to this point is designated as <s>grāhyasamāpatti</s> (attainment pertaining to the knowable). When the <s>sattva</s> (luminosity) of the inner instrument, tinged with slight <s>rajas</s> (activity) and <s>tamas</s> (inertia), is meditated upon, then due to the quality of the <s>guṇas</s>, because of the predominance of <s>sattva</s>, which is of the nature of happiness and luminosity, when it is being meditated upon, <s>sānanda samādhi</s> arises. In that very <s>samādhi</s>, those whose understanding is fixed and who do not see the further reality—the nature of <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter) and <s>Puruṣa</s>—being free from the ego of embodiment, are called by the term <s>videha</s> (bodiless). This is <s>grahaṇasamāpatti</s> (attainment pertaining to the grasper). Beyond that, when meditation proceeds taking pure <s>sattva</s> not overwhelmed by even a trace of <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s> as its object, in that [meditation], because the knowable recedes and the power of consciousness (<s>citiśakti</s>) predominates, the <s>samādhi</s> in which only bare existence remains is called <s>sāsmita</s>. One should not suspect that <s>ahaṃkāra</s> (ego) and <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness) are identical, for where the inner instrument cognizes objects with the notion 'I,' that is <s>ahaṃkāra</s>. Where, turned inward, in the reverse transformation, when the mind has dissolved into <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature), only bare existence shines forth—that is <s>asmitā</s>. In this very <s>samādhi</s>, those who are satisfied and do not see the supreme <s>Paramātman</s> (Supreme Self), the <s>Puruṣa</s>—when their mind has merged into its cause—are called <s>prakṛtilaya</s> (merged in Prakṛti). Those who, having known the supreme <s>Puruṣa</s>, proceed in meditation, for them this discriminative knowledge (<s>vivekakhyāti</s>) is called <s>grahītṛsamāpatti</s> (attainment pertaining to the grasper/knower). In <s>samprajñāta samādhi</s>, four stages remain in the form of latent power. In each of these, the abandonment [of the preceding stage constitutes] the progressively higher ones—thus this <s>samprajñāta samādhi</s> has four stages. ||17|| He now describes <s>asamprajñāta</s>:

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- viramyate+aneneti virāmo vitarkādicintātyāgaḥ| virāmaścāsau
                        pratyayaśceti virāmapratyayaḥ| tasyābhyāsaḥ paunaḥpunyena cetasi niveśanam|
                        tatra yā kācidvṛttirullasati tasyā neti netīti nairantaryeṇa paryudasanaṃ
                        virāmapratyayābhyāsaḥ| tatpūrvaḥ samprajñātasamādhiḥ|
                        saṃskāraśeṣo+anyastadvilakṣaṇo+ayamasamprajñāta ityarthaḥ| na tatra
                        kiñcidvedyam| asamprajñāto nirbījaḥ samādhiḥ| iha caturvidhaścittasya
                        pariṇāmaḥ --- vyutthānaṃ samādhiprārambha ekāgratā nirodhaśca| tatra
                        kṣiptamūḍhe cittabhūmī vyutthānam| vikṣiptā bhūmiḥ satvodrekāt
                        samādhiprārambhaḥ| niruddhaikāgrate ca paryantabhūmī| pratipariṇāmaṃ ca
                        saṃskārāḥ| tatra vyutthānajanitāḥ saṃskārāḥ samādhiprārambhajaiḥ saṃskāraiḥ
                        pratyāhanyante| tajjāścaikāgratājaiḥ| nirodhajanitairekāgratājā nirodhajāḥ
                        saṃskārāḥ svarūpaṃ ca hanyante| yathā suvarṇasaṃvalitaṃ dhmāyamānaṃ
                        sīsakamātmānaṃ suvarṇamalaṃ ca nirdahati| evamekāgratājanitān saṃskārān
                        nirodhajāḥ svātmānaṃ ca nirdahanti ||18||
children.translated_text: Commentary: That by which one ceases is <s>virāma</s> (cessation)—the abandonment of deliberation (<s>vitarka</s>) and the rest. <s>Virāma</s> itself being the content (<s>pratyaya</s>) is <s>virāmapratyaya</s>. Its <s>abhyāsa</s> (practice) is the repeated fixing in consciousness. Therein, whatever <s>vṛtti</s> (modification) arises, its continuous negation with 'not this, not this' (<s>neti neti</s>) is the practice of the cessation-content (<s>virāmapratyayābhyāsa</s>). That is preceded by <s>samprajñāta samādhi</s>. 'Having only <s>saṃskāras</s> remaining, the other'—different from that [<s>samprajñāta</s>], this is <s>asamprajñāta</s>—this is the meaning. Nothing is cognized therein. <s>Asamprajñāta</s> is seedless (<s>nirbīja</s>) <s>samādhi</s>. Here, the transformation of the mind is fourfold: emergence (<s>vyutthāna</s>), the beginning of <s>samādhi</s>, one-pointedness (<s>ekāgratā</s>), and cessation (<s>nirodha</s>). Among these, the scattered and deluded mental states constitute emergence. The distracted state, due to the predominance of <s>sattva</s>, constitutes the beginning of <s>samādhi</s>. Cessation and one-pointedness are the final stages. And the <s>saṃskāras</s> correspond to each transformation. Among these, the <s>saṃskāras</s> born of emergence are counteracted by those born of the beginning of <s>samādhi</s>. Those in turn [are counteracted] by those born of one-pointedness. Those born of one-pointedness—the <s>saṃskāras</s> born of cessation destroy both them and their own nature. Just as lead being smelted together with gold burns away both itself and the impurity of the gold, so the [<s>saṃskāras</s>] born of cessation burn away the <s>saṃskāras</s> born of one-pointedness and their own selves. ||18||

children.text:
tadevaṃ yogasya svarūpaṃ bhedaṃ ca saṃkṣepeṇopāyāṃścābhidhāya
                        vistārarūpeṇopāyaṃ yogābhyāsapradarśanapūrvakamupakramate ---
children.translated_text: Having thus briefly described the essential nature, varieties, and means of <s>yoga</s>, he now begins [an exposition] in the form of an elaboration of the means, preceded by a demonstration of the practice of <s>yoga</s>:
For the <s>videhas</s> (bodiless ones) and the <s>prakṛtilayas</s> (those merged in Prakṛti), [<s>samādhi</s>] is caused by [continued] existence (<s>bhava</s>). ||Samādhi 19||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- videhāḥ prakṛtilayāśca vitarkādibhūmikāsūtre (1|17) vyākhyātāḥ|
                        teṣāṃ samādhirbhavapratyayaḥ| bhavaḥ saṃsāraḥ sa eva pratyayaḥ kāraṇaṃ yasya
                        sa bhavapratyayaḥ| ayamarthaḥ --- ādhimātrāntarbhūtā eva te saṃsāre

tathāvidhasamādhibhājo bhavanti|
                        teṣāṃ paratattvā+adarśanādyogābhāso+ayam| ataḥ paratattvajñāne tadbhāvanāyāṃ
                        ca muktikāmena mahān yatno vidheya ityetadarthamupadiṣṭam ||19||
children.translated_text: become participants in such a <s>samādhi</s> while still in <s>saṃsāra</s>. Since they do not see the supreme reality, this is a semblance of <s>yoga</s>. Therefore, one who desires liberation should make great effort in the knowledge of the supreme reality and its meditation—this is what has been taught. ||19||

Commentary: The <s>videhas</s> and the <s>prakṛtilayas</s> have been explained in the sūtra on the stages beginning with <s>vitarka</s> (1.17). Their <s>samādhi</s> is <s>bhavapratyaya</s> (caused by existence). <s>Bhava</s> is <s>saṃsāra</s> (the cycle of existence); that alone is the <s>pratyaya</s> (cause) of which—that is <s>bhavapratyaya</s>. The meaning is: those who are included within the highest intensity [of practice]
But for the others:
[<s>Samādhi</s>] for the others is preceded by faith, energy, mindfulness, <s>samādhi</s>, and <s>prajñā</s> (wisdom). ||Samādhi 20||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- videhaprakṛtilayavyatiriktānāṃ śraddhādipūrvakaḥ śraddhādayaḥ
                        pūrve upāyā yasya sa śraddhādipūrvakaḥ| te ca śraddhādayaḥ
                        kramādupāyopeyabhāvena pravartamānāḥ samprajñātasamādherupāyatāṃ
                        pratipadyante| tatra śraddhā yogaviṣaye cetasaḥ prasādaḥ| vīryamutsāhaḥ|
                        smṛtiranubhūtāsampramoṣaḥ| samādhirekāgratā| prajñā prajñātavyavivekaḥ|
                        tatra śraddhāvato vīryaṃ jāyate yogaviṣaya utsāhavān bhavati| sotsāhasya ca
                        pāścātyāsu bhūmiṣu smṛtirutpadyate| tatsmaraṇācca cetaḥ samādhīyate|
                        samāhitacittaśca bhāvyaṃ samyagvivekena jānāti| ta ete samprajñātasya
                        samādherupāyāstasyābhyāsāt parācca vairāgyādbhavatyasamprajñātaḥ ||20||
children.translated_text: Commentary: For those other than the <s>videhas</s> and <s>prakṛtilayas</s>, [<s>samādhi</s>] is preceded by faith and the rest—faith and the others are the prior means of which—that is 'preceded by faith and the rest.' And those [means] beginning with faith, operating in sequence as means and end, serve as the means to <s>samprajñāta samādhi</s>. Among these, <s>śraddhā</s> (faith) is the serenity of mind regarding the subject of <s>yoga</s>. <s>Vīrya</s> (energy) is exertion. <s>Smṛti</s> (mindfulness) is the non-forgetting of what has been experienced. <s>Samādhi</s> is one-pointedness. <s>Prajñā</s> (wisdom) is the discernment of what is to be known. Among these, for one who has faith, energy arises—one becomes enthusiastic regarding the subject of <s>yoga</s>. For one who is enthusiastic, mindfulness arises in the subsequent stages. From that remembrance, the mind becomes concentrated (<s>samādhīyate</s>). And one whose mind is concentrated knows the object of meditation correctly through discernment. These are the means of <s>samprajñāta samādhi</s>; from its practice and from supreme <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion), <s>asamprajñāta</s> [samādhi] arises. ||20||
He describes the varieties [of yogins] based on the differences in means among yogins who possess the aforementioned means:
For those with intense ardor, [<s>samādhi</s>] is near. ||Samādhi 21||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- samādhilābha iti śeṣaḥ| saṃvegaḥ kriyāheturdṛḍhataraḥ saṃskāraḥ|
                        sa tīvro yeṣāmadhimātropāyānāṃ teṣāmāsannaḥ samādhilābhaḥ samādhiphalaṃ
                        cāsannaṃ bhavati| śīghrameva sampadyata ityarthaḥ ||21||
children.translated_text: Commentary: 'The attainment of <s>samādhi</s>' is to be supplied. <s>Saṃvega</s> (ardor) is a firm impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) that is the strongest cause of action. For those of the most intense means, for whom that [ardor] is intense, the attainment of <s>samādhi</s> and the fruit of <s>samādhi</s> are near—it is accomplished swiftly, this is the meaning. ||21||
He asks: who are those with intense ardor?
There is further distinction due to the mild, moderate, and intense [degrees]. ||Samādhi 22||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tebhya upāyebhyo mṛdvādibhedabhinnebhya upāyavatāṃ viśeṣo bhavati|
                        mṛdurmadhyo+adhimātra ityupāyabhedāḥ| te pratyekaṃ
                        mṛdusaṃvegamadhyasaṃvegatīvrasaṃvegabhedāt tridhā| tadbhedena ca nava yogino
                        bhavanti --- mṛdūpāyo mṛdusaṃvego madhyasaṃvegastīvrasaṃvegaśca| madhyopāyo
                        mṛdusaṃvego madhyasaṃvegastīvrasaṃvegaśca| adhimātropāyo mṛdusaṃvego
                        madhyasaṃvegastīvrasaṃvegaśca| adhimātra upāye tīvre saṃvege ca mahān yatnaḥ
                        kartavya iti bhedopadeśaḥ ||22||
children.translated_text: Commentary: From those means, differentiated by the distinctions of mild and so forth, a distinction arises among those who possess the means. Mild, moderate, and intense are the distinctions of means. Each is threefold according to the distinction of mild ardor, moderate ardor, and intense ardor. By that distinction, there are nine [types of] yogins: one with mild means and mild ardor, moderate ardor, or intense ardor; one with moderate means and mild ardor, moderate ardor, or intense ardor; one with intense means and mild ardor, moderate ardor, or intense ardor. When the means are intense and the ardor is intense, great effort should be made—this is the teaching of the distinctions. ||22||
Now, to show another means, different from these means and easy [to practice], he says:
Or by devotion to <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord). ||Samādhi 23||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- īśvaro vakṣyamāṇalakṣaṇaḥ| tatra praṇidhānaṃ bhaktiviśeṣo
                        viśiṣṭamupāsanaṃ sarvakriyāṇāṃ tatrārpaṇam| viṣayasukhādikaṃ phalamanicchan
                        sarvāḥ kriyāstasmin paramagurāvarpayati| tatpraṇidhānaṃ
                        samādhestatphalalābhasya ca prakṛṣṭa upāyaḥ ||23||
children.translated_text: Commentary: <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord) has the characteristics to be described. There, <s>praṇidhāna</s> (devotion) is a special kind of <s>bhakti</s> (devotion), a distinguished form of worship, the offering of all actions to Him. Not desiring fruits such as sense-pleasures and the like, one offers all actions to that supreme teacher. That <s>praṇidhāna</s> is an excellent means for <s>samādhi</s> and for obtaining its fruit. || 23 ||

children.text:
īśvarasya praṇidhānāt samādhilābha ityuktam| tatreśvarasya svarūpaṃ pramāṇaṃ
                        prabhāvaṃ vācakamupāsanākramaṃ tatphalaṃ ca krameṇa vaktumāha ---
children.translated_text: It has been said that from devotion to <s>Īśvara</s>, <s>samādhi</s> is attained. Now, to explain in order His essential nature, His proof, His power, His designator, the method of worship, and its fruit, he says—

<s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord) is a special <s>Puruṣa</s> (consciousness), untouched by <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), <s>karma</s> (actions), <s>vipāka</s> (fruitions), and <s>āśayas</s> (latent impressions). || Samādhi 24 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- kliśnantīti kleśā avidyādayo vakṣyamāṇāḥ|
                        vihitaniṣiddhavyāmiśrarūpāṇi karmāṇi| vipacyanta iti vipākāḥ karmaphalāni
                        jātyāyurbhogāḥ| āphalavipākāccittabhūmau śerata ityāśayo
                        vāsanākhyasaṃskāraḥ| tairaparāmṛṣṭastriṣvapi kāleṣu na saṃspṛṣṭaḥ|
                        puruṣaviśeṣo+anyebhyaḥ puruṣebhyo viśiṣyate iti viśeṣa īśvaraḥ īśanaśīla
                        icchāmātreṇa sakalajagaduddharaṇakṣamaḥ| yadyapi sarveṣāmātmaṇāṃ
                        kleśādisparśo nāsti tathāpi cittagatāsteṣāmupadiśyante| yathā yoddhṛgato
                        jayaparājayau svāminaḥ| asya tu triṣvapi kāleṣu tathāvidho+api
                        kleśādiparāmarśo nāsti| ataḥ savilakṣaṇa eva bhagavānīśvaraḥ| tasya ca
                        tathāvidhamaiśvaryamanādeḥ sattvotkarṣāt| tasya sattvotkarṣasya
                        prakṛṣṭājjñānādeva| na cānayorjñānaiśvaryayoritaretarāśrayatvaṃ
                        parasparānapekṣatvāt| te dve jñānaiśvarye īśvarasattve vartamāne anādibhūte
                        tena tathāvidhena sattvena tasyānādireva sambandhaḥ|
                        prakṛtipuruṣasaṃyogaviyogayorīśvarecchāvyatirekeṇānupapatteḥ| yathetareṣāṃ
                        prāṇināṃ sukhaduḥkhamohātmakatayā pariṇataṃ cittaṃ nirmale sāttvike
                        dharmānuprakhye pratisaṅkrāntaṃ cicchāyāsaṃkrānte saṃvedyaṃ bhavati
                        naivamīśvarasya| tasya kevala eva sāttvikaḥ pariṇāma
                        utkarṣavānanādisambandhena bhogyatayā vyavasthitaḥ| ataḥ
                        puruṣāntaravilakṣaṇatayā sa eva īśvaraḥ| muktātmanāntu punaḥpunaḥ
                        kleśādiyogastaistaiḥ śāstroktairupāyairnivartitaḥ| asya punaḥ sarvadaiva
                        tathāvidhatvānna muktātmatulyatvam| na ceśvarāṇāmanekatvam| teṣāṃ tulyatve
                        bhinnābhiprāyatvāt kāryasyaivānupapatteḥ| utkarṣāpakarṣayuktatve ya
                        evotkṛṣṭaḥ sa eveśvarastatraiva kāṣṭhāprāptatvādaiśvaryasya ||24||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Those that afflict are <s>kleśas</s> — <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) and others, to be described later. <s>Karmas</s> are actions of three kinds: prescribed, prohibited, and mixed. <s>Vipākas</s> (fruitions) are the ripening — the fruits of <s>karma</s>, namely birth, lifespan, and enjoyment. <s>Āśaya</s> — because they rest in the field of the mind until the ripening of their fruit — is the latent impression called <s>vāsanā</s> (residual tendency). By these untouched — not touched in any of the three times. A special <s>Puruṣa</s> — one who is distinguished from other <s>puruṣas</s>, that special one is <s>Īśvara</s>, whose nature is sovereignty, capable of uplifting the entire universe by mere will. Although for all selves there is no actual contact with <s>kleśas</s> and the like, still these are spoken of as belonging to the mind associated with them — just as victory and defeat belonging to the warrior are attributed to the master. But for Him, in all three times, there is no such contact with <s>kleśas</s> and the like whatsoever. Therefore the Lord <s>Īśvara</s> is indeed of a distinct character. And His such sovereignty is beginningless, due to the excellence of <s>sattva</s>. That excellence of <s>sattva</s> is due to supreme knowledge alone. Nor is there mutual dependency between knowledge and sovereignty, since they are independent of each other. Those two — knowledge and sovereignty — existing in the nature of <s>Īśvara</s>, being beginningless, His connection with such a nature is indeed beginningless. Because the union and separation of <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) and <s>Puruṣa</s> are impossible without the will of <s>Īśvara</s>. Just as the mind of other beings, transformed into the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion, when reflected in the pure <s>sāttvika</s> quality that resembles <s>dharma</s>, becomes knowable when the shadow of consciousness falls upon it — it is not so with <s>Īśvara</s>. His is a purely <s>sāttvika</s> transformation, of supreme excellence, established through beginningless connection as something to be experienced. Therefore, being distinct from other <s>puruṣas</s>, He alone is <s>Īśvara</s>. For liberated selves, the connection with <s>kleśas</s> and the like was removed through various means taught in the scriptures. But since His nature has always been thus, He is not equal to liberated selves. Nor is there plurality of <s>Īśvaras</s>. If they were equal, because of differing intentions, action itself would be impossible. If there were gradations of superiority and inferiority, the one who is supreme alone would be <s>Īśvara</s>, since sovereignty reaches its culmination there alone. || 24 ||
Having thus described the essential nature of <s>Īśvara</s>, he states the proof—
In Him, the seed of omniscience (<s>sārvajñya</s>) is unsurpassed. || Samādhi 25 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tasmin bhagavati sarvajñatvasya
                        yadbījamatītānāgatādigrahaṇasyālpatvaṃ mahatvaṃ ca mūlatvādbījamiva bījam|
                        tat tatra niratiśayaṃ kāṣṭhāṃ prāptam| dṛṣṭā hyalpatvamahatvādīnāṃ dharmāṇāṃ
                        sātiśayānāṃ kāṣṭhāprāptiḥ| yathā paramāṇāvalpatvasyākāśe paramamahatvasya|
                        evaṃ jñānādayo+api cittadharmāstāratamyena paridṛśyamānāḥ
                        kvacinniratiśayatāmāsādayanti| yatra caite niratiśayāḥ sa īśvaraḥ| yadyapi
                        sāmānyamātre+anumānasya paryavasitatvānna viśeṣāvagatiḥ sambhavati tathāpi
                        śāstrādasya sarvajñatvādayo viśeṣā avagantavyāḥ| tasya svaprayojanābhāve
                        kathaṃ prakṛtipuruṣayoḥ saṃyogaviyogāvāpādayatīti nā+a+aśaṅkanīyaṃ tasya
                        kāruṇikatvādbhūtānugraha eva prayojanam| kalpapralayamahāpralayeṣu niḥśeṣān
                        saṃsāriṇa uddhariṣyāmīti tasyādhyavasāyaḥ| yadyasyeṣṭaṃ tattasya
                        prayojanamiti ||25||
children.translated_text: Commentary: In that Lord, the seed of omniscience — the capacity for grasping the past, future, and so forth, in its smallness and greatness — is called 'seed' because it is the root, like a seed. That seed is unsurpassed therein, having reached its culmination. For it is observed that qualities such as smallness and greatness, which admit of degrees, reach their culmination — as the smallness of the atom and the supreme greatness of space. Similarly, knowledge and other properties of the mind, observed in gradation, somewhere reach the state of being unsurpassed. Where these are unsurpassed, that is <s>Īśvara</s>. Although inference, concluding only in a generality, cannot yield knowledge of particulars, still from scripture His specific qualities such as omniscience should be understood. One should not doubt how He brings about the union and separation of <s>Prakṛti</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s> when there is no purpose for Himself — because of His compassionate nature, the benefit of beings alone is the purpose. His resolve is: 'I shall liberate all beings in <s>saṃsāra</s> without remainder during <s>kalpa</s>-dissolution and <s>mahāpralaya</s> (great dissolution).' Whatever is desired by Him — that is His purpose. || 25 ||
Having thus stated the proof of <s>Īśvara</s>, he states His power—
He is the <s>guru</s> (teacher) even of the ancients, because He is not limited by time. || Samādhi 26 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- ādyānāṃ sraṣṭṝṇāṃ brahmādīnāmapi sa gururupadeṣṭā yataḥ sa kālena
                        nāvacchidyate+anāditvāt| teṣāṃ brahmādīnāṃ punarādimattvādasti
                        kālenāvacchedaḥ ||26||
children.translated_text: Commentary: He is the <s>guru</s>, the instructor, even of the first creators such as <s>Brahmā</s> and others, because He is not limited by time, being beginningless. For <s>Brahmā</s> and others, since they have a beginning, there is limitation by time. || 26 ||
Having thus stated His power, for the purpose of worship he states the designator—
His designator is <s>Praṇava</s> (<s>Oṃ</s>). || Samādhi 27 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- itthamuktasvarūpasyeśvarasya vācako+abhidhāyakaḥ prakarṣeṇa nūyate
                        stūyate+aneneti nauti stautīti vā praṇava oṃkāraḥ| tayośca
                        vācyavācakalakṣaṇaḥ sambandho nityaḥ saṃketena prakāśyate na tu kenacit
                        kriyate| yathā pitāputrayorvidyamāna eva sambandho+asyāyaṃ pitā+asyāyaṃ
                        putra iti kenacit prakāśyate ||27||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Of <s>Īśvara</s>, whose essential nature has been thus described, the designator — the denoting word — is <s>Praṇava</s>, the syllable <s>Oṃ</s>, so called because one praises (nauti) or lauds (stauti) eminently (prakarṣeṇa) by means of it. The relation between the signified and the signifier is eternal — it is made manifest by convention but is not created by anyone. Just as the relationship between father and son, which exists inherently, is made manifest by someone as 'this is his father, this is his son.' || 27 ||
He states the method of worship—
Its <s>japa</s> (repetition) and meditation on its meaning. || Samādhi 28 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tasya sārdhatrimātrikasya praṇavasya japo yathāvaduccāraṇaṃ
                        tadvācyasya ceśvarasya bhāvanaṃ punaḥpunaścetasi niveśanamekāgratāyā upāyaḥ|
                        ataḥ samādhisiddhaye yoginā praṇavo japyastadartha īśvaraśca bhāvanīya
                        ityuktaṃ bhavati ||28||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The <s>japa</s> (repetition) of that <s>Praṇava</s> of three-and-a-half <s>mātrās</s> (measures) — its proper utterance — and the <s>bhāvana</s> (meditation) on its signified, <s>Īśvara</s> — the repeated fixing of Him in the mind — is the means for one-pointedness. Therefore, for the attainment of <s>samādhi</s>, the <s>yogin</s> should repeat <s>Praṇava</s> and meditate on its meaning, <s>Īśvara</s> — this is what is stated. || 28 ||
He states the fruit of worship—
From that comes the attainment of inward consciousness and also the absence of obstacles. || Samādhi 29 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tasmājjapāttadarthabhāvanāyāśca yoginaḥ pratyakcetanā+adhigamo
                        bhavati| viṣayaprātikūlyena svāntaḥkaraṇābhimukhamañcati yā cetanā dṛkśaktiḥ
                        sā pratyakcetanā tadadhigamo jñānaṃ bhavatītyarthaḥ| antarāyā vakṣyamāṇāḥ|
                        teṣāmabhāvaḥ śaktipratibandho+api bhavati ||29||
children.translated_text: Commentary: From that <s>japa</s> and meditation on its meaning, the <s>yogin</s> attains inward consciousness. The consciousness — the power of seeing — that moves toward one's own inner faculty, turning away from external objects, is inward consciousness; its attainment means that knowledge arises — this is the meaning. The obstacles will be described. Their absence — the removal of the obstruction of power — also occurs. || 29 ||
Now, anticipating the question 'What are the obstacles?' he says—
Disease, dullness, doubt, negligence, laziness, non-abstention, erroneous perception, failure to attain a stage, and instability — these distractions of the mind are the obstacles. || Samādhi 30 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- navaite rajastamobalāt pravartamānāścittasya vikṣepā bhavanti|
                        tairekāgratāvirodhibhiścittaṃ vikṣipyata ityarthaḥ| tatra
                        vyādhirdhātuvaiṣamyanimitto jvarādiḥ| styānamakarmaṇyatā cittasya|
                        ubhayakoṭyālambanaṃ jñānaṃ saṃśayaḥ --- yogaḥ sādhyo na veti|
                        pramādo+anavadhānatā samādhisādhaneṣvaudāsīnyam| ālasyaṃ
                        kāyacittayorgurutvaṃ yogaviṣaye pravṛttyabhāvahetuḥ| aviratiścittasya
                        viṣayasamprayogātmā gardhaḥ| bhrāntidarśanaṃ śuktikāyāṃ
                        rajatavadviparyayajñānam| alabdhabhūmikatvaṃ kutaścinnimittāt
                        samādhibhūmeralābho+asamprāptiḥ| anavasthitattvaṃ labdhāyāmapi bhūmau
                        cittasya tatrāpratiṣṭhā| ta ete samādherekāgratāyā yathāyogaṃ
                        pratipakṣatvādantarāyā ityucyate ||30||
children.translated_text: Commentary: These nine, arising from the force of <s>rajas</s> (passion) and <s>tamas</s> (inertia), become distractions of the mind. By these, which are contrary to one-pointedness, the mind is distracted — this is the meaning. Among these: disease (<s>vyādhi</s>) is illness such as fever, caused by imbalance of the <s>dhātus</s> (bodily constituents). Dullness (<s>styāna</s>) is the unfitness for action of the mind. Knowledge that grasps both alternatives is doubt (<s>saṃśaya</s>) — 'Is <s>yoga</s> achievable or not?' Negligence (<s>pramāda</s>) is inattentiveness, indifference toward the means of <s>samādhi</s>. Laziness (<s>ālasya</s>) is heaviness of body and mind, the cause of non-engagement in the subject of <s>yoga</s>. Non-abstention (<s>avirati</s>) is the greed that takes the form of the mind's contact with sense-objects. Erroneous perception (<s>bhrāntidarśana</s>) is false knowledge, like mistaking a shell for silver. Failure to attain a stage (<s>alabdhabhūmikatva</s>) is the non-attainment, the non-reaching of the ground of <s>samādhi</s> due to some cause. Instability (<s>anavasthitatva</s>) is the mind's failure to establish itself even on a stage that has been attained. These are called obstacles because they are, as appropriate, contrary to the one-pointedness of <s>samādhi</s>. || 30 ||
To teach other obstacles too that accompany the distractions of the mind, he says—
Pain, depression, trembling of the limbs, inhalation, and exhalation are the accompaniments of distraction. || Samādhi 31 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- kutaścinnimittādutpanneṣu vikṣepeṣu ete duḥkhādayaḥ pravartante|
                        tatra duḥkhaṃ cittasya rajasaḥ pariṇāmo bādhanālakṣaṇo yadbādhāt
                        prāṇinastadupaghātāya pravartante| daurmanasyaṃ bāhyābhyantaraiḥ
                        kāraṇairmanaso dauḥsthyam| aṅgamejayatvaṃ sarvāṅgīno
                        vepathurāsanamanaḥsthairyasya bādhakaḥ| prāṇo yadbāhyaṃ vāyumācāmati sa
                        śvāsaḥ, yat kauṣṭhyaṃ vāyuṃ niḥśvasiti sa praśvāsaḥ| ete vikṣepaiḥ saha
                        pravartamānā yathoditābhyāsavairāgyābhyāṃ niroddhavyā ityeṣāmupadeśaḥ
                        ||31||
children.translated_text: Commentary: When distractions arise from some cause, these — pain and the rest — manifest. Among these: pain (<s>duḥkha</s>) is a transformation of <s>rajas</s> in the mind, characterized by affliction, impelled by which beings strive to remove it. Depression (<s>daurmanasya</s>) is the distress of the mind caused by external and internal factors. Trembling of the limbs (<s>aṅgamejayatva</s>) is a tremor of all the limbs that obstructs steadiness of posture and mind. <s>Śvāsa</s> (inhalation) is when one draws in external air; <s>praśvāsa</s> (exhalation) is when one exhales the internal air. These, which manifest along with distractions, should be restrained through practice and dispassion as previously taught — this is the instruction. || 31 ||
To state another means for preventing distraction along with its accompanying troubles, he says—
For their prevention, the practice of concentration on a single principle. || Samādhi 32 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- teṣāṃ vikṣepāṇāṃ pratiṣedhārthamekasmin kasmiṃścidabhimate
                        tattve+abhyāsaścetasaḥ punaḥpunarniveśanaṃ kāryaḥ| yadbalāt
                        pratyuditāyāmekāgratāyāṃ te vikṣepāḥ praṇāśamupayānti ||32||
children.translated_text: Commentary: For the prevention of those distractions, the practice on any one chosen principle — the repeated fixing of the mind upon it — should be performed. By the force of which, when one-pointedness arises, those distractions are destroyed. || 32 ||
Now, to state another means — the description of the mental purification that produces proper dispositions of the mind, he says—

By cultivating attitudes of <s>maitrī</s> (friendliness), <s>karuṇā</s> (compassion), <s>muditā</s> (gladness), and <s>upekṣā</s> (equanimity) toward those who are happy, suffering, virtuous, and non-virtuous respectively, there comes <s>cittaprasādana</s> (purification of the mind). || Samādhi 33 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- maitrī sauhārdam| karuṇā kṛpā| muditā harṣaḥ| upekṣaudāsīnyam| etā
                        yathākramaṃ sukhiteṣu duḥkhiteṣu puṇyavatsvapuṇyavatsu ca vibhāvayet|
                        tathāhi --- sukhiteṣu sādhuṣu eṣāṃ sukhitvamiti maitrīṃ kuryānna tu īrṣyām|
                        duḥkhiteṣu kathaṃ nu nāmaiṣāṃ duḥkhanivṛttiḥ syāditi kṛpāmeva kuryānna
                        tāṭasthyam| puṇyavatsu puṇyānumodanena harṣameva kuryānna tu kimete
