                        puṇyavanta iti vidveṣam| apuṇyavatsu caudāsīnyameva bhāvayennānumodanaṃ na
                        vā dveṣam| sūtre sukhaduḥkhādiśabdaistadvantaḥ pratipāditāḥ| tadevaṃ
                        maitryādiparikarmaṇā citte prasīdati sukhena samādherāvirbhāvo bhavati|
                        parikarma caitadbāhyaṃ karma| yathā gaṇite miśrakādivyavahāro
                        gaṇitaniṣpattaye saṃkalitādikarmopakārakatvena pradhānakarmaniṣpattaye
                        bhavatyevaṃ dveṣarāgādipratipakṣabhūtamaitryādibhāvanayā samutpāditaprasādaṃ
                        cittaṃ samprajñātādisamādhiyogyaṃ sampadyate| rāgadveṣāveva mukhyatayā
                        vikṣepamutpādayataḥ| tau cet samūlamunmūlitau syātāṃ tadā prasannatvānmanaso
                        bhavatyekāgratā ||33||
children.translated_text: Commentary: <s>Maitrī</s> is friendliness. <s>Karuṇā</s> is compassion. <s>Muditā</s> is joy. <s>Upekṣā</s> is equanimity. These should be cultivated, respectively, toward those who are happy, suffering, virtuous, and non-virtuous. Thus: toward those who are happy and good, one should practice friendliness, thinking 'they are happy'—not envy. Toward those who suffer, one should practice only compassion, thinking 'how might their suffering be removed?'—not indifference. Toward the virtuous, one should practice only joy through rejoicing in their merit—not hatred, thinking 'why are they virtuous?' Toward the non-virtuous, one should cultivate only equanimity—neither rejoicing nor hatred. In the <s>sūtra</s>, the words 'happiness,' 'suffering,' etc. indicate those who possess them. Thus, through the preparatory practice of <s>maitrī</s> and the rest, when the mind becomes serene, the manifestation of <s>samādhi</s> occurs easily. This preparatory practice is an external action. Just as in mathematics, operations with mixtures and the like, being auxiliary to the principal operation, serve for the accomplishment of the calculation—so, through the cultivation of <s>maitrī</s> and the rest, which are antidotes to hatred and attachment, the mind, having generated serenity, becomes fit for <s>samprajñāta</s> and other <s>samādhis</s>. Attachment and hatred primarily produce distraction. If those two are uprooted completely, then due to the serenity of mind, one-pointedness arises. ||33||
He states another means:
Or by exhalation and retention of <s>prāṇa</s> (breath). ||Samādhi 34||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- pracchardanaṃ kauṣṭyasya vāyoḥ prayatnaviśeṣānmātrāpramāṇena
                        bahirniḥsāraṇam| mātrāpramāṇenaiva prāṇasya vāyorbahirgativicchedo
                        vidhāraṇā| sā ca dvābhyāṃ prakārābhyāṃ bāhyasyābhyantarāpūraṇena pūritasya
                        vā tatraiva nirodhena| tadevaṃ recakapūrakakumbhakastrividhaḥ
                        prāṇāyāmaścittasya sthitimekāgratāyāṃ nibadhnāti sarvāsāmindriyavṛttīnāṃ
                        prāṇavṛttipūrvakatvāt| manaḥprāṇayośca
                        svavyāpāraparasparamekayogakṣematvājjīyamāṇaḥ prāṇaḥ
                        samastendriyavṛttinirodhadvāreṇa cittasyaikāgratāyāṃ prabhavati|
                        samastadoṣakṣayakāritvaṃ cāsyāgame śrūyate| doṣakṛtāśca sarvā
                        vikṣepavṛttayaḥ| ato doṣanirharaṇadvāreṇāpyasyaikāgratāyāṃ sāmarthyam
                        ||34||
children.translated_text: Commentary: <s>Pracchardana</s> (exhalation) is the expulsion outward of the internal breath by a special effort, in measured proportion. <s>Vidhāraṇā</s> (retention) is the stopping of the outward movement of <s>prāṇa</s> (breath), also in measured proportion. And that is of two kinds: by filling the interior with external [air], or by retaining the filled [air] right there. Thus, <s>prāṇāyāma</s> (breath control), which is threefold as <s>recaka</s> (exhalation), <s>pūraka</s> (inhalation), and <s>kumbhaka</s> (retention), binds the mind's steadiness to one-pointedness, because all activities of the sense organs are preceded by the activity of <s>prāṇa</s>. And because the mind and <s>prāṇa</s> share a single mutual welfare in their respective functions, <s>prāṇa</s>, when subdued, is capable of bringing about one-pointedness of the mind through the cessation of all sense-organ activities. Its ability to destroy all defects is heard in the <s>Āgama</s> (scriptures). And all distracting modifications are caused by defects. Therefore, through the removal of defects also, it has the power to bring about one-pointedness. ||34||
Now, by way of showing another means, he describes the preliminary to <s>samprajñāta samādhi</s>:
Or, a sensory activity that has arisen binds the mind to steadiness. ||Samādhi 35||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- manasa iti vākyaśeṣaḥ| viṣayā gandharasarūpasparśaśabdāste
                        vidyante phalatvena yasyāḥ sā viṣayavatī pravṛttirmanasaḥ sthairyaṃ karoti|
                        tathāhi nāsāgre cittaṃ dhārayato divyagandhasaṃvidupajāyate| tādṛśya eva
                        jihvāgre rasasaṃbit| tālvagre rūpasaṃvit| jihvāmadhye sparśasaṃvit|
                        jihvāmūle śabdasaṃvit| tadevaṃ tattadindriyadvāreṇa tasmiṃstasminviṣaye
                        divye jāyamānā saṃviccittasyaikāgratāyā heturbhavati| asti yogasya phalamiti
                        yoginaḥ samāśvāsotpādanāt ||35||
children.translated_text: Commentary: 'Of the mind'—this is the completion of the sentence. The objects are smell, taste, form, touch, and sound; that activity which has these as its fruit is 'having objects' (<s>viṣayavatī</s>)—such activity of the mind produces steadiness. Thus: when one fixes the mind on the tip of the nose, a perception of divine fragrance arises. Similarly, on the tip of the tongue, a perception of taste; on the palate, a perception of form; in the middle of the tongue, a perception of touch; at the root of the tongue, a perception of sound. Thus, the perception arising through each respective sense-door regarding each respective divine object becomes the cause of one-pointedness of the mind—because it generates confidence in the yogin that 'there is fruit of <s>yoga</s>.' ||35||
He states another means of the same kind:
Or the sorrowless, luminous [activity]. ||Samādhi 36||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- pravṛttirutpannā cittasya sthitinibandhinīti vākyaśeṣaḥ|
                        jyotiḥśabdena sāttvikaḥ prakāśa ucyate| sa praśasto bhūyānatiśayavāṃśca
                        vidyate yasyāḥ sā jyotiṣmatī pravṛttiḥ| viśokā vigataḥ
                        sukhamayasattvābhyāsavaśācchoko rajaḥpariṇāmo yasyāḥ sā viśokā cetasaḥ
                        sthitinibandhinī| ayamarthaḥ --- hṛtpadmasampūṭamadhye
                        praśāntakallolakṣīrodadhiprakhyaṃ cittasya sattvaṃ bhāvayataḥ prajñālokāt
                        sarvavṛttikṣaye cetasaḥ sthairyamutpadyate ||36||
children.translated_text: Commentary: 'An activity that has arisen, binding the mind to steadiness'—this is the completion of the sentence. By the word 'light' (<s>jyotis</s>), the <s>sāttvika</s> (pure) radiance is meant. That activity in which this excellent, abundant, and supremely radiant [light] exists is called 'luminous' (<s>jyotiṣmatī</s>). 'Sorrowless' (<s>viśokā</s>) means that from which sorrow—which is a transformation of <s>rajas</s> (activity)—has departed through the practice of bliss-pervaded <s>sattva</s>; that is 'sorrowless' and binds the mind to steadiness. The meaning is: when one meditates on the <s>sattva</s> of the mind within the lotus of the heart, resembling an ocean of milk with calmed waves, through the light of <s>prajñā</s> (wisdom), when all <s>vṛttis</s> (modifications) cease, steadiness of the mind arises. ||36||
By way of showing another means, he presents the object of <s>samprajñāta samādhi</s>:
Or the mind [directed toward one who is] free from attachment. ||Samādhi 37||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- manasaḥ sthitinibandhanaṃ bhavatīti śeṣaḥ| vītarāgaḥ
                        parityaktaviṣayābhilāṣastasya yaccittaṃ parihṛtakleśaṃ tadālambanīkṛtaṃ
                        cetasaḥ sthitiheturbhavati ||37||
children.translated_text: Commentary: 'Becomes the means of binding the mind to steadiness'—this is the completion. One who is <s>vītarāga</s> (free from attachment) is one who has abandoned desire for objects; the mind of such a one, free from <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), when taken as the object [of meditation], becomes the cause of the mind's steadiness. ||37||
He states another means of the same kind:
Or [the mind] supported by the knowledge [arising from] dream or sleep. ||Samādhi 38||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- pratyastamitabāhyendriyavṛttermanomātreṇaiva yatra
                        bhoktṛtvamātmanaḥ sa svapnaḥ| nidrā pūrvoktalakṣaṇā| tadālambanaṃ
                        svapnālambanaṃ nidrālambanaṃ vā jñānamālambyamānaṃ cetasaḥ sthitiṃ karoti
                        ||38||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Where the external sense activities have subsided and the self experiences [objects] by the mind alone—that is dream (<s>svapna</s>). Sleep (<s>nidrā</s>) has the characteristic previously stated. Taking either of these as the support—knowledge supported by dream or by sleep, when contemplated, brings about steadiness of the mind. ||38||

children.text:
nānārucitvāt prāṇināṃ yasmin kasmiṃścidvastuni yoginaḥ śraddhā bhavati| tasya
                        dhyānenāpīṣṭasiddhiriti pratipādayitumāha ---
children.translated_text: Due to the diversity of inclinations among beings, the yogin may have faith in any particular object; to establish that through its meditation too the desired accomplishment [occurs], he says:
Or by meditation on whatever is agreeable. ||Samādhi 39||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- yathābhiprete vastuni bāhye candrādāvabhyantare nāḍicakrādau vā
                        bhāvyamāne cetaḥ sthirībhavati ||39||
children.translated_text: Commentary: When meditating on a desired object—external, such as the moon, or internal, such as the <s>nāḍī</s>-<s>cakra</s> (energy centers)—the mind becomes steady. ||39||
Having thus shown the means, to show the result, he says:
His mastery extends from the smallest atom to the greatest magnitude. ||Samādhi 40||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- ebhirupāyaiścittasya sthairyaṃ bhāvayato yoginaḥ
                        sūkṣmaviṣayabhāvanādvāreṇa paramāṇvanto vaśīkāro+apratighātarūpo jāyate| na
                        kvacit paramāṇuparyante sūkṣme viṣaye+asya manaḥ pratihanyate ityarthaḥ|
                        evaṃ sthūlamākāśādiparamamahatvaparyantaṃ bhāvayato na kvaciccetasaḥ
                        pratighāta utpadyate sarvatra svātantryaṃ bhavatītyarthaḥ ||40||
children.translated_text: Commentary: For the yogin who cultivates the steadiness of the mind through these means, through the meditation on subtle objects, mastery in the form of non-obstruction arises, extending to the atomic level. Nowhere is his mind obstructed regarding the subtlest object, down to the atom—this is the meaning. Likewise, when meditating on gross objects up to the greatest magnitude, such as space, no obstruction of the mind arises anywhere; there is independence everywhere—this is the meaning. ||40||
He describes what the nature of the mind thus refined by these means becomes:
<s>Samāpatti</s> (attainment) is the state of being colored by and absorbed in the grasper, grasping, and grasped, like a pure crystal. ||Samādhi 41||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- kṣīṇā vṛttayo yasya sa kṣīṇavṛttistasya
                        grahītṛgrahaṇagrāhyeṣvātmendriyaviṣayeṣu tatsthatadañjanatā
                        samāpattirbhavati| tatsthatvaṃ tatraikāgratā| tadañjanatā tanmayatvam|
                        kṣīṇabhūte citte viṣayasya bhāvyamānasyaivotkarṣaḥ| tathāvidhā
                        samāpattistadrūpaḥ pariṇāmo bhavatītyarthaḥ| dṛṣṭāntamāhā+abhijātasyeva
                        maṇeriti| yathā+abhijātasya nirmalasphaṭikamaṇestattadupādhivaśāt
                        tattadrūpāpattirevaṃ nirmalasya cittasya
                        tattadbhāvanīyavastūparāgāttattadrūpāpattiḥ| yadyapi grahītṛgrahaṇagrāhyeṣu
                        ityuktaṃ tathāpi bhūmikākramavaśādgrāhyagrahaṇagrahītṛṣu iti bodhyam| yataḥ
                        prathamaṃ grāhyaniṣṭha eva samādhistato grahaṇaniṣṭhastato+asmitāmātrarūpo
                        grahītṛniṣṭhaḥ kevalasya puruṣasya grahīturbhāvyatvāsambhavāt| tataśca
                        sthūlasūkṣmagrāhyoparaktaṃ cittaṃ tatra samāpannaṃ bhavati| evaṃ grahaṇe
                        grahītari ca samāpannaṃ bodhyavyam ||41||
children.translated_text: Commentary: One whose <s>vṛttis</s> (modifications) have diminished is <s>kṣīṇavṛtti</s>; for that [mind], <s>samāpatti</s> is the state of being placed in and colored by the grasper, grasping, and grasped—i.e., the self, the senses, and the objects. 'Being placed in' (<s>tatsthatva</s>) means one-pointedness there. 'Being colored by' (<s>tadañjanatā</s>) means being pervaded by that. When the mind has become diminished, only the excellence of the object being meditated upon [remains]; such <s>samāpatti</s>—a transformation of that nature—arises, this is the meaning. He gives an illustration: 'like a pure crystal.' Just as a pure, flawless crystal gem takes on the appearance of whatever object is placed near it, so the clear mind takes on the appearance of whatever object of meditation colors it. Although it is said 'grasper, grasping, and grasped,' it should be understood according to the sequence of stages as 'grasped, grasping, and grasper'—since the <s>samādhi</s> first rests on the grasped (object), then on the grasping (process), then in the form of mere <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness) on the grasper, because the bare <s>Puruṣa</s> as grasper cannot be an object of meditation. Thus the mind colored by the gross and subtle grasped [objects] attains <s>samāpatti</s> there. Likewise, it should be understood as attaining [<s>samāpatti</s>] in grasping and in the grasper. ||41||
Now he describes the fourfold nature of the very <s>samāpatti</s> that has been described:
<s>Savitarkā samāpatti</s> (deliberative attainment) is that which is mixed with word, meaning, and knowledge as conceptual constructs. ||Samādhi 42||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- śrotrendiyagrāhyaḥ sphoṭarūpo vā śabdaḥ| artho jātyādiḥ| jñānaṃ
                        sattvapradhānā buddhivṛttiḥ| vikalpa uktalakṣaṇaḥ| taiḥ saṃkīrṇāḥ| yasyāmete
                        śabdādayastrayaḥ parasparādhyāsena vikalparūpeṇa pratibhāsante gauriti śabdo
                        gaurityartho gauriti jñānamityanenākāreṇa sā savitarkā samāpattirucyate
                        ||42||
children.translated_text: Commentary: <s>Śabda</s> (word) is that which is grasped by the ear-organ, or the <s>sphoṭa</s> (meaning-unit). <s>Artha</s> (meaning) is the universal and so forth. <s>Jñāna</s> (knowledge) is the mental modification predominated by <s>sattva</s>. <s>Vikalpa</s> (conceptual construct) has the characteristic previously stated. 'Mixed with' these—in which these three, word and the rest, appear through mutual superimposition in the form of conceptual construction: the word 'cow,' the meaning 'cow,' the knowledge 'cow'—in this manner, that is called <s>savitarkā samāpatti</s>. ||42||
He describes <s>nirvitarkā</s> (non-deliberative), which is opposite in character to what has been described:
When memory is purified, as if empty of its own form, shining forth as the object alone—that is <s>nirvitarkā</s> (non-deliberative). ||Samādhi 43||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- śabdārthasmṛtipravilaye sati
                        pratyuditaspaṣṭagrāhyākārapratibhāsatayā nyagbhūtajñānāṃśatvena
                        svarūpaśūnyeva nirvitarkā samāpattiḥ ||43||
children.translated_text: Commentary: When the memory of word and meaning has dissolved, through the appearance of the vividly clear form of the grasped [object], with the knowledge-aspect subdued, as if empty of its own nature—that is <s>nirvitarkā samāpatti</s>. ||43||
To explain another distinction, he says:

children.text: etayaiva savicārā nirvicārā ca sūkṣmaviṣayā vyākhyātā ||samādhi 44||
children.translated_text: By this very [explanation], <s>savicārā</s> (reflective) and <s>nirvicārā</s> (non-reflective), having subtle objects, are also explained. ||Samādhi 44||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- etayaiva savitarkayā nirvitarkayā ca samāpatyā savicārā nirvicārā
                        ca vyākhyātā| kīdṛśī| sūkṣmaviṣayā sūkṣmastanmātrendriyādirviṣayo yasyāḥ sā
                        tathoktā| etena pūrvasyāḥ sthūlaviṣayatvaṃ pratipāditaṃ bhavati| sā hi
                        mahābhūtendriyālambanā| śabdārthaviṣayatvena śabdārthavikalpasahitatvena
                        deśakāladharmādyavacchinnaḥ sūkṣmo+arthaḥ pratibhāti yasyāṃ sā savicārā|
                        deśakāladharmādirahito dharmimātratayā sūkṣmārthastanmātrendriyarūpaḥ
                        pratibhāti yasyāṃ sā nirvicārā ||44||
children.translated_text: Commentary: By this very [explanation] of <s>savitarkā</s> and <s>nirvitarkā samāpatti</s>, <s>savicārā</s> and <s>nirvicārā</s> are also explained. Of what kind? Having subtle objects—that whose object is the subtle, such as the <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements), senses, and so forth, is thus designated. By this, the gross-object nature of the former [<s>savitarkā</s>/<s>nirvitarkā</s>] is established. For that [former <s>samāpatti</s>] has the gross elements and senses as its support. That in which the subtle object—delimited by space, time, attribute, and so forth—appears in its word-and-meaning aspect, mixed with word-meaning conceptual constructs, is <s>savicārā</s>. That in which the subtle object, in the form of <s>tanmātras</s> and senses, appears as the bare <s>dharmin</s> (substance) without delimitation by space, time, attribute, and so forth, is <s>nirvicārā</s>. ||44||

children.text: asyā eva sūkṣmaviṣayāyāḥ kimparyantaḥ sūkṣmaviṣaya ityāha ---
children.translated_text: He asks: for this [<s>samāpatti</s>] having subtle objects, what is the limit of subtle objecthood?
And the subtle objecthood extends up to <s>aliṅga</s> (the unmanifest). ||Samādhi 45||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- savicāranirvicārayoḥ samāpattyoryat sūkṣmaviṣayatvamuktaṃ
                        tadaliṅgaparyavasānam| na kvacillīyate na vā kiñcilliṅgati gamayatītyaliṅgaṃ
                        pradhānam| tatparyantaṃ sūkṣmaviṣayatvam| tathāhi --- guṇānāṃ pariṇāme
                        catvāri parvāṇi --- viśiṣṭaliṅgamaviśiṣṭaliṅgaṃ liṅgamātramaliṅgaṃ ceti|
                        viśiṣṭaliṅgaṃ bhūtendriyāṇi| aviśiṣṭaliṅgāṃ tanmātrāntaḥkaraṇāni|
                        liṅgamātraṃ buddhiḥ| aliṅgam pradhānamiti| nātaḥ paraṃ sūkṣmamastītyuktaṃ
                        bhavati ||45||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The subtle objecthood stated for the <s>savicārā</s> and <s>nirvicārā samāpattis</s> extends up to <s>aliṅga</s>. That which neither dissolves into anything nor indicates (i.e., points to, or produces) anything is <s>aliṅga</s>—<s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter). The subtle objecthood extends up to that limit. Thus, in the transformation of the <s>guṇas</s> (constituents of nature), there are four levels: <s>viśeṣa</s> (particularized), <s>aviśeṣa</s> (unparticularized), <s>liṅgamātra</s> (mere indicator), and <s>aliṅga</s> (unmanifest). The particularized are the elements and sense organs. The unparticularized are the <s>tanmātras</s> and the inner instruments. The mere indicator is <s>buddhi</s> (intellect). The unmanifest is <s>Pradhāna</s>. Nothing subtler than this exists—this is what has been stated. ||45||
He states the purpose of these <s>samāpattis</s> in the present context:
These very [<s>samāpattis</s>] constitute the seeded <s>samādhi</s>. ||Samādhi 46||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tā evoktalakṣanāḥ samāpattayaḥ sabījaḥ saha bījenālambanena
                        vartata iti sabījaḥ samprajñātaḥ samādhirucyate sarvāsāṃ sālambanatvāt
                        ||46||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Those very attainments (<s>samāpattis</s>) with the stated characteristics—<s>sabīja</s> (with seed), meaning they operate together with the seed, which is the support (<s>ālambana</s>)—hence it is called <s>sabīja samprajñāta samādhi</s>, since all of them have a support. ||46||
Now, since the fruit of the other attainments pertains to <s>nirvicāra</s> (without reflection) by virtue of its being their culmination, he states the fruit of <s>nirvicāra</s>:
When there is clarity in <s>nirvicāra</s> [samāpatti], there is inner luminosity (<s>adhyātmaprasāda</s>). ||Samādhi 47||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- nirvicāratvaṃ vyākhyātam (1|44)| vaiśāradyaṃ nairmalyam|
                        savitarkāṃ sthūlaviṣayāmapekṣya nirvitarkāyāḥ prādhānyam| tato+api
                        sūkṣmaviṣayāyāḥ savicārāyāḥ| tato+api nirvicārāyāḥ| tasyāstu
                        nirvikalparūpāyāḥ prakṛṣṭābhyāsavaśādvaiśāradye nairmalye
                        satyadhyātmaprasādaḥ samupajāyate| cittaṃ kleśavāsanārahitaṃ
                        sthitipravāhayogyaṃ bhavati| etadeva cittasya vaiśāradyaṃ yat sthitau
                        dārḍhyam ||47
children.translated_text: Commentary: <s>Nirvicāratva</s> (the state of being without reflection) has been explained (1.44). <s>Vaiśāradya</s> is purity (<s>nairmalya</s>). Compared to <s>savitarka</s> (with deliberation), which has a gross object, <s>nirvitarka</s> (without deliberation) has superiority. More than that, <s>savicāra</s> (with reflection), which has a subtle object. More than that, <s>nirvicāra</s> (without reflection). But for that <s>nirvicāra</s>, which is of the nature of being free from conceptualization (<s>nirvikalpa</s>), through the force of excellent practice, when clarity or purity is truly present, inner luminosity (<s>adhyātmaprasāda</s>) arises. The mind becomes free from <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) and <s>vāsanās</s> (impressions), fit for the flow of stability. This indeed is the clarity of the mind—firmness in stability. ||47||
When that exists, what happens?—he says:
Therein, the wisdom is <s>ṛtambharā</s> (truth-bearing). ||Samādhi 48||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- ṛtaṃ satyaṃ vibharti kadācidapi na viparyayeṇācchādyate sā
                        ṛtambharā prajñā tasmin bhavatītyarthaḥ| tasmācca prajñālokāt sarvaṃ
                        yathāvat paśyan yogī prakṛṣṭaṃ yogaṃ prāpnoti ||48||
children.translated_text: Commentary: '<s>Ṛtam</s>' means truth; '[that which] bears' it—it is never obscured by error. That is <s>ṛtambharā prajñā</s> (truth-bearing wisdom); it arises therein—this is the meaning. And from that light of wisdom, seeing everything as it truly is, the <s>yogin</s> attains the highest <s>yoga</s>. ||48||
He states the distinction of this wisdom from other types of wisdom:
This wisdom has a different domain from that born of scripture and inference, since it pertains to particulars. ||Samādhi 49||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- śrutamāgamajñānam| anumānamuktalakṣaṇam (1|7)| tābhyāṃ yā jāyate
                        prajñā sā sāmānyaviṣayā| na hi śabdaliṅgayorindriyavadviśeṣapratipattau
                        sāmarthyam| iyaṃ punaḥ nirvicāravaiśāradyasamudbhavā prajñā tābhyāṃ
                        vilakṣaṇā viśeṣaviṣayatvāt| asyāṃ hi prajñāyāṃ
                        sūkṣmavyavahitaviprakṛṣṭānāmapi viśeṣaḥ sphuṭenaiva rūpeṇa bhāsate|
                        atastasyāmeva yoginā paraḥ prayatnaḥ kartavya ityupadiṣṭaṃ bhavati
                        ||49||
children.translated_text: Commentary: <s>Śruta</s> is knowledge from scripture (<s>āgama</s>). <s>Anumāna</s> (inference) has already been defined (1.7). The wisdom born from these two has generals as its object. For neither words nor inferential signs have the capacity, like the senses, to cognize particulars. But this wisdom, born from the clarity of <s>nirvicāra</s>, is different from those two because it has particulars as its object. For in this wisdom, even the particular nature of the subtle, the hidden, and the distant shines forth in a clear form. Therefore, the <s>yogin</s> should make supreme effort in this very wisdom—this is what has been taught. ||49||
He states the fruit of this wisdom:
The latent impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) born of that wisdom obstructs other latent impressions. ||Samādhi 50||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tayā prajñayā janito yaḥ saṃskāraḥ so+anyān saṃskārān vyutthānajān
                        samādhijāṃśca saṃskārān pratibadhnāti svakāryakaraṇākṣamān karotītyarthaḥ|
                        yatastattvarūpatayā+anayā janitāḥ saṃskārā
                        balavatvādatattvarūpaprajñājanitān saṃskārān bādhituṃ śaknuvanti| atastāmeva
                        prajñāmabhyasedityuktaṃ bhavati ||50||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The <s>saṃskāra</s> generated by that wisdom obstructs other <s>saṃskāras</s>—both those born of emergence (<s>vyutthāna</s>) and those born of <s>samādhi</s>—it renders them incapable of producing their effects, this is the meaning. Since the <s>saṃskāras</s> generated by this wisdom, being of the nature of reality, are powerful, they can overpower the <s>saṃskāras</s> generated by wisdom not of the nature of reality. Therefore one should practice this very wisdom—this is what has been stated. ||50||
Having thus described <s>samprajñāta samādhi</s>, in order to describe <s>asamprajñāta</s>, he says:
When even that is ceased, from the cessation of all, seedless (<s>nirbīja</s>) <s>samādhi</s> arises. ||Samādhi 51||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tasyāpi samprajñātasya nirodhe vilaye sati sarvāsāṃ cittavṛttīnāṃ
                        kāraṇe pravilayādyā saṃskāramātrādvṛttirudeti tasyāṃ neti neti kevalaṃ
                        paryudasanānnirbījaḥ samādhirbhavati yasmin sati puruṣaḥ svarūpaniṣṭhaḥ
                        śuddho bhavati ||51||
children.translated_text: Commentary: When even that <s>samprajñāta</s> ceases, when it dissolves—since all the <s>cittavṛttis</s> (mental modifications) dissolve into their cause—when the modification that arises merely from <s>saṃskāras</s> (latent impressions) is continuously negated with '<s>neti neti</s>' (not this, not this), seedless (<s>nirbīja</s>) <s>samādhi</s> arises, in which <s>Puruṣa</s> (the spirit), established in its own nature, becomes pure. ||51||

children.text:
tadatrādhikṛtasya yogasya lakṣaṇaṃ cittavṛttinirodhapadānāṃ
                        vyākhyānamabhyāsavairāgyalakṣaṇasyopāyadvayasya svarūpaṃ bhedaṃ cābhidhāya
                        samprajñātāsamprajñātabhedena yogasya mukhyāmukhyabhedamuktvā
                        yogābhyāsapradarśanapūrvakaṃ vistāreṇopāyān pradarśya
                        sugamopāyapradarśanaparatayā īśvarasya svarūpapramāṇaprabhāvavācakopāsanāni
                        tatphalāni ca nirṇīya cittavikṣepāṃstattatsahabhuvaśca duḥkhādīn vistareṇa
                        ca tatpratiṣedhopāyānekatvābhyāsamaitryādiprāṇāyāmādīn
                        samprajñātāsamprajñātapūrvāṅgabhūtaviṣayavatī
                        pravṛttirityādīnākhyāyopasaṃhāradvāreṇa ca samāpattiṃ lakṣaṇaphalasahitāṃ
                        svasvaviṣayasahitāṃ coktvā samprajñātāsamprajñātayorupasaṃhāramabhidhāya
                        sabījapūrvakanirbījasamādhirabhihita iti vyākṛto yogapādaḥ|
children.translated_text: Herein, having stated the definition of <s>yoga</s> which is the subject under discussion, having explained the terms '<s>citta</s>,' '<s>vṛtti</s>,' and '<s>nirodha</s>,' having described the essential nature and divisions of the two means characterized as <s>abhyāsa</s> (practice) and <s>vairāgya</s> (detachment), having stated the principal and secondary divisions of <s>yoga</s> in the form of <s>samprajñāta</s> and <s>asamprajñāta</s>, having elaborately shown the means preceded by a demonstration of the practice of <s>yoga</s>, having, through the presentation of easy means, determined the nature, proof, power, designation, and worship of <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord) and their fruits, having described in detail the obstacles of mind-scattering and the accompanying sufferings, and the means for their removal—one-pointedness practice, <s>maitrī</s> (friendliness) and such, <s>prāṇāyāma</s> (breath control) and such—and the activity directed toward objects which forms the preliminary stage of <s>samprajñāta</s> and <s>asamprajñāta</s>, and having described by way of conclusion the <s>samāpatti</s> (attainment) together with its definition, fruit, and respective objects, and having stated the conclusion of <s>samprajñāta</s> and <s>asamprajñāta</s>, the seedless <s>samādhi</s> preceded by the seeded has been described—thus the <s>Yogapāda</s> (Chapter on Yoga) has been explained.

children.text:
dhāreśvarabhojadevaviracitāyāṃ rājamārtaṇḍābhidhāyāṃ pātañjalavṛttau
                    samādhipādaḥ ||1|| iti samādhipādaḥ ||1||
children.translated_text: In the <s>Rājamārtaṇḍa</s>, the commentary on <s>Patañjali</s>'s [<s>Yoga Sūtras</s>] composed by <s>Bhojadeva</s>, Lord of <s>Dhārā</s>, this is the <s>Samādhipāda</s> (Chapter on Concentration). ||1|| Thus ends the <s>Samādhipāda</s>. ||1||
<s>Sādhanapāda</s> (Chapter on Practice)
Now, the chapter on <s>Sādhana</s> (practice). ||2||

children.text:
te te duṣprāpayogarddhisiddhaye yena darśitāḥ| upāyāḥ sa
                        jagannāthastryakṣo+astu prārthitāptaye|| tadevaṃ prathame pāde
                        samāhitacittasya sopāyaṃ yogamabhidhāya vyutthitacittasyāpi
                        kathamupāyābhyāsapūrvako yogaḥ svāsthyamupayātīti
                        tatsādhanānuṣṭhānapratipādanāya kriyāyogamāha ---
children.translated_text: May that three-eyed Lord of the World (<s>Tryakṣa</s>), who has shown those various difficult-to-attain means for the perfection and accomplishment of <s>yoga</s>, be for the fulfillment of what is desired. Thus, in the first chapter, having described <s>yoga</s> together with its means for the concentrated mind, in order to demonstrate the performance of the means of practice—how <s>yoga</s> returns to its own state even for the emergent mind through the prior practice of means—he states <s>kriyāyoga</s> (yoga of action):
<s>Tapas</s> (austerity), <s>svādhyāya</s> (self-study), and <s>Īśvarapraṇidhāna</s> (devotion to the Lord) constitute <s>Kriyāyoga</s> (the yoga of action). ||Sādhana 1||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tapaḥ śāstrāntaropadiṣṭaṃ kṛcchracāndrāyaṇādi| svādhyāyaḥ
                        praṇavapūrvāṇāṃ mantrāṇāṃ japaḥ| īśvarapranidhānaṃ sarvakriyāṇāṃ tasmin
                        paramagurau phalanirapekṣatayā samarpaṇam| etāni kriyāyoga ityucyate
                        ||1||
children.translated_text: Commentary: <s>Tapas</s> (austerity) is that prescribed in other treatises, such as <s>kṛcchra</s> and <s>cāndrāyaṇa</s> fasts and the like. <s>Svādhyāya</s> (self-study) is the recitation of <s>mantras</s> preceded by <s>Praṇava</s> (<s>Oṃ</s>). <s>Īśvarapraṇidhāna</s> (devotion to the Lord) is the surrender of all actions to that supreme teacher without regard for their fruit. These are called <s>Kriyāyoga</s>. ||1||
'For what purpose is that?'—he says:
[It is] for the purpose of cultivating <s>samādhi</s> and for attenuating the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions). ||Sādhana 2||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- kleśā vakṣyamāṇāsteṣāṃ tanūkaraṇaṃ svakāryakaraṇapratibandhaḥ|
                        samādhiruktalakṣaṇaḥ (1|17)| tasya bhāvanā cetasi punaḥpunarniveśanaṃ
                        sā+arthaḥ prayojanaṃ yasya sa tathoktaḥ| etaduktaṃ bhavati --- ete
                        tapaḥprabhṛtayo+abhyasyamānāścittagatānavidyādīn kleśān śithilīkurvantaḥ
                        samādherupakārakatāṃ bhajante| tasmāt prathamaṃ kriyāyogavidhānapareṇa
                        yoginā bhavitavyamityupadiṣṭam ||2||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) are those to be described; their attenuation is the obstruction of their capacity to produce their effects. <s>Samādhi</s> has already been defined (1.17). Its cultivation (<s>bhāvanā</s>) is the repeated installation in consciousness—that is the purpose of which, hence it is so called. This amounts to saying: these practices beginning with <s>tapas</s>, when being practiced, weaken the afflictions such as <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) present in the mind, and serve as aids to <s>samādhi</s>. Therefore, the <s>yogin</s> should first be devoted to the practice of <s>kriyāyoga</s>—this is what has been taught. ||2||

children.text: kleśatanūkaraṇārtha ityuktam| tatra ke kleśā ityāha ---
children.translated_text: It has been said 'for the purpose of attenuating the <s>kleśas</s>.' Therein, 'What are the <s>kleśas</s>?'—he says:
<s>Avidyā</s> (ignorance), <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness), <s>rāga</s> (attachment), <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion), and <s>abhiniveśa</s> (clinging to life) are the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions). ||Sādhana 3||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- avidyādayāḥ vakṣyamāṇalakṣaṇāḥ pañca| te bādhanālakṣaṇaṃ
                        paritāpamupajanayantaḥ kleśaśabdavācyā bhavanti| te hi cetasi pravartamānāḥ
                        saṃskāralakṣaṇaṃ guṇapariṇāmaṃ draḍhayanti ||3||
children.translated_text: Commentary: <s>Avidyā</s> and the rest, whose characteristics will be described, are five. They, producing <s>paritāpa</s> (torment) of the nature of distress, are denoted by the word <s>kleśa</s>. For they, operating in the mind, strengthen the transformation of the <s>guṇas</s> (qualities) in the form of <s>saṃskāras</s> (latent impressions). ||3||

children.text:
satyapi sarveṣāṃ tulyakleśatve mūlabhūtatvādavidyāyāḥ prādhānyaṃ
                        pratipādayitumāha ---
children.translated_text: Even though all afflictions share equally in being afflictions, in order to demonstrate the primacy of <s>avidyā</s> due to its being the root, he says:
<s>Avidyā</s> (ignorance) is the field for the others, whether dormant, attenuated, alternating, or fully active. ||Sādhana 4||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- avidyā moho+anātmanyātmābhimāna iti yāvat| sā kṣetraṃ
                        prasavabhūmiruttareṣāmasmitādīnāṃ pratyekaṃ prasuptatanvādibhedena
                        caturvidhānām| ato yatrāvidyā viparyayajñānarūpā śithilībhavati tatra
                        kleśānāmasmitādīnāṃ nodbhavo dṛśyate| viparyayajñānasadbhāve ca
                        teṣāmudbhavadarśanāt sthitameva mūlatvamavidyāyāḥ|
                        prasuptatanuvicchinnodārāṇāmiti| tatra ye kleśāścittabhūmau sthitāḥ
                        prabodhakābhāve svakāryaṃ nārabhante te prasuptā ityucyante| yathā
                        bālāvasthāyāṃ bālasya hi vāsanārūpāḥ sthitā api kleśāḥ
                        prabodhakasahakāryabhāve nābhivyajyante| te tanavo ye
                        svasvapratipakṣabhāvanayā śithilīkṛtakāryasampādanaśaktayo
                        vāsanā+avaśeṣatayā cetasyavasthitāḥ prabhūtāṃ sāmagrīmantareṇa
                        svakāryamārabdhumakṣamā yathā+abhyāsavato yoginaḥ| te vicchinnā ye
                        kenacidbalavatā kleśenābhibhūtaśaktayastiṣṭhanti yathā dveṣāvasthāyāṃ rāgo
                        rāgāvasthāyāṃ vā dveṣaḥ| na hyanayoḥ parasparaviruddhayoryugapat
                        sambhavo+asti| te udārā ye prāptasahakārisannidhayaḥ svaṃ svaṃ
                        kāryamabhinirvartayanti yathā sadaiva yogaparipanthino vyutthānadaśāyām|
                        eṣāṃ pratyekaṃ caturvidhānāmapi mūlabhūtatvena sthitā+apyavidyā+anvayitvena
                        pratīyate| na hi kvacidapi kleśānāṃ viparyayānvayanirapekṣāṇāṃ
                        svarūpamupalabhyate| tasmāt

mithyājñānarūpāyāmavidyāyāṃ samyagjñānena nivartitāyāṃ
                        dagdhabījakalpānāmeṣāṃ na kvacit praroho+asti|
                        ato+avidyānimittatvamavidyānvayaścaiteṣāṃ niścīyate| ataḥ
                        sarve+apyavidyāvyapadeśabhājaḥ| sarveṣāṃ ca kleśānāṃ
                        cittavikṣepakāritvādyoginā prathamameva taducchede yatnaḥ kārya iti
                        ||4||
children.translated_text: when <s>avidyā</s>, which is of the nature of false knowledge, is removed by right knowledge, these afflictions, like burnt seeds, have no sprouting anywhere. Thus, the causal role of <s>avidyā</s> and its constant connection are established. Therefore, all afflictions are designated by the term <s>avidyā</s>. And since all afflictions cause the scattering of the mind, the <s>yogin</s> should first make effort toward their eradication—this is what is taught. ||4||

Commentary: <s>Avidyā</s> is delusion—the false identification of the Self with what is not the Self, that is the extent of its definition. It is the field, the breeding ground, for the others—<s>asmitā</s> and the rest—each being fourfold as dormant, attenuated, and so forth. Therefore, wherever <s>avidyā</s>, which is of the nature of erroneous knowledge, becomes weakened, there the arising of the afflictions such as <s>asmitā</s> is not seen. And since their arising is seen when erroneous knowledge exists, the rootness of <s>avidyā</s> is established. 'Whether dormant, attenuated, alternating, or fully active'—therein, those afflictions which, present in the mental ground, do not begin their effect in the absence of an activator are called 'dormant' (<s>prasupta</s>). As in childhood—although the afflictions are present in the form of <s>vāsanās</s> (impressions), in the absence of an activating co-cause, they are not manifested. Those are 'attenuated' (<s>tanu</s>) which, having their power to produce effects weakened by the cultivation of their respective antidotes, remain in the mind as mere residual impressions, unable to commence their effect without abundant supporting conditions—as in the case of a practicing <s>yogin</s>. Those are 'alternating' (<s>vicchinna</s>) which stand with their power overwhelmed by some stronger affliction—as attachment during a state of aversion, or aversion during a state of attachment. For these two, being mutually opposed, cannot occur simultaneously. Those are 'fully active' (<s>udāra</s>) which, having obtained the proximity of supporting conditions, accomplish their respective effects—as always, the obstacles to <s>yoga</s> in the state of emergence. Of these, each being fourfold, <s>avidyā</s>, though established as the root, is perceived through its constant connection with the others. For nowhere is the essential nature of the afflictions found independent of the connection with error. Therefore,
He states the definition of <s>avidyā</s>:
<s>Avidyā</s> (ignorance) is seeing the eternal, pure, pleasurable, and the Self in what is non-eternal, impure, painful, and not-Self. ||Sādhana 5||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- atasmiṃstatpratibhāso+avidyetyavidyāyāḥ sāmānyalakṣaṇam| tasyā eva
                        bhedapratipādanam --- anityeṣu ghaṭādiṣu nityatvābhimāno+avidyetyucyate|
                        evamaśuciṣu kāyādiṣu śucityābhimāno duḥkheṣu viṣayeṣu
                        sukhābhimāno+anātmaśarīra ātmābhimānaḥ| etenāpuṇye
                        puṇyabhramo+anarthe+arthabhramo vyākhyātaḥ ||5||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The appearance of 'that' in what is 'not-that' is <s>avidyā</s>—this is the general definition of <s>avidyā</s>. Its specific exposition: the notion of permanence in impermanent things like pots and the like is called <s>avidyā</s>. Similarly, the notion of purity in impure things like the body and the like, the notion of pleasure in painful objects, and the notion of Self in the not-Self body. By this, the error of merit in what is without merit, and the error of purpose in what is without purpose, are also explained. ||5||
In order to define <s>asmitā</s>, he says:
<s>Asmitā</s> (I-am-ness) is the seeming identity of the power of seeing and the power of the instrument of seeing. ||Sādhana 6||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- dṛkśaktiḥ puruṣaḥ| darśanaśaktī rajastamobhyāmanabhibhūtaḥ
                        sātvikaḥ pariṇāmo+antaḥkaraṇarūpaḥ| anayorbhoktṛbhogyatvena
                        jaḍājaḍatvenātyantabhinnarūpayorekatābhimāno+asmitetyucyate| yathā
                        prakṛtirvastutaḥ kartṛtvabhoktṛtvarahitāpi kartryahamityabhimanyate

children.translated_text: this erroneous identification called <s>asmitā</s> is an affliction (<s>kleśa</s>). ||6||

Commentary: The power of seeing (<s>dṛkśakti</s>) is <s>Puruṣa</s> (the spirit). The power of the instrument of seeing (<s>darśanaśakti</s>) is the <s>sāttvika</s> (lucid) transformation, having the form of the inner instrument (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>), not overwhelmed by <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>. The false identification as one of these two, though utterly different in nature as experiencer and experienced, as sentient and insentient—that is called <s>asmitā</s>. Just as <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature), though in reality devoid of agency and experience, falsely identifies as 'I am the agent'—
He states the definition of <s>rāga</s> (attachment):
<s>Rāga</s> (attachment) follows upon pleasure. ||Sādhana 7||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- sukhamanuśeta iti sukhānuśayī| sukhajñasya sukhānubhūtipūrvakaḥ
                        sukhasādhaneṣu tṛṣṇārūpo gardho rāgasaṃjñakaḥ kleśaḥ ||7||
children.translated_text: Commentary: 'It follows pleasure'—hence '<s>sukhānuśayī</s>' (following upon pleasure). For one who knows pleasure, the craving toward the means of pleasure, preceded by the experience of pleasure, the greed in the form of thirst—that is the affliction called <s>rāga</s>. ||7||
He states the definition of <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion):
<s>Dveṣa</s> (aversion) follows upon pain. ||Sādhana 8||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- duḥkhamuktalakṣaṇam| tadabhijñasya tadanusmṛtipūrvakaṃ
                        tatsādhaneṣvanabhilaṣato yo+ayaṃ nindātmakaḥ krodhaḥ sa dveṣalakṣaṇaḥ kleśaḥ
                        ||8||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The characteristic of [<s>dveṣa</s>] has been stated as pain. The anger that is of the nature of blame, arising in one who knows [pain] and preceded by the recollection of it, who does not desire its means [of production]—that is the <s>kleśa</s> (affliction) characterized as <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion). || 8 ||
He states the characteristic of <s>abhiniveśa</s> (clinging to life):
Flowing by its own momentum, established even in the wise—[this is] <s>abhiniveśa</s> (clinging to life). || <s>Sādhana</s> 9 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- pūrvajanmānubhūtamaraṇaduḥkhānubhavavāsanābalādbhayarūpaḥ
                        samupajāyamānaḥ śarīraviṣayādibhirmama viyogo mā
                        bhūdityanvahamanubandharūpaḥ sarvasyaivā+a+akṛmerbrahmaparyantaṃ
                        nimittamantareṇa pravartamāno+abhiniveśākhyaḥ kleśaḥ ||9||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Arising in the form of fear due to the force of latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) from the experience of the suffering of death experienced in previous births, taking the form of a continuous attachment [thinking] 'may there be no separation from my body, sense-objects, and so forth'—this <s>kleśa</s> called <s>abhiniveśa</s> operates in everyone from the worm to <s>Brahmā</s>, without any external cause. || 9 ||

children.text:
tadevaṃ vyutthānasya kleśātmakatvādekāgratā+abhyāsakāmena prathamaṃ kleśāḥ
                        parihartavyāḥ| na cājñātānāṃ teṣāṃ parihāraḥ kartuṃ śakya iti tajjñānāya
                        teṣāmuddeśaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ kṣetraṃ vibhāgaṃ cābhidhāya sthūlasūkṣmabhedabhinnānāṃ
                        teṣāṃ prahāṇopāyavibhāgamāha ---
children.translated_text: Thus, since distraction (<s>vyutthāna</s>) is of the nature of <s>kleśas</s>, one desiring to practice one-pointedness (<s>ekāgratā</s>) must first remove the <s>kleśas</s>. And since it is not possible to remove them without knowing them, having stated their enumeration, characteristics, field, and classification for the purpose of knowing them, he now states the method of abandoning them, which differ according to their gross and subtle divisions:
Those subtle ones are to be abandoned by involution (<s>pratiprasava</s>). || <s>Sādhana</s> 10 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- te sukṣmāḥ kleśāḥ ye vāsanārūpeṇaiva sthitāḥ svavṛttirūpaṃ
                        pariṇāmaṃ nārabhante| te pratiprasavena pratilomapariṇāmena heyāstyaktavyāḥ|
                        svakāraṇe+asmitāyāṃ kṛtārthaṃ savāsanaṃ cittaṃ yadā praviṣṭaṃ bhavati tadā
                        kutasteṣāṃ nirmūlānāṃ sambhavaḥ ||10||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Those subtle <s>kleśas</s> which remain merely in the form of latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) and do not commence their transformation into their active form—they are to be abandoned, to be relinquished, through <s>pratiprasava</s> (involution), i.e., reverse transformation. When the mind (<s>citta</s>), having fulfilled its purpose, along with its latent impressions, has entered into its own cause, <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness), then how can there be any arising of those which have been uprooted? || 10 ||
He states the method of removing the gross ones:
Their active manifestations (<s>vṛttis</s>) are to be abandoned through <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation). || <s>Sādhana</s> 11 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- teṣāṃ kleśānāmārabdhakāryāṇāṃ yāḥ sukhaduḥkhamohātmikā vṛttayastā
                        dhyānaheyāḥ| dhyānenaiva cittaikāgratālakṣaṇena hātavyā ityarthaḥ|
                        cittaparikarmābhyāsamātreṇaiva sthūlatvāt tāsāṃ nivṛttirbhavati| yathā
                        vastrādau sthūlo malaḥ prakṣālanamātreṇaiva nivartate| yastatra sūkṣmāṃśaḥ
                        sa taistairupāyairuttāpanaprabhṛtibhireva nivartayituṃ śakyate ||11||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The <s>vṛttis</s> (modifications) of those <s>kleśas</s> which have commenced their activity, being of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion, are to be abandoned through <s>dhyāna</s>—they are to be removed through meditation, characterized by one-pointedness of mind. Through mere practice of mental purification, because of their grossness, their cessation occurs. Just as gross dirt on cloth is removed by mere washing, while the subtle portion can only be removed through particular means such as heating and the like. || 11 ||
Having thus stated the true nature of the <s>kleśas</s>, he states that of the <s>karmāśaya</s> (repository of karma):
The <s>karmāśaya</s> (repository of karma), rooted in <s>kleśas</s>, is to be experienced in seen or unseen births. || <s>Sādhana</s> 12 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- karmāśaya ityanena svarūpaṃ tasyābhihitam| ato vāsanārūpāṇyeva
                        karmāṇi| kleśamūla ityanena kāraṇamabhihitaṃ yataḥ karmaṇāṃ śubhāśubhānāṃ
                        kleśā eva nimittam| dṛṣṭādṛṣṭajanmavedanīya ityanena phalamuktam| asminneva
                        janmani anubhavanīyo dṛṣṭajanmavedanīyaḥ|
                        janmāntarānubhavanīyo+adṛṣṭajanmavedanīyaḥ| tathāhi --- kānicit puṇyāni
                        devatārādhanādīni tīvrasaṃvegena kṛtāni ihaiva janmani jātyāyurbhogalakṣaṇaṃ
                        phalaṃ prayacchanti yathā nandīśvarasya bhagavanmaheśvarārādhanabalādihaiva
                        janmani jātyādayo viśiṣṭāḥ prādurbhūtāḥ| evamanveṣāṃ viśvāmitrādīnāṃ
                        tapaḥprabhāvājjātyāyuṣī| keṣāñcijjātireva yathā tīvrasaṃvegena
                        duṣṭakarmakṛtāṃ nahuṣādīnāṃ jātyantarādipariṇāmaḥ| urvaśyāśca kārtikeyavane
                        latārūpatayā| evaṃ vyastasamastatvena yathāyogyaṃ yojyamiti ||12||
children.translated_text: Commentary: By the term <s>karmāśaya</s>, its own nature is stated—therefore <s>karmas</s> exist only in the form of latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>). By 'rooted in <s>kleśas</s>,' the cause is stated, since the <s>kleśas</s> alone are the occasion for good and bad <s>karmas</s>. By 'to be experienced in seen or unseen births,' the fruit is stated. That which is to be experienced in this very birth is 'experienced in a seen birth'; that which is to be experienced in another birth is 'experienced in an unseen birth.' For example: certain meritorious deeds such as worship of deities, performed with intense fervor, yield their fruit—characterized as birth, lifespan, and enjoyment—in this very life, as in the case of <s>Nandīśvara</s>, whose distinguished birth and so forth manifested in this very life through the power of worshipping Lord <s>Maheśvara</s>. Similarly for <s>Viśvāmitra</s> and others, birth and lifespan [resulted] from the power of austerity. For some, only birth [changes], as in the case of <s>Nahuṣa</s> and others who performed evil deeds with intense fervor, [resulting in] transformation into another birth. And [the case of] <s>Urvaśī</s> [taking] the form of a creeper in <s>Kārtikeya</s>'s forest. Thus, in separate and combined ways, this should be applied as appropriate. || 12 ||
Now he states the fruit of the <s>karmāśaya</s>, differentiated according to its own divisions:
When the root exists, its fruition is birth, lifespan, and experience. || <s>Sādhana</s> 13 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- mūlamuktalakṣaṇāḥ kleśāḥ| teṣvanabhibhūteṣu satsu karmaṇāṃ
                        kuśalākuśalarūupāṇāṃ vipākaḥ phalaṃ jātyāyurbhogā bhavanti| jātirmanuṣyādiḥ|
                        āyuścirakālamekaśarīrasambandhaḥ| bhogā viṣayā indriyāṇi
                        sukhasaṃvidduḥkhasaṃvicca sukhaduḥkhādīni karmakaraṇabhāvabodhanavyutpatyā
                        bhogaśabdasya| idamatra tātparyam --- cittabhūmāvanādikālasañcitāḥ
                        karmavāsanā yathā yathā pākamupayānti tathā tathā guṇapradhānabhāvena sthitā
                        jātyāyurbhogalakṣaṇaṃ svakāryamārabhante ||13||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The root is the <s>kleśas</s>, whose characteristics have been stated. When these are not overpowered, the <s>vipāka</s> (fruition), the fruit of <s>karmas</s> of wholesome and unwholesome nature, consists of birth, lifespan, and enjoyment. Birth means [being born as] human and so forth. Lifespan is the long-term connection with a single body. Enjoyments are sense-objects, sense-organs, the experience of pleasure, the experience of pain, pleasure, pain, and so forth—the word 'enjoyment' (<s>bhoga</s>) being understood through its etymology as the instrument-agent relationship of <s>karma</s>. The purport here is: the <s>karma</s>-impressions accumulated from beginningless time in the field of mind, as they progressively ripen, standing in the relation of predominance of one or another <s>guṇa</s>, commence their own effect characterized as birth, lifespan, and enjoyment. || 13 ||
He states that birth and so forth, mentioned as fruits of <s>karma</s>, following their respective causal <s>karmas</s>, produce effects:
They bear the fruit of pleasure and pain, owing to [their] having merit and demerit as causes. || <s>Sādhana</s> 14 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- hlādaḥ sukhamṃ paritāpo duḥkhaṃ tau phalaṃ yeṣāṃ te tathoktāḥ|
                        puṇyaṃ kuśalaṃ karma tadviparītamapuṇyaṃ te karmaṇī kāraṇaṃ yeṣāṃ teṣāṃ
                        bhāvastasmāt| etaduktaṃ bhavati --- puṇyakarmārabdhā jātyāyurbhogā
                        hlādaphalāḥ| apuṇyakarmārabdhāstu paritāpaphalāḥ| etacca prāṇimātrāpekṣayā
                        dvaividhyam ||14|| yoginastatsarvaṃ duḥkhamityāha ---

children.translated_text: Due to the sufferings of transformation, anguish, and latent impressions, and due to the conflict of the activities of the <s>guṇas</s>,
everything is indeed suffering for the discerning one. || <s>Sādhana</s> 15 ||

Commentary: Joy is pleasure; affliction is pain; those for which these are the fruit are called thus. Merit (<s>puṇya</s>) is wholesome <s>karma</s>; its opposite is demerit (<s>apuṇya</s>); those for which these two <s>karmas</s> are the cause—their state is due to that. What is stated is this: birth, lifespan, and enjoyment commenced by meritorious <s>karma</s> bear the fruit of joy; those commenced by demeritorious <s>karma</s> bear the fruit of affliction. And this twofold division is with respect to living beings in general. || 14 || For the yogin, he states that all of this is suffering:

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- vivekinaḥ parijñātakleśādivivekasya dṛśyamātraṃ sakalameva
                        bhogasādhanaṃ saviṣaṃ svādvannamiva duḥkhameva
                        pratikūlavedanīyamevetyarthaḥ| yasmādatyantābhijāto yogī
                        duḥkhaleśenāpyudvijate| yathā --- akṣipātramūrṇātantusparśamātreṇaiva
                        mahatīṃ pīḍāmanubhavati netaradaṅgaṃ tathā vivekī
                        svalpaduḥkhānubandhenāpyudvijate| kathamityāha ---
                        pariṇāmatāpasaṃskāraduḥkhaiḥ| viṣayāṇāmupabhujyamānānāṃ yathāyathaṃ
                        gardhābhivṛddhestadaprāptikṛtasya sukhaduḥkhasyāparihāryatayā
                        duḥkhāntarasādhanatvānnāstyeva sukharūpateti pariṇāmaduḥkhatvam|
                        upagṛhyamāṇeṣu sukhasādhaneṣu tatpratipanthinaṃ prati dveṣasya
                        sarvadaivāvasthitatvāt sukhānubhavakāle+api tāpaduḥkhaṃ duṣpariharamiti
                        tāpaduḥkhatā| saṃskāraduḥkhaṃ tu svābhimatānabhimataviṣayasannidhāne
                        sukhasaṃvidduḥkhasaṃviccopajāyamānā tathāvidhameva svakṣetre
                        saṃskāramārabhate| saṃskārācca punastathāvidhasaṃvidanubhava
                        ityaparimitasaṃskārotpattidvāreṇa sarvasyaiva duḥkhānuvedhādduḥkhatvam|
                        evamuktaṃ bhavati --- kleśakarmāśayavipākasaṃskārānucchedāt sarvasyaiva
                        duḥkhatvam| guṇavṛttivirodhācceti| guṇānāṃ satvarajastamasāṃ yā vṛttayaḥ
                        sukhaduḥkhamoharūpāḥ parasparamabhibhāvyābhibhāvakatvena viruddhā jāyante|
                        tāsāṃ sarvatraiva duḥkhānuvedhād duḥkhatvam| etaduktaṃ bhavati ---
                        aikāntikīmātyantikīṃ ca duḥkhanivṛttimicchato vivekina
                        uktarūpakāraṇacatuṣṭayāḥ sarve viṣayā duḥkharūpatayā pratibhānti| tasmācca
                        sarvakarmavipāko duḥkharūpa evetyuktaṃ bhavati ||15||
children.translated_text: Commentary: For the discerning one (<s>vivekin</s>)—one who has known the discrimination of <s>kleśas</s> and so forth—everything that serves as a means of experience, the entire visible [world], is indeed suffering, like delicious food mixed with poison—meaning it is to be experienced as adverse. Because the yogin who is extremely refined is distressed even by a trace of suffering. Just as the surface of the eye experiences great pain from the mere touch of a wool thread, while other body parts do not, so the discerning one is distressed even by a slight association with suffering. How so? He explains: through the sufferings of transformation, anguish, and latent impressions. Since sense objects, as they are being enjoyed, progressively increase craving, and since the pleasure-pain caused by not attaining them is unavoidable, being the means to further suffering, there is no existence as pleasure—this is the suffering of transformation (<s>pariṇāma-duḥkha</s>). Since, regarding the means of pleasure being grasped, aversion toward whatever opposes them is always present, even during the experience of pleasure the suffering of anguish (<s>tāpa-duḥkha</s>) is difficult to avoid. As for the suffering of latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra-duḥkha</s>): in the presence of desired and undesired objects, the experience of pleasure and pain that arises creates a corresponding impression in its own field; and from that impression comes again the experience of a similar kind—thus through the door of unlimited generation of impressions, everything is pervaded by suffering, hence everything is suffering. Thus what is stated is: because the <s>kleśas</s>, <s>karmāśaya</s>, fruition, and impressions are not cut off, everything is of the nature of suffering. 'Due to the conflict of the activities of the <s>guṇas</s>': the modifications of the <s>guṇas</s>—<s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s>—being of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion, arise in mutual conflict, each overpowering and being overpowered by the others. Because these are pervaded everywhere by suffering, all is suffering. What is stated is this: for the discerning one who desires absolute and permanent cessation of suffering, all sense-objects appear as being of the nature of suffering, due to the fourfold cause described. And therefore, all fruition of <s>karma</s> is indeed of the nature of suffering. || 15 ||

children.text:
tadevamuktasya kleśakarmāśayavipākarāśeravidyāprabhavatvādavidyāyāśca
                        mithyājñānarūpatayā samyagjñānocchedyatvāt samyagjñānasya ca
                        sasādhanaheyopādeyāvadhāraṇarūpatvāt tadabhidhānamāha ---
children.translated_text: Thus, since the stated mass of <s>kleśas</s>, <s>karmāśaya</s>, and fruition has its origin in <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), and since <s>avidyā</s>, being of the nature of false knowledge, is to be destroyed by right knowledge, and since right knowledge is of the nature of determining what is to be accepted and rejected along with its means—he states that:
The suffering that is yet to come is to be avoided. || <s>Sādhana</s> 16 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- bhūtasyātikrāntatvādanubhūyamānasya tyaktumaśakyatvādanāgatameva
                        saṃsāraduḥkhaṃ hātavyamityuktaṃ bhavati ||16||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Since what is past has already gone, and since what is being experienced cannot be abandoned, only the future suffering of <s>saṃsāra</s> (cyclical existence) is to be avoided—this is what is stated. || 16 ||
He states the cause of what is to be avoided:
The conjunction of the seer and the seen is the cause of what is to be avoided. || <s>Sādhana</s> 17 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- draṣṭā cidrūpaḥ puruṣaḥ| dṛśyaṃ buddhisattvaṃ|
                        tayoravivekakhyātipūrvako yo+asau saṃyogo bhoktṛbhogyatvena sannidhānaṃ sa
                        heyasya duḥkhasya guṇapariṇāmarūpasya saṃsārasya hetuḥ kāraṇam| tannivṛtyā
                        saṃsāranivṛttirbhavatītyarthaḥ ||17||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The seer (<s>draṣṭṛ</s>) is <s>Puruṣa</s>, of the nature of consciousness. The seen (<s>dṛśya</s>) is the <s>sattva</s> of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect). Their conjunction, preceded by the non-discriminative cognition (<s>aviveka-khyāti</s>), which is the association as experiencer and experienced—that is the cause, the reason, of the suffering to be avoided, which is of the nature of the transformation of the <s>guṇas</s>, i.e., <s>saṃsāra</s>. By its cessation, the cessation of <s>saṃsāra</s> occurs—this is the meaning. || 17 ||

children.text:
draṣṭṛdṛśyayoḥ saṃyoga ityuktam| tatra dṛśyasya svarūpaṃ kāryaṃ prayojanaṃ
                        cāha ---
children.translated_text: The conjunction of the seer and the seen has been stated. Regarding the seen, he states its own nature, its effect, and its purpose:

Having the character of illumination, activity, and stability, consisting of the elements and sense-organs, serving the purposes of experience and liberation—[such is] the seen. || <s>Sādhana</s> 18 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- prakāśaḥ sattvasya dharmaḥ| kriyā pravṛttirūpā rajasaḥ|
                        sthitirniyamarūpā tamasaḥ| tāḥ prakāśakriyāsthitayaḥ śīlaṃ svābhāvikaṃ rūpaṃ
                        yasya tattathāvidhamiti svarūpamasya nirdiṣṭam| bhūtendriyātmakamiti|
                        bhūtāni sthūlasūkṣmabhedena dvividhāni pṛthivyādīni gandhatanmātrādīni ca|
                        indriyāṇi buddhīndriyakarmendriyāntaḥkaraṇabhedena trividhāni|
                        ubhayametadgrāhyagrahaṇarūpātmā svarūpābhinnaḥ pariṇāmo yasya
                        tattathāvidhamityanenāsya kāryamuktam| bhogaḥ kathitalakṣaṇaḥ| apavargo
                        vivekakhyātipūrvikā saṃsāranivṛttiḥ| tau bhogāpavargavarthaḥ prayojanaṃ
                        yasya tattathāvidhaṃ dṛśyamityarthaḥ ||18||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Illumination (<s>prakāśa</s>) is the property of <s>sattva</s>. Activity (<s>kriyā</s>), being of the nature of movement, belongs to <s>rajas</s>. Stability (<s>sthiti</s>), being of the nature of restraint, belongs to <s>tamas</s>. These—illumination, activity, and stability—constitute the character, the natural form, of that [seen]; its own nature is thus indicated. 'Consisting of the elements and sense-organs': the elements are of two kinds as gross and subtle—earth and so forth, and the smell-<s>tanmātra</s> and so forth. The sense-organs are of three kinds as cognitive organs, motor organs, and the inner instrument (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>). Both of these constitute the transformation, identical with its own nature, of what is to be grasped and the grasping—thus its effect is stated. <s>Bhoga</s> (experience) is as previously defined. <s>Apavarga</s> (liberation) is the cessation of <s>saṃsāra</s> preceded by discriminative knowledge (<s>viveka-khyāti</s>). These two—experience and liberation—constitute its purpose; the seen is that which has these as its purpose. || 18 ||

children.text:
tasya dṛśyasya nānāvasthārūpapariṇāmātmakasya heyatvena jñātavyatvāt
                        tadavasthāḥ kathayitumāha ---
children.translated_text: Since the seen, being of the nature of transformation in various states, is to be known for the purpose of being avoided, he begins to state its states:
The specific, the unspecific, the merely indicated, and the unmanifest are the stages of the <s>guṇas</s>. || <s>Sādhana</s> 19 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- guṇānāṃ parvāṇyavasthāviśeṣāścatvāro jñātavyā ityupadiṣṭaṃ
                        bhavati| tatra viśeṣā mahābhūtendriyāṇi| aviśeṣāstanmātrāntaḥkaraṇāni|
                        liṅgamātraṃ buddhiḥ| aliṅgamavyaktamityuktam| sarvatra
                        triguṇarūpasyāvyaktasyānvayitvena pratyabhijñānādavaśyaṃ jñātavyatvena
                        yogakāle catvāri parvāṇi nirdiṣṭāni ||19||
children.translated_text: Commentary: It is taught that four stages, or particular states, of the <s>guṇas</s> are to be known. Among these, the 'specific' (<s>viśeṣa</s>) are the gross elements and sense-organs. The 'unspecific' (<s>aviśeṣa</s>) are the <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements) and the <s>antaḥkaraṇa</s> (inner instrument). The 'merely indicated' (<s>liṅgamātra</s>) is <s>buddhi</s> (intellect). The 'unmanifest' (<s>aliṅga</s>) is the <s>avyakta</s> (unmanifest <s>Prakṛti</s>). Since everywhere the three-<s>guṇa</s>-natured <s>avyakta</s> is recognized as pervading, necessarily four stages are specified for knowing during the practice of <s>yoga</s>. || 19 ||

children.text:
evaṃ heyatvena dṛśyasya prathamaṃ jñātavyatvāt tadavasthāsahitaṃ
                        vyākhyāyopādeyaṃ draṣṭāraṃ vyākhyātumāha ---
children.translated_text: Having thus explained the seen along with its states as that which is to be known for being avoided, he begins to explain the seer, who is to be accepted:
The seer is consciousness only; though pure, he perceives through mental modifications. || <s>Sādhana</s> 20 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- draṣṭā puruṣo dṛśimātraścetanāmātram| mātragrahaṇaṃ
                        dharmadharminirāsārtham| keciddhi cetanāmātmano dharmamicchanti| sa
                        śuddho+api pariṇāmitvādyabhāvena svapratiṣṭho+api pratyayānupaśyaḥ| pratyayā
                        viṣayoparaktāni vijñānāni tāni anu avyavadhānena pratisaṃkramādyabhāvena
                        paśyati| etaduktaṃ bhavati --- jātaviṣayoparāgāyāmeva buddhau
                        sannidhimātreṇaiva puruṣasya draṣṭutvamiti ||20||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The seer is <s>Puruṣa</s>, pure consciousness alone. The word 'alone' (mātra) is used for the purpose of negating properties and their substrates. For some indeed consider consciousness to be a property of the self. He, though pure, without transformation and the like, though self-established, is a witness of conditions. Conditions are cognitions colored by objects; he sees them continuously, without interruption, without transmigration and the like. The meaning is: Only when the intellect has become colored by objects, by mere proximity alone, does <s>Puruṣa</s> become a seer. ||20||
That very one is the experiencer—he says:
The essence of the seen exists for the sake of that [the seer]. ||Sādhana 21||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- dṛśyasya prāguktalakṣaṇasya ya ātmā yat svarūpaṃ tadartha eva|
                        tasya puruṣārthabhoktṛtvasampādanaṃ nāma svārthaparihāreṇa proyojanam| na hi
                        pradhānaṃ pravartamānamātmanaḥ kiñcit prayojanamapekṣya pravartate kintu
                        puruṣasya bhoktṛtvaṃ sampādayitumiti ||21||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The essence (ātmā), the own-form, of the seen whose characteristics were described earlier, exists for the sake of that alone. The accomplishment of the purpose of serving as the object of experience for <s>Puruṣa</s> is its function, by setting aside its own interest. For <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial nature), when it evolves, does not evolve with regard to any purpose of its own, but rather to accomplish the experiencer-ship of <s>Puruṣa</s>. ||21||

children.text:
yadyevaṃ puruṣsya bhogasampādanameva proyojanaṃ tadā smpādite
                        tasmiṃstanniṣprayojanaṃ viratavyāpāraṃ syāt| tasmiṃśca pariṇāmaśūnye
                        śuddhatvāt sarve draṣṭāro bandharahitāḥ syuḥ| tataśca saṃsāroccheda
                        ityāśaṅkyāha ---
children.translated_text: If this is so—if the accomplishment of experience for <s>Puruṣa</s> is the sole purpose—then when that is accomplished, it would be purposeless and cease its activity. And in the absence of transformation, due to purity, all seers would be free from bondage. Then there would be the destruction of <s>saṃsāra</s>—anticipating this objection, he says:
Though destroyed for one who has accomplished his purpose, it is not destroyed, because of being common to others. ||Sādhana 22||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- yadyapi vivekakhyātiparyantādbhogasampādanāt kamapi kṛtārthaṃ
                        puruṣaṃ prati tannaṣṭaṃ viratavyāpāraṃ tathāpi sarvapuruṣasādhāraṇatvādanyān
                        pratyanaṣṭavyāpāramavatiṣṭhate| ataḥ pradhānasya sakalabhoktṛsādhāraṇatvānna
                        kadācidapi vināśaḥ| ekasya muktau vā na sarvamuktiprasaṅga ityuktaṃ bhavati
                        ||22||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Although, up to the culmination of discriminative discernment, from the accomplishment of experience, for some <s>Puruṣa</s> who has accomplished his purpose, it has ceased its activity; nonetheless, because of being common to all <s>Puruṣas</s>, for others it remains with unceased activity. Therefore, there is never destruction of <s>Pradhāna</s>, because it is common to all experiencers. Nor from the liberation of one is there the consequence of liberation of all—thus is the meaning. ||22||
Having explained the seen and the seer, to explain their conjunction he says:
The conjunction is the cause of the apprehension of the nature of the power of the owned and the owner. ||Sādhana 23||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- kāryadvāreṇāsya lakṣaṇaṃ karoti| svaśaktirdṛśyasya svabhāvaḥ|
                        svāmiśaktirdraṣṭuḥ svarūpam| tayordvayorapi saṃvedyasaṃvedakatvena
                        vyavasthitayoryā svarūpopalabdhistasyāḥ kāraṇaṃ yaḥ sa saṃyogaḥ| sa ca
                        sahajo bhogyabhoktṛbhāvasvarūpānanyaḥ

| na hi
                        tayornityayorvyāpakayoḥ svarūpādatiriktaḥ kaścit saṃyogaḥ| yadeva bhogyasya
                        bhogyatvaṃ bhoktuśca bhoktṛtvamanādisiddhaṃ sa eva saṃyogaḥ ||23||
children.translated_text: for there is no conjunction of these two, who are eternal and all-pervading, other than their own nature. That the enjoyability of the enjoyable and the enjoyer-ship of the enjoyer are established from beginningless time—that itself is the conjunction. ||23||

Commentary: He defines its characteristic through its effect. The power of the self (sva-śakti) is the nature of the seen. The power of the master (svāmi-śakti) is the own-form of the seer. Of both these two, established as the experienced and the experiencer,
He states its cause as well:
<s>Avidyā</s> (ignorance) is its cause. ||Sādhana 24||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- yā pūrvaṃ viparyāsātmikā moharūpā+avidyā vyākhyātā (2|4-5) sā
                        tasyāvivekakhyātirūpasya saṃyogasya kāraṇam ||24||
children.translated_text: Commentary: That <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), which was previously explained (2.4–5) as consisting of error, in the form of delusion—that is the cause of this conjunction, which has the form of the absence of discriminative discernment. ||24||
The abandonable and the act of abandonment are stated. What then is that abandonment? He says:
In its absence, the absence of conjunction—that is the abandonment; that is the <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation) of the seer. ||Sādhana 25||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tasyā avidyāyāḥ svarūpaviruddhena samyagjñānenonmūlitāyā
                        yo+ayamabhāvastasmin sati tatkāryasya saṃyogasyāpyabhāvastaddhānamityucyate|
                        ayamarthaḥ --- naitasyā+amūrtavastuno vibhāgo yujyate

kintu jātāyāṃ
                        vivekakhyātavavivekanimittaḥ saṃyogaḥ svayameva nivartata iti tasya hānam|
                        yadeva ca saṃyogasya hānaṃ tadeva nityaṃ kevalasyāpi puruṣasya kaivalyaṃ
                        vyapadiśyate ||25||
children.translated_text: Rather, when discriminative discernment arises, the conjunction, whose cause is the absence of discrimination, ceases by itself—that is its abandonment. And this abandonment of conjunction is itself the <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation) of the eternal, pure <s>Puruṣa</s> as well.

Commentary: Of that <s>avidyā</s>, uprooted by right knowledge which is opposed to its own nature—the absence that follows; when that exists, the absence of conjunction which is its effect also arises—that is called abandonment. This meaning:

children.text:
tadevaṃ dṛśyasaṃyogasya svarūpaṃ kāraṇaṃ kāryaṃ cābhihitam| atha
                        hānopāyakathanadvāreṇa upādeyakāraṇamāha ---
children.translated_text: Thus the nature, cause, and effect of the conjunction with the seen have been stated. Now, by way of stating the means of abandonment, he states the cause that is to be adopted:
Uninterrupted discriminative discernment is the means of abandonment. ||Sādhana 26||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- anye guṇā anyaḥ puruṣa ityevaṃvidhasya vivekasya yā khyātiḥ
                        prakhyā sā+asya hānasya dṛśyaduḥkhaparityāgasyopāyaḥ kāraṇam| kīdṛśī|
                        aviplavā na vidyate viplavo vicchedo+antarā+antarā+abhyutthānarūpo yasyāḥ sā
                        aviplavā| idamatra tātparyam --- pratipakṣabhāvanābalādavidyāpralaye
                        vinivṛttakartṛtvabhoktṛtvābhimānāyā rajastamomalānabhibhūtāyā
                        buddherantarmukhā yā cicchāyāsaṃkrāntiḥ sā vivekakhyātirucyate| tasyāṃ ca
                        santatatvena pravṛttāyāṃ satyāṃ dṛśyasyādhikāranivṛtterbhavatyeva kaivalyam
                        ||26||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The discernment, the illumination, of the discrimination 'the <s>guṇas</s> are different, <s>Puruṣa</s> is different'—that is the means, the cause, of this abandonment, the relinquishment of the suffering associated with the seen. Of what kind? Uninterrupted—

children.text:
utpannavivekakhyāteḥ puruṣasya yādṛśī prajñā bhavati tāṃ kathayan
                        vivekakhyātereva svarūpamāha ---
children.translated_text: Describing the kind of wisdom that arises for <s>Puruṣa</s> in whom discriminative discernment has arisen, he states the nature of discriminative discernment itself:
His wisdom at the final stage is sevenfold. ||Sādhana 27||

children.text: tasya saptadhā prāntabhūmiḥ prajñā iti vā bahusammataḥ sūtrapāṭhaḥ|

vṛttiḥ --- tasyotpannavivekajñānasya jñātavyavivekarūpā prajñā prāntabhūmau
                        sakalasālambanasamādhiparyante saptaprakārā bhavantītyarthaḥ| tatra
                        kāryavimuktirūpā catuṣprakārā ---
children.translated_text: Commentary: For him in whom discriminative knowledge has arisen, the wisdom consisting of the nature of what is to be known through discrimination, at the final stage—at the culmination of all object-supported <s>samādhi</s>—is of seven kinds. In that context, the liberations of the mind:

children.text: 1| jñātaṃ mayā jñeyam| jñātavyaṃ na kiñcidasti|
children.translated_text: 1. What was to be known has been known by me; there is nothing more to be known.

children.text: 2| kṣīṇā me kleśāḥ| na kiñcit kṣetavyamasti|
children.translated_text: 2. My <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) are destroyed; there is nothing more to be destroyed.
3. Knowledge has been attained by me.

children.text:
4| prāptā mayā vivekakhyātiriti| pratyayāntaraparihāreṇa
                            tasyāmavasthāyāmīdṛśyeva prajñā jāyate| īdṛśī prajñā kāryaviṣayaṃ
                            nirmalaṃ jñānaṃ kāryavimuktirityucyate| cittavimuktistridhā ---
children.translated_text: 4. Discriminative discernment has been attained by me. In that state, by the exclusion of other conditions, such wisdom alone arises. Such wisdom is the effect-domain,

children.text:
5| caritārthā me buddhiḥ| guṇā hṛtādhikārā giriśikharanipatitā iva
                            grāvāṇo na punaḥ sthitiṃ yāsyanti|
children.translated_text: 5. My intellect has accomplished its purpose. The <s>guṇas</s>, having lost their authority, like boulders fallen from a mountain peak, will not regain stability.

children.text:
6| svakāraṇe pravilayābhimukhānāṃ guṇānāṃ
                            mohābhidhānamūlakāraṇābhāvānniṣprayojanatvāccāmīṣāṃ kutaḥ praroho
                            bhavet|
children.translated_text: 6. Of the <s>guṇas</s>, headed toward dissolution into their own cause, due to the absence of the root cause called delusion and due to their purposelessness—whence could there be growth?

children.text:
me samādhistasmin
                            sati svarupapratiṣṭho+ahamiti| īdṛśī triprakārā cittavimuktiḥ|
children.translated_text: my <s>samādhi</s> is stable; when that exists, I am established in my own nature. Such is the threefold liberation of the mind.
7. And having become established in oneself,
Thus, when such sevenfold wisdom of the stages has arisen, <s>Puruṣa</s> is called 'isolated.' ||27||

children.text:
vivekakhyātiḥ saṃyogābhāvaheturityuktam| tasyāstu utpattau kiṃ nimittamityāha
                        ---
children.translated_text: It was stated that discriminative discernment is the cause of the absence of conjunction. What then is the cause of its arising? He says:
Through the practice of the limbs of <s>yoga</s>, with the destruction of impurity, the light of knowledge shines forth unto discriminative discernment. ||Sādhana 28||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- yogāṅgāni vakṣyamāṇāni|
                        teṣāmanuṣṭhānājjñānapūrvakābhyāsādāvivekakhyāteraśuddhikṣaye cittasattvasya
                        prakāśāvaraṇarūpakleśātmakāśuddhikṣaye yā jñānadīptistāratamyena sāttvikaḥ
                        pariṇāmo vivekakhyātiparyantastasyāḥ khyāterheturityarthaḥ ||28||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The limbs of <s>yoga</s> are those that will be described. Through their practice, through cultivation preceded by knowledge, unto discriminative discernment, with the destruction of impurity—of the impurity in the form of obstructions to the luminosity of the mind-<s>sattva</s>—

children.text:
yogāṅgānāmanuṣṭhānādaśuddhikṣaya ityuktam| kāni punastāni yogāṅgānīti
                        teṣāmuddeśamāha ---
children.translated_text: It was stated that through the practice of the limbs of <s>yoga</s> there is the destruction of impurity. What then are those limbs of <s>yoga</s>? He states their enumeration:

<s>Yama</s> (restraints), <s>niyama</s> (observances), <s>āsana</s> (posture), <s>prāṇāyāma</s> (breath control), <s>pratyāhāra</s> (sense withdrawal), <s>dhāraṇā</s> (concentration), <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation), and <s>samādhi</s> (absorption)—these are the eight limbs. ||Sādhana 29||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- iha kānicit samādheḥ sākṣādupakārakāṇi yathā dhāraṇādīni kānicit
                        pratipakṣabhūtahiṃsādivitarkonmūlanadvāreṇa samādhimupakurvanti yathā
                        yamādayaḥ| tatrāsanādīnāmuttarotaramupakārakatvam| tadyathā ---
                        satyāsanajaye prāṇāyāmasthairyam| evamuttaratrāpi yojyam ||29||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Here, some directly assist <s>samādhi</s>, such as <s>dhāraṇā</s> and the rest; some assist <s>samādhi</s> through the uprooting of contrary thoughts such as violence, such as the <s>yamas</s> and the rest.
He states their nature in order:

<s>Ahiṃsā</s> (non-violence), <s>satya</s> (truthfulness), <s>asteya</s> (non-stealing), <s>brahmacarya</s> (celibacy), and <s>aparigraha</s> (non-possessiveness) are the <s>yamas</s> (restraints). ||Sādhana 30||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tatra prāṇaviyogaprayojanavyāpāro hiṃsā| sā ca sarvānarthahetuḥ|
                        tadabhāvo+ahiṃsā| hiṃsāyāḥ sarvaprakāreṇaiva parihāryatvāt prathamaṃ
                        tadabhāvarūpāyā ahiṃsāyā nirdeśaḥ| satyaṃ vāṅmanasoryathārthatvam| steyaṃ
                        parasvāpaharaṇaṃ tadabhāvo+asteyam| brahmacaryamupasthasaṃyamaḥ| aparigraho
                        bhogasādhanānāmanaṅgīkāraḥ| ta ete+ahiṃsādayaḥ pañca yamaśabdavācyā
                        yogāṅgatvena nirdiṣṭāḥ ||30||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Among these, activity aimed at the purpose of separating the life-breath is violence (<s>hiṃsā</s>). And that is the cause of all misfortune. Its absence is non-violence (<s>ahiṃsā</s>). Because violence is to be avoided in every way, first its absence is mentioned.
He states their special qualification:
When not limited by class, place, time, or circumstance, they are universal and constitute the great vow. ||Sādhana 31||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- jātirbrāhmaṇatvādiḥ| deśastīrthādiḥ| kālaścaturdaśyādiḥ| samayo
                        brāhmaṇaprayojanādiḥ| etaiścaturbhiranavacchinnāḥ pūrvoktā ahiṃsādayo yamāḥ
                        sarvāsu kṣiptādiṣu cittabhūmiṣu bhavā mahāvratamityucyate| tadyathā ---
                        brāhmaṇaṃ na haniṣyāmi tīrthe na kaṃcana haniṣyāmi caturdaśyāṃ na haniṣyāmi
                        devabrāhmaṇaprayojanavyatirekeṇa kamapi na haniṣyāmīti| evaṃ
                        caturvidhāvacchedavyatirekeṇa kiṃcit kadācit kasmiṃścidarthe na
                        haniṣyāmītyanavacchinnāḥ| evaṃ satyādiṣu yathāyogaṃ yojyam|
                        itthamaniyatīkṛtāḥ sāmānyenaiva pravṛttā mahāvratamityucyate na punaḥ
                        parakīyaparicchinnāvadhāraṇam
children.translated_text: Commentary: Class (jāti) means being a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> and so on. Place (deśa) means a holy ford and so on. Time (kāla) means the fourteenth day and so on. Circumstance (samaya) means the purpose of a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> and so on. Not limited by these four, the previously mentioned <s>yamas</s> beginning with non-violence are universal.
He states the <s>niyamas</s> (observances):

<s>Śauca</s> (purity), <s>santoṣa</s> (contentment), <s>tapas</s> (austerity), <s>svādhyāya</s> (self-study), and <s>Īśvarapraṇidhāna</s> (devotion to the Lord) are the <s>niyamas</s> (observances). ||Sādhana 32||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- śaucaṃ dvividham --- bāhyamābhyantaraṃ ca| bāhyaṃ mṛjjalādibhiḥ
                        kāyādiprakṣālanam| ābhyantaraṃ maitryādibhiścittamalānāṃ prakṣālanam|
                        santoṣastuṣṭiḥ| śeṣāḥ prāgeva (2|1) kṛtavyākhyānāḥ| ete śaucādayo
                        niyamaśabdavācyāḥ ||32||
