children.translated_text: Commentary: <s>Śauca</s> (purity) is twofold—external and internal. External is the cleansing of the body and so forth with earth, water, and the like. Internal is the cleansing of mental impurities through <s>maitrī</s> (friendliness) and the like. <s>Santoṣa</s> (contentment)—
How are these limbs of <s>yoga</s>? He says:
<s>Pratipakṣa bhāvanā</s> (cultivation of the opposite) when obstructed by contrary thoughts. ||Sādhana 33||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- vitarkyante iti vitarkā yogaparipanthino hiṃsādayaḥ| teṣāṃ
                        pratipakṣabhāvane sati yadā bādhā bhavati tadā yogaḥ sukaro bhavatīti
                        bhavatyeva yamaniyamayoryogāṅgatvam ||33||
children.translated_text: Commentary: <s>Vitarkas</s> (contrary thoughts) are those which are deliberated upon—they are impediments to <s>yoga</s> such as violence and the rest. When the cultivation of their opposites takes place, when there is obstruction of those thoughts, then <s>yoga</s> becomes easy—thus these are indeed limbs of <s>yoga</s>.

children.text: idānīṃ vitarkāṇāṃ svarūpaṃ bhedaprakāraṃ phalaṃ ca krameṇāha ---
children.translated_text: Now he states the nature, types, and fruits of the contrary thoughts in order:

children.text:
vitarkā hiṃsādayaḥ kṛtakāritānumoditā lobhakrodhamohapūrvakā
                        mṛdumadhyādhimātrā duḥkhājñānānantaphalā iti pratipakṣabhāvanam ||sādhana
                        34||
children.translated_text: The contrary thoughts—violence and the rest—whether done, caused to be done, or approved; preceded by greed, anger, or delusion; mild, moderate, or intense—result in endless suffering and ignorance. This is the cultivation of the opposite. ||Sādhana 34||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- ete pūrvoktā hiṃsādayaḥ prathamaṃ tridhā bhidyante
                        kṛtakāritānumodanabhedena| tatra svayaṃ niṣpāditāḥ kṛtāḥ| kuru kurviti
                        prayojakavyāpāreṇa samutpāditāḥ kāritāḥ| anyena kriyamāṇāḥ sādhvityaṅgīkṛtā
                        anumoditāḥ| etacca traividhyaṃ parasparaṃ vyāmohanirākaraṇāvadhāraṇāyocyate|
                        anyathā mandamatirevaṃ manyeta na mayā svayaṃ hiṃsā kṛteti nāsti me doṣaḥ|
                        eteṣāṃ kāraṇapratipādanāya lobhakrodhamohapūrvakā iti| yadyapi lobhaḥ
                        prathamaṃ nirdiṣṭastathā+api sarvakleśānāṃ
                        mohasyā+anātmanyātmābhimānalakṣaṇasya nidānatvāt tasmin sati
                        svaparavibhāgapūrvakatvena lobhakrodhādīnāmudbhavānmūlatvamavaseyam|
                        mohapūrvikā sarvā doṣajātirityarthaḥ| lobhastṛṣṇā| krodhaḥ
                        kṛtyākṛtyavivekonmūlakaḥ prajvalanātmakaścittadharmaḥ| pratyekaṃ
                        kṛtādibhedena triprakārā api hiṃsādayo mohādikāraṇatvena tridhā bhidyante|
                        eṣāmeva punaravasthābhedena traividhyamāha --- mṛdumadhyādhimātrāḥ| mṛdavo
                        mandāḥ na tīvrā nāpi madhyāḥ| madhyā nāpi mandā nāpi tīvrāḥ|
                        adhimātrāstīvrāḥ| pāścāttyā navabhedāḥ| itthaṃ traividhye sati
                        saptaviṃśatirbhavati| mṛdvādīnāmapi pratyekaṃ mṛdumadhyādhimātrabhedāt
                        traividhyaṃ sambhavati| tadyathāyogaṃ yojyam| tadyathā ---
                        mṛdumṛdurmṛdumadhyo mṛdutīvra iti| eṣāṃ phalamāha --- duḥkhājñānānantaphalā
                        duḥkhaṃ pratikūlatayā+avabhāsamāno rājasaścittadharmaḥ| ajñānaṃ mithyājñānaṃ
                        saṃśayaviparyayarūpam| te duḥkhājñāne+anantamaparicchinnaṃ phalaṃ yeṣāṃ te
                        tathoktāḥ| itthaṃ teṣāṃ svarūpakāraṇādibhedena jñātānāṃ pratipakṣabhāvanayā
                        yoginā parihāraḥ kartavya ityupadiṣṭaṃ bhavati ||34||
children.translated_text: Commentary: These previously mentioned [violations] beginning with <s>hiṃsā</s> (violence) are first divided threefold according to the distinction of done, caused to be done, and approved. Among these: those performed by oneself are 'done' (<s>kṛta</s>). Those produced through the agent's prompting, 'do it, do it,' are 'caused to be done' (<s>kārita</s>). Those performed by another and sanctioned with approval are 'approved' (<s>anumodita</s>). This threefold division is stated for the purpose of removing mutual confusion and for establishing certainty. Otherwise, a dull-witted person would think, 'Violence was not done by me personally, so I have no fault.' To establish the causes of these, [it is said:] 'preceded by greed, anger, and delusion.' Although greed is mentioned first, nevertheless, since <s>moha</s> (delusion), characterized by the superimposition of selfhood on the non-self, is the root cause of all <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions)—and from its presence, greed, anger, and the rest arise preceded by the distinction between self and other—its status as the root cause should be understood. The entire class of faults is preceded by delusion—this is the meaning. Greed is craving. Anger is a mental quality of blazing nature that uproots the discrimination between what should and should not be done. The [violations] beginning with violence, though threefold by the distinction of done and the rest, are further divided threefold by the causation of delusion and the rest. He states another threefold division of these very [violations] by distinction of degree: mild, moderate, and intense. Mild are weak—neither intense nor moderate. Moderate are neither weak nor intense. Intense are severe. The latter are ninefold divisions. Thus, with this threefold division, there are twenty-seven. The mild and the rest can each be further divided threefold as mild-mild, mild-moderate, and mild-intense—this should be applied as appropriate. For example: mild-mild, mild-moderate, mild-intense. He states their result: 'having endless fruit of suffering and ignorance.' Suffering is a mental quality of <s>rajas</s> manifesting as what is adverse. Ignorance is false knowledge in the form of doubt and error. Those whose fruit—suffering and ignorance—is endless, unlimited, are thus described. Thus, when these [violations] are known through the distinctions of their nature, cause, and so forth, the yogin should counteract them by cultivating the opposite (<s>pratipakṣabhāvanā</s>)—this is what has been taught. ||34||

children.text:
eṣāmabhyāsavaśāt prakarṣamāgacchatāmanuniṣpādinyaḥ siddhayo yathā bhavanti
                        tathā krameṇa pratipādayitumāha ---
children.translated_text: To demonstrate how, through the force of practice of these [virtues], the supernatural powers that arise as they reach their culmination, he says in sequence:
When <s>ahiṃsā</s> (non-violence) is firmly established, hostility is abandoned in one's presence. ||Sādhana 35||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tasyā+ahiṃsāṃ bhāvayataḥ sannidhau
                        sahajavirodhināmapyahinakulādīnāṃ vairatyāgo nirmatsaratayā+avasthānaṃ
                        bhavati| hiṃsrasvabhāvā api hiṃsāṃ tyajantītyarthaḥ

children.translated_text: Even those whose nature is violent abandon violence—this is the meaning. ||35||
Commentary: In the presence of one who cultivates <s>ahiṃsā</s>, even those who are natural enemies, such as snakes and mongooses, abandon hostility, remaining without enmity.
He asks: what happens for one who practices truthfulness?
When <s>satya</s> (truthfulness) is firmly established, actions and their fruits become dependent [on one's word]. ||Sādhana 36||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- kriyamāṇā hi kriyā yāgādikāḥ phalaṃ svargādikaṃ prayacchanti|
                        tasya tu satyābhyāsavato yoginastathā satyaṃ prakṛṣyate yathā
                        kriyāyāmakṛtāyāmapi yogī phalamāpnoti| tadvacanādyasya kasyacit
                        kriyāmakurvato+api kriyāphalaṃ bhavatītyarthaḥ ||36||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Actions that are performed, such as sacrifices and the like, yield their fruits such as heaven. But for that yogin who practices truthfulness, truthfulness is so perfected that even without performing the action, the yogin obtains the fruit. By his word, even for someone who does not perform an action, the fruit of action arises—this is the meaning. ||36||
He states the fruit of practicing non-stealing:
When <s>asteya</s> (non-stealing) is firmly established, all gems present themselves. ||Sādhana 37||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- asteyaṃ yadā+abhyasati tadāsya tatprakarṣānnirabhilāṣasyāpi
                        sarvato divyāni ratnānyupatiṣṭhante ||37||
children.translated_text: Commentary: When one practices non-stealing, through its culmination, even though one has no desire for them, divine gems present themselves from all directions. ||37||
He states the fruit of practicing celibacy:
When <s>brahmacarya</s> (celibacy) is firmly established, vigor is obtained. ||Sādhana 38||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- yaḥ kila brahmacaryamabhyasyati tasya tatprakarṣānniratiśayaṃ
                        vīryaṃ sāmarthyamāvirbhavati| vīryanirodhe hi brahmacaryasya
                        prakarṣāccharīrendriyamanaḥsu vīryaṃ prakarṣamāgacchati ||38||
children.translated_text: Commentary: One who indeed practices <s>brahmacarya</s>, through its culmination, unsurpassed vigor and power manifest. For through the celibate restraint of vital energy, vigor reaches its culmination in the body, sense organs, and mind. ||38||
He states the fruit of non-possessiveness:
When <s>aparigraha</s> (non-possessiveness) is firm, knowledge of the 'how' of births [arises]. ||Sādhana 39||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- kathamityasya bhāvaḥ kathantā| janmanaḥ kathantā janmakathantā|
                        tasyāḥ sambodhaḥ samyagjñānaṃ janmāntare ko+ahamāsaṃ kīdṛśaḥ kiṃkāryakārīti
                        jijñāsāyāṃ sarvameva samyagjānātītyarthaḥ| na kevalaṃ bhogasādhanaparigraha
                        eva parigraho yāvadātmanaḥ śarīraparigraho+api parigraho
                        bhogasādhanatvāccharīrasya| tasmin sati rāgānubandhādbahirmukhāyāmeva
                        pravṛttau na tāttvikajñānaprādurbhāvaḥ| yadā punaḥ
                        śarīrādiparigrahanairapekṣyeṇa mādhyasthyamavalambate tadā madhyasthasya
                        rāgādityāgāt samyagjñānaheturbhavatyeva pūrvāparajanmasambodhaḥ ||39||
children.translated_text: Commentary: <s>Kathantā</s> is the abstract noun of 'how.' <s>Janmakathantā</s> is the 'how' of birth. Its <s>sambodha</s> (complete knowledge) is perfect understanding—'who was I in a previous birth, of what kind, doing what?'—when such inquiry arises, one knows everything perfectly, this is the meaning. Not only the possession of means of enjoyment constitutes <s>parigraha</s> (possession), but also the possession of one's own body, since the body is a means of enjoyment. When that exists, due to the subsequent bond of attachment, when activity is directed outward alone, the arising of true knowledge does not occur. But when, through indifference to the possession of body and so forth, one relies on equanimity, then for the equanimous one, through the abandonment of attachment and the rest, the complete knowledge of past and future births naturally becomes a cause of right knowledge. ||39||
The supernatural powers of the <s>yamas</s> have been stated. Now he states those of the <s>niyamas</s>:
From <s>śauca</s> (purity) [comes] disgust toward one's own body and non-contact with others. ||Sādhana 40||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- yaḥ śaucaṃ bhāvayati tasya svāṅgeṣvapi
                        kāraṇasvarūpaparyālocanadvāreṇa jugupsā ghṛṇā samupajāyate --- aśucirayaṃ
                        kāyo nātrāgrahaḥ kārya iti| amunaiva hetunā parairanyaiśca
                        kāyavadbhirasaṃsargaḥ samparkābhāvaḥ saṃsargaparivarjanamityarthaḥ| yaḥ kila
                        svameva kāyaṃ jugupsate tattadavadyadarśanāt sa kathaṃ
                        parakīyaistathābhūtaiśca kāyaiḥ saṃsargamanubhavati ||40||
children.translated_text: Commentary: One who cultivates purity develops disgust, revulsion, even toward one's own limbs, through contemplation of the nature of its causes—'this body is impure; attachment to it should not be maintained.' For this very reason, non-contact, absence of association, avoidance of contact with others who are embodied—this is the meaning. Indeed, one who is disgusted with one's own body, seeing its various faults, how would one enjoy contact with others' bodies of the same nature? ||40||
He states another fruit of purity:
And purity of <s>sattva</s>, cheerfulness, one-pointedness, mastery of the senses, and fitness for the vision of the Self. ||Sādhana 41||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- bhavantīti vākyaśeṣaḥ| sattvaṃ prakāśasukhādyātmakaṃ tasya śuddhī
                        rajastamobhyāmanabhibhavaḥ| saumanasyaṃ khedānanubhavena mānasī prītiḥ|
                        ekāgratā niyataviṣaye cetasaḥ sthairyam| indriyajayo
                        viṣayaparāṅmukhāṇāmindriyāṇāmātmanyavasthānam| ātmadarśane vivekakhyātirūpe
                        cittasya yogyatvaṃ samarthatvam| śaucābhyāsavata eva ete sattvaśuddhyādayaḥ
                        krameṇa prādurbhavanti| tathāhi --- sattvaśuddheḥ saumanasyam|
                        saumanasyādekāgratā| ekāgratāyā indriyajayaḥ| tasmādātmadarśanayogyateti
                        ||41||
children.translated_text: Commentary: 'Arise'—this is the completion of the sentence. <s>Sattva</s>, whose nature is luminosity, happiness, and the like—its purity is its being unoverwhelmed by <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>. Cheerfulness (<s>saumanasya</s>) is mental delight through not experiencing distress. One-pointedness (<s>ekāgratā</s>) is the steadiness of the mind on a fixed object. Mastery of the senses (<s>indriyajaya</s>) is the establishment of the senses, turned away from objects, in the Self. Fitness for the vision of the Self (<s>ātmadarśanayogyatva</s>) is the capacity, the ability of the mind for <s>vivekakhyāti</s> (discriminative discernment). These, beginning with the purity of <s>sattva</s>, progressively manifest for one who practices purity. Thus: from the purity of <s>sattva</s> comes cheerfulness; from cheerfulness, one-pointedness; from one-pointedness, mastery of the senses; from that, fitness for the vision of the Self. ||41||
He states the fruit of practicing contentment:
From <s>santoṣa</s> (contentment), unsurpassed happiness is obtained. ||Sādhana 42||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- santoṣaprakarṣeṇa yoginastathāvidhamāntaraṃ sukhamāvirbhavati
                        yasya bāhyaṃ viṣayasukhaṃ śatāṃśenāpi na samam ||42||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Through the culmination of contentment, such an inner happiness manifests for the yogin that external sensory happiness does not equal even a hundredth part of it. ||42||
He states the fruit of austerity:
Perfection of the body and senses [comes] from <s>tapas</s> (austerity), through the destruction of impurity. ||Sādhana 43||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ ---tapaḥ samabhyasyamānaṃ cetasaḥ kleśādilakṣaṇāśuddhikṣayadvāreṇa
                        kāyendriyāṇāṃ siddhiprakarṣamādadhāti| ayamarthaḥ --- cāndrāyaṇādinā
                        cittakleśakṣayastatkṣayādindriyādīnāṃ
                        sūkṣmavyavahitaviprakṛṣṭadarśanādisāmarthyamāvirbhavati kāyasya yatheccham
                        aṇutvamahattvādīni ||43||
children.translated_text: Commentary: <s>Tapas</s>, when well-practiced, brings about the culmination of perfection of the body and senses through the destruction of impurity characterized by <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) and the like in the mind. The meaning is: through practices like <s>cāndrāyaṇa</s> (lunar fast), the <s>kleśas</s> of the mind are destroyed; through their destruction, the ability of the senses and such to perceive subtle, hidden, and distant things manifests; and the body [gains] powers such as becoming minute or great at will. ||43||
He states the fruit of self-study:
From <s>svādhyāya</s> (self-study), union with the desired deity [is achieved]. ||Sādhana 44||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- abhipretamantrajapādilakṣaṇe svādhyāye prakṛṣyamāṇe yogina
                        iṣṭayā+abhipretayā devatayā samprayogo bhavati| sā devatā pratyakṣā
                        bhatītyarthaḥ ||44||
children.translated_text: Commentary: When self-study, characterized by the repetition of one's chosen <s>mantra</s> and the like, is perfected, the yogin achieves union with the desired, chosen deity. That deity becomes directly visible—this is the meaning. ||44||
He states the fruit of devotion to the Lord:
Perfection of <s>samādhi</s> [comes] from <s>Īśvarapraṇidhāna</s> (devotion to the Lord). ||Sādhana 45||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- īśvare yat praṇidhānaṃ bhaktiviśeṣastasmāt
                        samādheruktalakṣaṇasyāvirbhāvo bhavati yasmāt sa bhagavānīśvaraḥ prasannaḥ
                        sannantarāyarūpān kleśān parihṛtya samādhiṃ sambodhayati ||45||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The <s>praṇidhāna</s> (devotion) toward <s>Īśvara</s>, which is a special form of <s>bhakti</s> (devotion)—from that, the manifestation of <s>samādhi</s> with the characteristics previously described occurs, because the Blessed Lord <s>Īśvara</s>, being pleased, having removed the <s>kleśas</s> in the form of obstacles, awakens <s>samādhi</s>. ||45||
Having stated the <s>yamas</s> and <s>niyamas</s>, he states <s>āsana</s>:
<s>Āsana</s> (posture) is steady and comfortable. ||Sādhana 46||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- āsyate+anenetyāsanaṃ padmāsanadaṇḍāsanasvastikāsanādi| tadyadā
                        sthiraṃ niṣkampaṃ sukhamanudvejanīyaṃ ca bhavati tadā yogāṅgatāṃ bhajate
                        ||46||
children.translated_text: Commentary: That by which one sits is <s>āsana</s>—<s>padmāsana</s> (lotus posture), <s>daṇḍāsana</s> (staff posture), <s>svastikāsana</s> (auspicious posture), and so forth. When that becomes steady, without trembling, and comfortable, not causing distress—then it becomes a limb of <s>yoga</s>. ||46||
To state the means for attaining that steadiness and comfort, he says:
By relaxation of effort and <s>samāpatti</s> (absorption) on the infinite. ||Sādhana 47||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tadāsanaṃ prayatnaśaithilyenā+a+anantyasamāpattyā ca sthiraṃ
                        sukhaṃ bhavatīti sambandhaḥ| yadā yadā+a+asanaṃ badhnāmīti icchāṃ karoti
                        prayatnaśaithilye+apyakleśenaiva tadā tadā+a+asanaṃ sampadyate| yadā
                        cākāśādigata ānantye cetasaḥ samāpattiḥ kriyate+avadhānena

tādātmyamāpadyate tadā dehāhaṃkārābhāvānnāsanaṃ
                        duḥkhajanakaṃ bhavati| asmiṃścāsanajaye sati samādhyantarāyabhūtā na
                        prabhavantyaṅgamejayatvādayaḥ ||47||
children.translated_text: one becomes identified with it; then, due to the absence of body-ego, the posture does not cause suffering. And when this mastery of posture is attained, the trembling of limbs and the like, which are obstacles to <s>samādhi</s>, do not prevail. ||47||

Commentary: That <s>āsana</s> becomes steady and comfortable through relaxation of effort and through <s>samāpatti</s> on the infinite—this is the connection. Whenever one forms the intention 'I shall assume the posture,' through relaxation of effort, effortlessly, the posture is accomplished. And when <s>samāpatti</s> of the mind is made through attention on the infinity [pervading] space and the like,
He states the consequent fruit of that very [mastery]:
From that, non-affliction by the pairs of opposites. ||Sādhana 48||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tasminnāsanajaye sati dvandvaiḥ śītoṣṇakṣuttṛṣṇādibhiryogī
                        nābhihanyata ityarthaḥ ||48||
children.translated_text: Commentary: When that mastery of posture is attained, the yogin is not afflicted by the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat, hunger and thirst, and the like—this is the meaning. ||48||
After mastery of posture, he states <s>prāṇāyāma</s>:
When that [āsana] is [mastered], the cutting off of the movement of inhalation and exhalation is <s>prāṇāyāma</s> (breath control). ||Sādhana 49||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- āsanasthairye sati tannimittakaprāṇāyāmalakṣaṇo
                        yogāṅgaviśeṣo+anuṣṭheyo bhavati| kīdṛśaḥ|
                        svāsapraśvāsayorgativicchedalakṣaṇaḥ| śvāsapraśvāsau niruktau (1|31)
                        tayostridhā recanastambhanapūraṇadvāreṇa bāhyābhyantareṣu sthāneṣu gateḥ
                        pravāhasya vicchedo dhāraṇaṃ prāṇāyāma ucyate ||49||
children.translated_text: Commentary: When steadiness of posture is attained, the special limb of <s>yoga</s> characterized by <s>prāṇāyāma</s>, occasioned by that, should be practiced. Of what kind? Characterized by the cutting off of the movement of inhalation and exhalation. Inhalation and exhalation have been defined [in 1.31]; through the three means of <s>recana</s> (exhaling), <s>stambhana</s> (holding), and <s>pūraṇa</s> (filling), the cutting off—the holding—of the flow of movement in the external and internal places is called <s>prāṇāyāma</s>. ||49||

children.text: tasyaiva sukhāvagamāya vibhajya svarūpaṃ kathayati --- sa tu
children.translated_text: For easy understanding, he describes its nature by dividing it: 'That [<s>prāṇāyāma</s>] indeed—'
has the operations of external, internal, and suspension, and is regulated by place, time, and number, [becoming] long and subtle. ||Sādhana 50||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- bāhyavṛttiḥ śvāso recakaḥ| antarvṛttiḥ praśvāsaḥ pūrakaḥ|
                        āntarastambhavṛttiḥ kumbhakaḥ| tasmin jalamiva kumbhe niścalatayā prāṇā
                        avasthāpyanta iti kumbhakaḥ| trividho+ayaṃ prāṇāyāmaḥ deśena kālena
                        saṃkhyayā copalakṣito dīrghasūkṣmasaṃjño bhavati| deśopalakṣito yathā
                        nāsāddvādaśāntādi nāsāmārabhya dvādaśāṅguliparyantamityarthaḥ| kālopalakṣito
                        yathā ṣaṭtriṃśanmātrādipramāṇaḥ| saṃkhyayopalakṣito yathā iyato vārān kṛta
                        etāvadbhiḥ śvāsapraśvāsaiḥ prathama udghāto bhavatīti| etajjñānāya
                        saṃkhyāgrahaṇamupāttam| udghāto nāma nābhimūlāt preritasya vāyoḥ
                        śirasyabhihananam ||50||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The external activity is exhalation (<s>śvāsa</s>), which is <s>recaka</s>. The internal activity is inhalation (<s>praśvāsa</s>), which is <s>pūraka</s>. The internal retention activity is <s>kumbhaka</s> — therein the <s>prāṇas</s> (vital breaths) are held motionless as water in a pot (<s>kumbha</s>), hence <s>kumbhaka</s>. This threefold <s>prāṇāyāma</s> (breath control), characterized by place, time, and number, becomes known as 'long and subtle.' Characterized by place, such as from the nose to the <s>dvādaśānta</s> (twelve finger-breadths beyond the nose) — meaning from the nose extending to twelve finger-breadths. Characterized by time, such as a measure of thirty-six <s>mātrās</s> (units). Characterized by number, such as 'having done so many rounds with so many inhalations and exhalations, the first <s>udghāta</s> (impulse) occurs.' The counting is taken up for this knowledge. <s>Udghāta</s> means the striking of the breath, impelled from the base of the navel, upon the head. || 50 ||
Having described three types of <s>prāṇāyāma</s>, to describe the fourth he says—
The fourth <s>prāṇāyāma</s> transcends the external and internal domains. || Sādhana 51 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- prāṇasya bāhyo viṣayo nāsāddvādaśāntādiḥ| ābhyantaro viṣayo
                        hṛdayanābhicakrādiḥ| tau dvau viṣayāvākṣipya paryālocya yaḥ stambharūpī
                        gativicchedaḥ sa caturthaḥ prāṇāyāmaḥ| tṛtīyasmāt kumbhakākhyādayamasya
                        viśeṣaḥ --- sa bāhyābhyantaraviṣayāvaparyālocyaiva sahasā
                        taptopalanipatitajalanyāyena yugapat stambhavṛttyā niṣpādyate

| asya tu viṣayadvayākṣepako nirodhaḥ| ayamapi
                        pūrvavaddeśakālasaṃkhyābhirupalakṣito draṣṭavyaḥ ||51||
children.translated_text: Its cessation, however, transcends both domains. This too should be seen as characterized by place, time, and number, as before. || 51 ||

Commentary: The external domain of <s>prāṇa</s> is the space from the nose to the <s>dvādaśānta</s> and so forth. The internal domain is the heart, navel-<s>cakra</s>, and so forth. Having examined and considered both these domains, the cessation of movement in the form of retention — that is the fourth <s>prāṇāyāma</s>. Its distinction from the third, called <s>kumbhaka</s>, is this: it is accomplished suddenly, without examining the external and internal domains, like water falling on a heated stone, simultaneously through the retention activity.
He states the fruit of this fourfold [<s>prāṇāyāma</s>]—
Thereby the covering of illumination is destroyed. || Sādhana 52 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tatastasmāt prāṇāyāmāt prakāśasya cittasattvagatasya yadāvaraṇaṃ
                        kleśarūpaṃ tat kṣīyate vinaśyatītyarthaḥ ||52||
children.translated_text: Commentary: From that <s>prāṇāyāma</s>, the covering of the illumination residing in the <s>sattva</s> quality of the mind — that covering which has the form of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) — is destroyed, meaning it perishes. || 52 ||
He states another fruit—
And the mind becomes fit for <s>dhāraṇā</s> (concentration). || Sādhana 53 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- dhāraṇā vakṣyamāṇalakṣaṇāstāsu prāṇāyāmaiḥ kṣīṇadoṣaṃ mano yatra
                        yatra dhāryate tatra tatra sthirībhavati na vikṣepaṃ bhajate ||53||
children.translated_text: Commentary: <s>Dhāraṇās</s> have the characteristics to be described; through <s>prāṇāyāma</s>, the mind whose defects have been diminished becomes steady wherever it is held — it does not become distracted. || 53 ||
He states the definition of <s>pratyāhāra</s> (sense-withdrawal)—
<s>Pratyāhāra</s> (sense-withdrawal) is, as it were, the imitation by the senses of the mind's own form, when they are disengaged from their respective objects. || Sādhana 54 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- indriyāṇi viṣayebhyaḥ pratīpamāhriyante+asminniti pratyāhāraḥ| sa
                        ca kathaṃ niṣpadyata ityāha --- cakṣurādīnāmindriyāṇāṃ svaviṣayo rūpādistena
                        samprayogastadābhimukhyena vartanam tadabhāvastadābhimukhyaṃ parityajya
                        svarūpamātre+avasthānam| tasmin sati cittamātrānukāriṇīndriyāṇi bhavanti
                        yataścittamanuvartamānāni madhukararājamiva makṣikāḥ sarvāṇīndriyāṇi
                        pratīyante| ataścittanirodhe tāni pratyāhṛtāni bhavanti| teṣāṃ
                        tatsvarūpānukāraḥ pratyāhāra uktaḥ ||54||
children.translated_text: Commentary: That in which the senses are withdrawn back from their objects is <s>pratyāhāra</s>. And how is it accomplished? He says: the proper objects of the senses such as the eye and so forth are form and the rest; their engagement with these is their functioning directed toward them; their disengagement is the abandonment of that directedness, remaining in their own essential nature alone. When that occurs, the senses become mere followers of the mind, for all the senses are seen to follow the mind, just as bees follow the queen bee. Therefore, when the mind is restrained, they become withdrawn. Their imitation of the mind's own form is called <s>pratyāhāra</s>. || 54 ||
He states the fruit of <s>pratyāhāra</s>—
From that comes the supreme mastery over the senses. || Sādhana 55 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- abhyasyamāne hi pratyāhāre tathā vaśyānyāyattānīndriyāṇi
                        sampadyante yathā bāhyaviṣayābhimukhatāṃ nīyamānānyapi na yāntītyarthaḥ
                        ||55||
children.translated_text: Commentary: When <s>pratyāhāra</s> is practiced, the senses become so mastered and obedient that even when being led toward external objects, they do not go — this is the meaning. || 55 ||

children.text:
tadevaṃ prathamapādoktalakṣaṇasya yogasyāṅgabhūtakleśatanūkaraṇaphalaṃ
                        kriyāyogamabhidhāya kleśānāmuddeśaṃ svarūpaṃ kāraṇaṃ kṣetraṃ phalaṃ coktvā
                        karmaṇāmapi bhedaṃ kāraṇaṃ svarūpaṃ phalaṃ cābhidhāya vipākasya kāraṇam
                        svarūpaṃ cābhihitam| tatastyājyatvāt kleśādināṃ jñānavyatirekeṇa
                        tyāgasyā+aśakyatvājjñānasya ca śāstrāyattatvāt śāstrasya
                        heyahānakāraṇopādeyopādānakāraṇabodhakatvena caturvyūhatvāt heyasya
                        hānavyatirekeṇa svarūpāniṣpatterhānasahitaṃ caturvyūhaṃ
                        svasvakāraṇasahitamabhidhāya upādeyakāraṇabhūtāyā vivekakhyāteḥ
                        kāraṇabhūtānāmantaraṅgabahiraṅgabhāvena sthitānāṃ yamādīnāṃ svarūpaṃ
                        phalasahitaṃ vyākṛtya āsanādīnāṃ dhāraṇāparyantānāṃ
                        parasparamupakāryopakārakabhāvenāvasthitānāmuddeśamabhidhāya pratyekaṃ
                        lakṣaṇakaraṇapūvakaṃ phalamabhihitam | tadayaṃ yogo yamaniyamādibhiḥ
                        prāptabījabhāva āsanaprāṇāyāmairaṅkuritaḥ pratyāhāreṇa puṣpito
                        dhyānadhāraṇāsamādhibhiḥ phaliṣyatīti vyākhyātaḥ sādhanapādaḥ|
children.translated_text: Thus, having described <s>kriyāyoga</s> whose fruit is the attenuation of the <s>kleśas</s> that constitute the limbs of <s>yoga</s> as defined in the first chapter, and having stated the enumeration, nature, cause, field, and fruit of the <s>kleśas</s>, and also having described the varieties, cause, nature, and fruit of <s>karma</s>, and having stated the cause and nature of <s>vipāka</s> (fruition), then — because <s>kleśas</s> and the rest must be abandoned, because abandonment is impossible without knowledge, because knowledge depends on scripture, and because scripture teaches the fourfold arrangement of what is to be avoided, avoidance, its cause, what is to be adopted, and its cause — having described the four categories together with their respective causes and accompanied by the means of avoidance, and having explained the nature and fruit of <s>yama</s> and the other [limbs] that stand in the relation of inner and outer means to <s>vivekakhyāti</s> (discriminative knowledge), which is the cause of what is to be adopted, and having enumerated from <s>āsana</s> up to <s>dhāraṇā</s> which stand in mutual relation of means and end, he has stated the fruit of each through its definition and means. Thus this <s>yoga</s>, having received its seed through <s>yama</s> and <s>niyama</s>, sprouted through <s>āsana</s> and <s>prāṇāyāma</s>, blossomed through <s>pratyāhāra</s>, will bear fruit through <s>dhyāna</s>, <s>dhāraṇā</s>, and <s>samādhi</s> — thus has the <s>Sādhanapāda</s> been explained.

children.text:
iti dhāreśvarabhojaviracitāyāṃ rājamārtaṇḍābhidhāyāṃ pātañjalavṛttau
                        sādhanapādaḥ ||2|| iti sādhanapādaḥ ||2||
children.translated_text: Thus ends the <s>Sādhanapāda</s> (Chapter on Practice), the second chapter of the <s>Rājamārtaṇḍa</s> commentary on <s>Patañjali</s>'s [Yoga Sūtras], composed by the sovereign lord <s>Bhoja</s>. || 2 || Thus ends the <s>Sādhanapāda</s>. || 2 ||
<s>Vibhūtipāda</s> (Chapter on Supernatural Powers)

children.text:
atha vibhūtipādaḥ ||3||
                        yatpādapadmasmaraṇādaṇimādivibhūtayaḥ | bhavanti bhavināmastu bhūtanāthaḥ sa
                        bhūtaye ||
children.translated_text: Now begins the <s>Vibhūtipāda</s>, the third chapter. || 3 || May He whose lotus feet, when remembered, cause <s>aṇimā</s> and other supernatural powers to arise in beings — may that Lord of beings be for our welfare.

children.text:
tadevaṃ pūrvoddiṣṭaṃ dhāraṇādyaṅgatrayaṃ nirṇetuṃ
                        saṃyamasaṃjñābhidhānapūrvakaṃ bāhyābhyantarādisiddhipratipādanāya
                        lakṣayitumupakramate| tatra dhāraṇāyāḥ svarūpamāha ---
children.translated_text: Thus, to determine the triad of limbs beginning with <s>dhāraṇā</s> that was previously enumerated, and to establish the internal and external <s>siddhis</s> (accomplishments) preceded by the designation called <s>saṃyama</s> (combined practice), he begins to define them. There, he states the nature of <s>dhāraṇā</s>—
<s>Dhāraṇā</s> (concentration) is the binding of the mind to a place. || Vibhūti 1 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- deśe nābhicakranāsāgrādau cittasya bandho viṣayāntaraparihāreṇa
                        yat sthirīkaraṇaṃ sā cittasya dhāraṇocyate| ayamarthaḥ ---
                        maitryādicittaparikarmavāsitāntaḥkaraṇena yamaniyamavatā jitāsanena
                        parihṛtaprāṇavikṣepeṇa pratyāhṛtendriyagrāmeṇa nirbādhe pradeśa ṛjukāyena
                        jitadvandvena yoginā nāsāgrādau samprajñātasya samādherabhyāsāya cittasya
                        sthirīkaraṇaṃ kartavyamiti ||1||
children.translated_text: Commentary: <s>Dhāraṇā</s> is the binding of the mind to a particular place — the navel-<s>cakra</s>, the tip of the nose, and so forth — its steadying by excluding other objects. The meaning is: the <s>yogin</s>, whose inner instrument has been purified by the preparatory practice of <s>maitrī</s> (friendliness) and the rest, who possesses <s>yama</s> and <s>niyama</s>, who has mastered <s>āsana</s>, who has removed the disturbances of <s>prāṇa</s>, whose senses have been withdrawn, sitting in an undisturbed place with an erect body, having conquered the pairs of opposites, should steady the mind on the tip of the nose and other points, for the practice of <s>samprajñāta samādhi</s> (cognitive absorption). || 1 ||
Having described <s>dhāraṇā</s>, to describe <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation) he says—
The continuous flow of cognition toward that [place] is <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation). || Vibhūti 2 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tatra tasmin pradeśe yatra cittaṃ dhṛtaṃ tatra pratyayasya
                        jñānasya yā ekatānatā visadṛśapariṇāmaparihāradvāreṇa yadeva
                        dhāraṇāyāmavalambanīkṛtaṃ tadavalambanatayaiva nirantaramutpattiḥ sā
                        dhyānamucyate ||2||
children.translated_text: Commentary: In that place where the mind has been held, the continuous flow of cognition — knowledge — means that, by excluding dissimilar modifications, what was held as support in <s>dhāraṇā</s> continues to arise uninterruptedly as that very support; this is called <s>dhyāna</s>. || 2 ||
He states the final limb of <s>yoga</s>, <s>samādhi</s>—
That very [meditation], shining forth as the object alone, as if empty of its own form, is <s>samādhi</s> (absorption). || Vibhūti 3 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tadevoktalakṣaṇaṃ dhyānaṃ
                        yatrārthamātranirbhāsamarthākārasamāveśādudbhūtārtharūpaṃ
                        nyagbhūtajñānasvarūpatvena svarūpaśūnyatāmivā+a+apadyate sa
                        samādhirityucyate| samyagādhīyata ekāgrīkriyate vikṣepān parihṛtya mano
                        yatra sa samādhiḥ ||3||
children.translated_text: Commentary: That very meditation with the described characteristics, in which the object alone shines forth — due to absorption in the form of the object, the form of the object having arisen, and the form of knowledge having become subdued — it attains, as it were, emptiness of its own form; that is called <s>samādhi</s>. <s>Samādhi</s> is where the mind is properly placed, made one-pointed, having removed distractions. || 3 ||

children.text:
uktalakṣaṇasya yogāṅgatrayasya vyavahārāya svaśāstre tāntrikīṃ saṃjñāṃ
                        kartumāha ---
children.translated_text: To create a technical term in his own system for the practical usage of the described triad of <s>yoga</s> limbs, he says—
The three together on a single [object] constitute <s>saṃyama</s> (combined practice). || Vibhūti 4 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- ekasmin viṣaye dhāraṇādhyānasamādhitrayaṃ pravartamānaṃ
                        saṃyamasaṃjñayā śāstre vyavahriyate ||4||
children.translated_text: Commentary: When <s>dhāraṇā</s>, <s>dhyāna</s>, and <s>samādhi</s> — the triad — are practiced together on a single object, they are designated in the scripture by the term <s>saṃyama</s>. || 4 ||
He states its fruit—
From mastery of that comes the light of <s>prajñā</s> (wisdom). || Vibhūti 5 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tasya saṃyamasya jayādabhyāsena sātmyotpādanāt prajñāyā
                        vivekakhyāterālokaḥ prasavo bhavati| prajñā jñeyaṃ
                        samyagavabhāsayatītyarthaḥ ||5||
children.translated_text: Commentary: From the mastery of that <s>saṃyama</s> — through practice producing familiarity — there arises the light, the dawning, of <s>prajñā</s>, which is <s>vivekakhyāti</s> (discriminative knowledge). <s>Prajñā</s> illuminates the knowable perfectly — this is the meaning. || 5 ||
He states its application—
Its application is by stages. || Vibhūti 6 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tasya saṃyamasya bhūmiṣu sthūlasūkṣmāvalambanabhedena sthitāsu
                        cittavṛttiṣu viniyogaḥ kartavyaḥ| adharāmadharāṃ cittabhūmiṃ jitāṃ jitāṃ
                        jñātvottarasyāṃ bhūmau saṃyamaḥ kāryaḥ| sa
                        hyanātmīīkṛtādharabhūmiruttarasyāṃ bhūmau saṃyamaṃ kurvāṇaḥ phalabhāgbhavati
                        ||6||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The application of that <s>saṃyama</s> should be made by stages — on the mental modifications that are arranged in the distinction between gross and subtle supports. Having known each lower stage of the mind as mastered, <s>saṃyama</s> should be practiced on the next higher stage. For one who has made the lower stage his own, practicing <s>saṃyama</s> on the higher stage, becomes the recipient of fruit. || 6 ||

children.text:
sādhanapāde yogāṅgānyaṣṭāvuddiśya pañcānāṃ lakṣaṇaṃ vidhāya trayāṇāṃ kathaṃ
                        na kṛtamityāśaṅkyāha ---
children.translated_text: In the <s>Sādhanapāda</s>, having enumerated eight limbs of <s>yoga</s> and defined five, one might ask why the definition of the [remaining] three was not given there. He says—
The three are internal compared to the preceding [limbs]. || Vibhūti 7 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- pūrvebhyo yamādibhyo yogāṅgebhyaḥ pāramparyeṇa
                        samādherūpakārakebhyo dhāraṇādiyogāṅgatrayaṃ samprajñātasya
                        samādherantaraṅgaṃ samādhisvarūpaniṣpādanāt ||7||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Compared to the preceding <s>yoga</s> limbs — <s>yama</s> and the rest — which progressively contribute to <s>samādhi</s>, the triad of <s>yoga</s> limbs beginning with <s>dhāraṇā</s> is internal to <s>samprajñāta samādhi</s>, because it directly accomplishes the nature of <s>samādhi</s>. || 7 ||
He states that even this is external in relation to another <s>samādhi</s>—
Even that is external to the seedless [<s>samādhi</s>]. || Vibhūti 8 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- nirbījasya nirālambanasya śūnyabhāvanā+aparaparyāyasya
                        samādheretadapi yogāṅgatrayaṃ bahiraṅgaṃ pāramparyeṇopakārakatvāt ||8||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Even this triad of <s>yoga</s> limbs is external to <s>nirbīja samādhi</s> (seedless absorption) — the supportless [absorption], also known by the synonym '<s>śūnyabhāvanā</s>' (meditation on the void) — because it contributes to it progressively. || 8 ||

children.text:
idānīṃ yogasiddhīrvyākhyātukāmaḥ saṃyamasya viṣayaviśuddhiṃ kartuṃ krameṇa
                        pariṇāmatrayamāha ---
children.translated_text: Now, wishing to explain the <s>yoga</s> <s>siddhis</s> (accomplishments), to purify the object of <s>saṃyama</s>, he states the three types of <s>pariṇāma</s> (transformation) in sequence—

<s>Nirodhapariṇāma</s> (transformation of cessation) is the connection of the mind with the moment of cessation, in which the <s>saṃskāra</s> (impression) of emergence is overcome and the <s>saṃskāra</s> of cessation manifests. || Vibhūti 9 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- vyutthānaṃ kṣiptamūḍhavikṣiptākhyaṃ bhūmitrayam| nirodhaḥ
                        prakṛṣṭasattvasyāṅgitayā cetasaḥ pariṇāmaḥ| tābhyāṃ vyutthānanirodhābhyāṃ
                        yau janitau saṃskārau tayoryathākramam abhibhavaprādurbhāvau yadā bhavataḥ|
                        abhibhavo nyagbhūtatayā kāryakaraṇāsāmarthyenāvasthānam| prādurbhāvo
                        vartamāne+adhvanyabhivyaktarūpatayā+a+avirbhābaḥ| tadā nirodhakṣaṇe
                        cittasyobhayakṣaṇavṛttitvādanvayo yaḥ sa nirodhapariṇāma ucyate| ayamarthaḥ
                        --- yadā vyutthānasaskārarūpo dharmastirobhūto bhavati
                        nirodhasaṃskārarūpaścāvirbhavati dharmirūpatayā ca cittamubhayānvayitve+api
                        nirodhātmanā+avasthitaṃ pratīyate tadā sa nirodhapariṇāmaśabdena
                        vyavahriyate| calatvādguṇavṛttasya yadyapi cetaso niścalatvaṃ nāsti
                        tathāpyevambhūtaḥ pariṇāmaḥ sthairyamucyate ||9||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Emergence (<s>vyutthāna</s>) refers to the three levels called scattered, stupefied, and distracted. Cessation (<s>nirodha</s>) is the transformation of the mind dominated by refined <s>sattva</s>. The <s>saṃskāras</s> (impressions) generated by these two — emergence and cessation — when their respective overcoming and manifestation occur: overcoming is remaining in a state of being subdued, with inability to produce effects; manifestation is appearing with a revealed form in the present moment. Then, at the moment of cessation, the mind, being connected with both moments due to its functioning in both — that is called <s>nirodhapariṇāma</s>. The meaning is: when the <s>dharma</s> in the form of the <s>saṃskāra</s> of emergence becomes concealed and the <s>dharma</s> in the form of the <s>saṃskāra</s> of cessation manifests, and the mind, as the <s>dharmin</s> (substance), though connected with both, is apprehended as abiding in the nature of cessation — then it is designated by the term <s>nirodhapariṇāma</s>. Although, due to the restless nature of the activity of the <s>guṇas</s> (constituents), the mind has no absolute stillness, still such a transformation is called steadiness. || 9 ||
He states the fruit of that very [transformation]—
Its calm flow is due to <s>saṃskāra</s> (impression). || Vibhūti 10 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tasya cetaso niruktānnirodhasaṃskārāt praśāntavāhitā bhavati|
                        parihṛtavikṣepatayā sadṛśapravāhapariṇāmi cittaṃ bhavatītyarthaḥ ||10||
children.translated_text: Commentary: From the cessation-<s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression of cessation) described above, the peaceful flow of that mind arises. Having abandoned distraction, the mind becomes one that transforms in a continuous, uniform flow—this is the meaning. ||10||
Having described <s>nirodha-pariṇāma</s> (cessation-transformation), he states <s>samādhi-pariṇāma</s> (concentration-transformation):
The <s>samādhi-pariṇāma</s> (concentration-transformation) of the mind is the decline and rise of all-objectness and one-pointedness. ||Vibhūti 11||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- sarvārthatā calatvānnānāvidhārthagrahaṇaṃ cittasya vikṣepo
                        dharmaḥ| ekasminnevālambane sadṛśapariṇāmitaikāgratā| sā+api cittasya
                        dharmaḥ| tayoryathākramaṃ kṣayodayau sarvārthatālakṣaṇasya dharmasya
                        kṣayo+atyantābhibhava ekāgratālakṣaṇasya dharmasya
                        prādurbhāvo+abhivyaktiścittasyodriktasattvasyānvayitayā+avasthānaṃ
                        samādhipariṇāma ityucyate| pūrvasmāt pariṇāmādasyāyaṃ viśeṣaḥ --- tatra
                        saṃskāralakṣaṇayoḥ dharmayorabhibhavaprādurbhāvau pūrvasya
                        vyutthānasaṃskārarūpasya nyagbhāva uttarasya
                        nirodhasaṃskārarūpasyodbhavo+anabhibhūtatvenāvasthānam| iha tu kṣayodayāviti
                        sarvātmatārūpasya vikṣepasyātyantatiraskārādanutpattiratīte+adhvani praveśaḥ
                        kṣaya ekāgratālakṣaṇasya dharmasyodbhavo vartamāne+adhvani prakaṭatvam
                        ||11||
children.translated_text: Commentary: <s>Sarvārthatā</s> (all-objectness) is distraction—a <s>dharma</s> (property) of the mind characterized by the grasping of manifold objects due to its restlessness. One-pointedness (<s>ekāgratā</s>) is the uniform transformation regarding one and the same support. That too is a <s>dharma</s> of the mind. Of these two respectively, the decline and rise—the decline, i.e., the utter suppression, of the <s>dharma</s> characterized by all-objectness, and the rise, i.e., the manifestation, of the <s>dharma</s> characterized by one-pointedness—the continuous abiding of the mind whose <s>sattva</s> is predominant, is called <s>samādhi-pariṇāma</s>. The distinction of this from the previous transformation is as follows: there, the suppression and manifestation were of two <s>dharmas</s> characterized by <s>saṃskāras</s>—the decline of the former, which was in the form of emergence-<s>saṃskāras</s>, and the rise of the latter, which was in the form of cessation-<s>saṃskāras</s>, its abiding in an unsuppressed state. Here, however, 'decline and rise': the utter concealment of distraction in the form of all-objectness, its non-arising, its entry into the past time, is 'decline'; the rise of the <s>dharma</s> characterized by one-pointedness, its becoming manifest in the present time. ||11||
He states the third transformation—<s>ekāgratā-pariṇāma</s> (one-pointedness-transformation):
When the subsided and the arisen mental contents are similar, that is the <s>ekāgratā-pariṇāma</s> (one-pointedness-transformation) of the mind. ||Vibhūti 12||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- samāhitasyaiva cittasyaikapratyayo vṛttiviśeṣaḥ
                        śānto+atītamadhvānaṃ praviṣṭaḥ| aparastūdito vartamāne+adhvani sphuritaḥ|
                        dvāvapi samāhitacittatvena tulyāvekarūpālambanatvena sadṛśau pratyayau|
                        ubhayatrāpi samāhitasyaiva cittasyānvayitvenāvasthānam| sa ekāgratāpariṇāma
                        ityucyate ||12||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Of the mind that is indeed concentrated, one mental content—a particular modification—is 'subsided' (<s>śānta</s>), having entered into the past time. Another is 'arisen' (<s>udita</s>), manifest in the present time, having left the future time. Both, by virtue of the mind being concentrated, are similar, uniform mental contents, having the same object as support. In both cases, the mind, being concentrated, abides in continuity. That is called <s>ekāgratā-pariṇāma</s>. ||12||
Extending the pattern of mind-transformation described [above] to other [entities] as well, he says:
By this, the transformations of <s>dharma</s> (property), <s>lakṣaṇa</s> (temporal character), and <s>avasthā</s> (condition) in the elements and sense organs are explained. ||Vibhūti 13||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- etena trividhenoktena cittapariṇāmena bhūteṣu
                        sthūlasūkṣmeṣvindriyeṣu buddhikarmāntaḥkaraṇabhedenāvasthiteṣu
                        dharmalakṣaṇāvasthābhedena trividhaḥ pariṇāmo vyākhyāto+avagantavyaḥ|
                        avasthitasya dharmiṇaḥ pūrvadharmanivṛttau dharmāntarāpattirdharmapariṇāmaḥ|
                        yathā --- mṛllakṣaṇasya dharmiṇaḥ piṇḍarūpadharmaparityāgena
                        ghaṭarūpadharmāntarasvīkāro dharmapariṇāma ityucyate| lakṣṇapariṇāmo yathā
                        --- tasyaiva ghaṭasyānāgatādhvaparityāgena vartamānādhvasvīkāraḥ|
                        tatparityāgenātītādhvaparigrahaḥ| avasthāpariṇāmo yathā --- tasyaiva
                        ghaṭasya prathamadvitīyayoḥ sadṛśayoḥ kālalakṣaṇayoranvayitvena| yataśca
                        guṇavṛttirnā+apariṇamyamānā kṣaṇamapyasti ||13||
children.translated_text: Commentary: By this threefold mind-transformation that has been described, a threefold transformation in the elements—both gross and subtle—and in the sense organs—established in the divisions of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), <s>karma</s> (action), and <s>antaḥkaraṇa</s> (inner instrument)—should be understood as explained, according to the distinction of <s>dharma</s>, <s>lakṣaṇa</s>, and <s>avasthā</s>. <s>Dharma-pariṇāma</s> (property-transformation) is the assumption of a different property when the previous property of a persisting <s>dharmin</s> (substance) ceases. For example: the <s>dharmin</s> characterized as clay, by abandoning the property in the form of a lump and assuming another property in the form of a pot—that is called <s>dharma-pariṇāma</s>. <s>Lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma</s> (temporal-character-transformation) is, for example: that very pot, by leaving the future time and entering the present time; and by leaving that, entering the past time. <s>Avasthā-pariṇāma</s> (condition-transformation) is, for example: of that very pot, the first and second similar moments characterized by time, with continuity. Because the activity of the <s>guṇas</s> does not exist even for a moment without undergoing transformation. ||13||
Anticipating the question 'What is this <s>dharmin</s> (substance)?', he states the characteristic of the <s>dharmin</s>:
The <s>dharmin</s> (substance) is that which follows the subsided, arisen, and indeterminate <s>dharmas</s> (properties). ||Vibhūti 14||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- śāntā ye kṛtasvasvavyāpārā atīte+adhvani anupraviṣṭāḥ| uditā ya
                        anāgatamadhvānaṃ parityajya vartamāne+adhvani svavyāpāraṃ kurvanti|
                        avyapadeśyā ye śaktirūpeṇa sthitā vyapadeṣṭuṃ na śakyante| teṣāṃ yathāsvaṃ
                        sarvātmakatvamityevamādayo niyatakāryakāraṇarūpayogyatayāvacchinnā
                        śaktireveha dharmaśabdenābhidhīyate| taṃ trividhamapi dharmaṃ
                        yo+anupatatyanuvartate+anvayitvena svīkaroti sa
                        śāntoditāvyapadeśyadharmānupātī dharmītyucyate| yathā --- suvarṇaṃ
                        rucakarūpadharmaparityāgena svastikarūpadharmāntaraparigrahe
                        suvarṇarūpatayā+anuvartamānaṃ teṣu dharmeṣu kathaṃcidbhinneṣu dharmirūpatayā
                        sāmānyātmanā dharmarūpatayā viśeṣātmanā sthitamanvayitvenāvabhāsate
                        ||14||
children.translated_text: Commentary: 'Subsided' (<s>śānta</s>) are those that have completed their own function and entered the past time. 'Arisen' (<s>udita</s>) are those that, having left the future time, perform their function in the present time. 'Indeterminate' (<s>avyapadeśya</s>) are those that exist in the form of latent power and cannot be designated. Their respective all-pervasiveness and so forth—capacities delimited by the fitness for fixed effect-cause relationships—this is what is here meant by the word <s>dharma</s> (property). That which follows, accompanies, assumes through continuity this threefold <s>dharma</s>—that is called the <s>dharmin</s>, the one that follows the subsided, arisen, and indeterminate properties. For example: gold, when abandoning the property of bracelet form and assuming another property of <s>svastika</s> (auspicious sign) form, persists in its gold nature and, in those properties that are in some way different, appears in continuity as the <s>dharmin</s>—in its general nature—and as the properties—in their particular natures. ||14||
To remove the doubt, 'How can a single <s>dharmin</s> have many transformations?', he says:
The difference in sequence is the cause of the difference in transformation. ||Vibhūti 15||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- dharmāṇāmuktalakṣaṇānāṃ yaḥ kramastasya yat pratikṣaṇamanyatvaṃ
                        paridṛśyamānaṃ pariṇāmasyoktalakṣaṇasyānyatve nānāvidhatve heturliṅgaṃ
                        jñāpakaṃ bhavati| ayamarthaḥ --- yo+ayaṃ niyataḥ kramo
                        mṛccūrṇānmṛtpiṇḍastataḥ kapālāni tebhyaśca ghaṭa ityevaṃ kramarūpaḥ
                        paridṛśyamānaḥ pariṇāmasyā+anyatvamāvedayati| tasminneva dharmiṇi yo
                        lakṣaṇapariṇāmasyā+avasthāpariṇāmasya ca kramaḥ so+apyanenaiva nyāyena
                        pariṇāmānyatve gamako+avagantavyaḥ| sarva eva bhāvā niyatenaiva krameṇa
                        pratikṣaṇaṃ pariṇamyamānāḥ paridṛśyante| ataḥ siddhaṃ kramānyatvāt
                        pariṇāmānyatvam| sarveṣāṃ cittādīnāṃ pariṇamamānānāṃ keciddharmāḥ
                        pratyakṣeṇaivopalabhyante| yathā sukhādayaḥ saṃsthānādayaśca|
                        kecidekāntenānumānagamyāḥ| yathā dharmasaṃskāraśaktiprabhṛtayaḥ| dharmiṇaśca
                        bhinnābhinnarūpatayā sarvatrānugamaḥ ||15||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The observed difference moment by moment in the sequence of the properties with the characteristics described—that is the cause, the indicator, the informant of the difference, the variety, of the transformation described. The meaning is: this fixed sequence that is observed—from clay powder to clay lump, from that to potsherds, from those to a pot—this sequence-pattern indicates the variety of transformation. In that very <s>dharmin</s>, the sequence of <s>lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma</s> and <s>avasthā-pariṇāma</s> should be understood as indicative of the variety of transformation by the same logic. All entities are observed as undergoing transformation moment by moment in a fixed sequence. Therefore, it is established that from the difference of sequence comes the difference of transformation. Among the properties of all transforming entities like the mind, some are perceived directly—such as happiness and the like, and shapes and the like. Some are knowable solely through inference—such as merit, <s>saṃskāras</s>, latent powers, and so forth. And the <s>dharmin</s> pervades all, in its aspect as both identical and different [from its properties]. ||15||
Now, to establish the supernatural powers by way of showing the objects of the <s>saṃyama</s> (concentration) that has been described, he says:
By <s>saṃyama</s> on the three transformations, knowledge of the past and future [arises]. ||Vibhūti 16||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- dharmalakṣaṇāvasthābhedena yat pariṇāmatrayamuktaṃ tatra saṃyamāt
                        tasmin viṣaye pūrvoktasaṃyamasya karaṇādatītānāgatajñānaṃ yoginaḥ
                        samādherbhavati| idamatra tātparyam --- asmin dharmiṇyayaṃ dharma idaṃ
                        lakṣaṇamiyamavasthā cā+anāgatādadhvanaḥ sametya vartamāne+adhvani
                        svavyāpāraṃ vidhāyātītamadhvānaṃ praviśatītyevaṃ parihṛtavikṣepatayā yadā
                        saṃyamaṃ karoti tadā yatkiṃcidanutpannamatikrāntaṃ vā tat sarvaṃ yogī
                        jānāti| yataścittasya śuddhasattvaprakāśarūpatvāt
                        sarvārthagrahaṇasāmarthyamavidyādibhirvikṣepairapakriyate| yadā tu
                        taistairupāyairvikṣepāḥ parihriyante tadā nivṛttamalasyevādarśasya
                        sarvārthagrahaṇasāmarthyamekāgratābalādāvirbhavati ||16||
children.translated_text: Commentary: By <s>saṃyama</s>—i.e., by performing the previously described <s>saṃyama</s>—on the threefold transformation described according to the distinction of <s>dharma</s>, <s>lakṣaṇa</s>, and <s>avasthā</s>, knowledge of the past and future arises from <s>samādhi</s> for the yogin. The purport here is: 'In this <s>dharmin</s>, this is the <s>dharma</s>, this is the temporal character, this is the condition—from the future time, having arrived in the present time and performed its function, it enters the past time'—when, with distraction removed, one performs <s>saṃyama</s> in this manner, then whatever has not yet arisen or has already passed—the yogin knows all of that. Because the mind, being of the nature of pure <s>sattva</s>-radiance, has the capacity to grasp all objects, [but] this is obstructed by distractions such as <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) and the rest. But when those distractions are removed by those various means, then, like a mirror whose impurity has been removed, the capacity to grasp all objects manifests through the power of one-pointedness. ||16||
He states another supernatural power:
Due to the mutual superimposition of word, meaning, and cognition, there is confusion; by <s>saṃyama</s> on their distinction, knowledge of the sounds of all beings [arises]. ||Vibhūti 17||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- śabdaḥ śrotrendriyagrāhyo niyatakramavarṇātmā
                        niyataikārthapratipattyavacchinnaḥ| yadi vā kramarahitasphoṭātmā
                        śāstrasaṃskṛtabuddhigrāhyaḥ

|
                        ubhayathā+api padarūpo vākyarūpaśca tayorekārthapratipattau sāmarthyāt|
                        artho jātiguṇakriyādiḥ| pratyayo jñānaṃ viṣayākārā buddhivṛttiḥ| eṣāṃ
                        śabdārthajñānānāṃ vyavahāre itaretarādhyāsādbhinnānāmapi
                        buddhyekarūpatāsampādanāt saṃkīrṇatvam| tathāhi --- gāmānayetyukte
                        kaścidgolakṣaṇamarthaṃ gotvajātyavacchinnaṃ sāsnādimat piṇḍarūpaṃ śabdaṃ ca
                        tadvācakaṃ jñānaṃ ca tadgrāhakamabhedenaivādhyavasyati na tvasya gośabdo
                        vācako+ayaṃ gośabdasya vācyastayoridaṃ grāhakaṃ jñānamiti bhedena
                        vyavaharati| tathāhi --- ko+ayamarthaḥ ko+ayaṃ śabdaḥ kimidaṃ jñānamiti
                        pṛṣṭaḥ sarvatraikarūpamevottaraṃ dadāti gauriti| sa yadyekarūpatāṃ na
                        pratipadyate kathamekarūpamuttaraṃ prayacchati| evaṃ tasminnavasthite
                        yo+ayaṃ
children.translated_text: In both views, it functions as both word and sentence, due to its capacity for conveying a single meaning. <s>Artha</s> (meaning) is universal, attribute, action, and so forth. <s>Pratyaya</s> (cognition) is knowledge, a mental modification in the form of the object. In ordinary usage, these—word, meaning, and cognition—though distinct, are confused due to their mutual superimposition, because the intellect makes them appear as one. Thus, when told 'Bring the cow,' someone understands the meaning characterized by the cow—endowed with dewlap and so forth, delimited by the universal 'cowness,' in a concrete form—and the word that denotes it, and the cognition that grasps it, as identical, without distinction. He does not distinguish: 'This is the denoting cow-word, this is the denoted [meaning] of the cow-word, this is the cognition that grasps them.' Thus, when asked 'What is this meaning? What is this word? What is this cognition?' he gives in every case the same uniform answer: 'cow.' If he did not apprehend them as identical, how would he give a uniform answer? Thus, when this [confusion] persists,

children.text: pā0 ekasmin viṣaye yo+ayam| etasmin sthite yo+ayam vā

pravibhāga idaṃ śabdasya tattvaṃ yadvācakatvaṃ nāma idamarthasya
                        yadvācyatvamidaṃ jñānasya yat prakāśakatvamiti pravibhāgaṃ vidhāya tasmin
                        pravibhāge yaḥ saṃyamaṃ karoti tasya sarveṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ
                        mṛgapakṣisarīsṛpādīnāṃ yadrutaṃ yaḥ śabdastatra jñānamutpadyate|
                        anenaivābhiprāyeṇa tena prāṇināyaṃ śabdaḥ samuccārita iti sarvaṃ jānāti
                        ||17||
children.translated_text: the distinction—'this is the nature of the word, namely its denotative capacity; this is the nature of the meaning, namely its being denoted; this is the nature of cognition, namely its illuminating capacity'—having made this distinction, one who performs <s>saṃyama</s> on that distinction gains knowledge of the sounds of all beings—animals, birds, reptiles, and so forth—whatever utterance, whatever sound they make. By this very intention, he knows everything: 'This sound was uttered by that creature with this [meaning].' ||17||

Commentary: <s>Śabda</s> (word) is what is grasped by the ear-organ, consisting of letters in a fixed sequence, delimited by the capacity to convey a fixed meaning. Or alternatively, it is of the nature of <s>sphoṭa</s> (meaning-unit), free from sequence, grasped by the intellect refined by grammar.
He states another supernatural power:
By direct perception of <s>saṃskāras</s> (latent impressions), knowledge of previous births [arises]. ||Vibhūti 18||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- dvividhāścittasya vāsanārūpāḥ saṃskārāḥ| kecit
                        smṛtimātrotpādanaphalāḥ kecijjātyāyurbhogalakṣaṇā vipākahetavo yathā
                        dharmādharmākhyāḥ| teṣu saṃskāreṣu yadā saṃyamaṃ karoti evaṃ mayā
                        so+artho+anubhūta evaṃ mayā sā kriyā niṣpāditeti pūrvavṛttamanusandadhāno
                        bhāvayanneva prabodhakamantareṇodbuddhasaṃskāraḥ sarvamatītaṃ smarati|
                        krameṇa sākṣātkṛteṣūdbuddheṣu saṃskāreṣu pūrvajanmāntarānubhūtānapi jātyādīn
                        pratyakṣeṇa paśyati ||18||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The <s>saṃskāras</s> of the mind, in the form of <s>vāsanās</s> (latent tendencies), are of two kinds. Some have only the production of memory as their fruit. Some are causes of fruition (<s>vipāka</s>) characterized by birth, lifespan, and enjoyment—such as those called merit and demerit. When one performs <s>saṃyama</s> on those <s>saṃskāras</s>, connecting the past events—'I experienced such-and-such an object, I performed such-and-such an action'—meditating in this very manner, when the <s>saṃskāras</s> are awakened without an external trigger, one remembers everything that is past. When, through sequential direct perception, the <s>saṃskāras</s> are awakened, one sees directly even the births and so forth experienced in previous lives. ||18||
He states another supernatural power:
Knowledge of another's mind [arises from <s>saṃyama</s>] on the mental content. ||Vibhūti 19||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- pratyayasya paracittasya kenacinmukharāgādinā liṅgena gṛhītasya
                        yadā saṃyamaṃ karoti tadā parakīyacittasya jñānamutpadyate sarāgamasya
                        cittaṃ vītarāgaṃ veti| paracittagatān sarvānapi dharmān jānātītyarthaḥ
                        ||19||
children.translated_text: Commentary: When one performs <s>saṃyama</s> on the mental content of another's mind, grasped through some indicator such as facial complexion and the like, then knowledge of another's mind arises—'This person's mind has attachment' or 'is free from attachment.' One knows all the properties present in another's mind—this is the meaning. ||19||
He states the specific knowledge regarding this very knowledge of another's mind:
But that [knowledge] is not together with its support, because [the support] has not become the object [of <s>saṃyama</s>]. ||Vibhūti 20||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tasya parasya yaccittaṃ tat sālambanaṃ svakīyenā+a+alambanena
                        sahitaṃ na śakyate jñātumālambanasya kenacilliṅgenāviṣayīkṛtatvāt| liṅgāddhi
                        cittamātraṃ parasyāvagataṃ na tu nīlaviṣayamasya cittaṃ pītaviṣayamiti vā|
                        yacca na gṛhītaṃ tatra saṃyamasya kartumaśakyatvānna bhavati paracittasya yo
                        viṣayastatra jñānam| tasmāt parakīyacittaṃ nā+a+alambanasahitaṃ gṛhyate
                        tasyā+a+alambanasyā+agṛhītatvāt| cittadharmāḥ punargṛhyanta eva| yadā tu
                        kimanenā+a+alambitamiti praṇidhānaṃ karoti tadā tatsaṃyamāttadviṣayamapi
                        jñānamutpadyata eva ||20||
children.translated_text: Commentary: His, the other person's, mind—together with its support (<s>ālambana</s>)—cannot be known, because the support has not been made an object by any sign. For from a sign, only another's bare mind is understood, not 'his mind has a blue object or a yellow object.' And since one cannot perform <s>saṃyama</s> on what has not been grasped, there is no knowledge of the object that is the content of another's mind. Therefore, another's mind is not grasped together with its support, because that support has not been grasped. But the mental properties are indeed grasped. However, when one makes the effort 'what has this mind taken as its object?', then from <s>saṃyama</s> on that, knowledge even of that object arises. ||20||
He states another supernatural power:
From <s>saṃyama</s> on the form of the body, when the power of being grasped by the eye is suspended, and the connection with the eye's light is broken, invisibility [results]. ||Vibhūti 21||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- kāyaḥ śarīraṃ tasya rūpaṃ cakṣurgrāhyo guṇastasminnastyasmin kāye
                        rūpamiti saṃyamāttasya rūpasya cakṣurgrāhyatvarūpā yā śaktistasyāḥ stambhe
                        bhāvanāvaśāt pratibandhe cakṣuṣprakāśāsaṃyoge cakṣuṣaḥ prakāśaḥ
                        sattvadharmastasyā+asaṃyoge tadgrahaṇavyāpārābhāve yogino+antardhānaṃ
                        bhavati| na kenacidasau dṛśyata ityarthaḥ| etenaiva
                        rūpāntardhānopāyapradarśanena śabdādīnāṃ śrotrādigrāhyāṇāmantardhānamuktaṃ
                        veditavyam ||21||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The body (<s>kāya</s>) is the physical frame. Its form (<s>rūpa</s>) is the quality graspable by the eye—it exists in this body, thus 'the body has form.' From <s>saṃyama</s> on that form, when the power of the form to be grasped by the eye—its graspability—is suspended, obstructed through the force of meditation, and there is disconnection from the eye's light—the eye's light being the <s>sattva</s>-property—when there is its disconnection, absence of the operation of grasping, the <s>yogin</s>'s invisibility occurs. He is not seen by anyone—this is the meaning. By this very demonstration of the means of invisibility of form, the invisibility of sounds and other qualities grasped by the ear and other senses should be understood as stated. ||21||
He states another supernatural power:

children.text:
sopakramaṃ nirupakramaṃ ca karma tatsaṃyamādaparāntajñānamariṣṭebhyo vā
                        ||vibhūti 22||
children.translated_text: <s>Karma</s> (action) is of two kinds—<s>sopakrama</s> (with onset) and <s>nirupakrama</s> (without onset). From <s>saṃyama</s> on that, knowledge of death [arises], or from portents. ||Vibhūti 22||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- āyurvipākaṃ yat pūrvakṛtaṃ karma taddviprakāraṃ sopakramaṃ
                        nirupakramaṃ ca| tatra sopakramaṃ yat phalajananāya sahopakrameṇa
                        kāryakaraṇābhimukhyena vartate yathoṣṇapradeśe prasāritārdravāsaḥ śīghrameva
                        śuṣyati| uktaviparītaṃ nirupakramaṃ yathā tadevārdravāsaḥ
                        saṃvartitamanuṣṇapradeśe cireṇa śuṣyati| tasmin dvividhe karmaṇi yaḥ
                        saṃyamaṃ karoti --- kiṃ mama karma śīghravipākaṃ ciravipākaṃ vā --- evaṃ
                        dhyānadārḍhyādaparāntajñānamasyotpadyate| aparāntaḥ
                        śarīraviyogastasmiñjñānamamuṣmin kāle+amuṣmin deśe mama śarīraviyogo
                        bhaviṣyatīti niḥsaṃśayaṃ jānāti| ariṣṭebhyo vā| ariṣṭāni trividhāni|
                        ādhyātmikādhibhautikādhidaivikāni| tatrādhyātmikāni --- pihitakaraṇaḥ
                        koṣṭhyasya vāyorghoṣaṃ na śṛṇotītyevamādīni| ādhibhautikāni ---
                        akasmādvikṛtapuruṣadarśanādīni| ādhidaivikāni --- akāṇḍa eva draṣṭumaśakyāni
                        svargādipadārthadarśanādīni| tebhyaḥ śarīraviyogakālaṃ jānāti|
                        yadyapyayogināmapyariṣṭebhyaḥ prāyeṇa tajjñānamutpadyate tathāpi teṣāṃ
                        sāmānyākāreṇa tat saṃśayarūpaṃ yogināṃ punarniyatadeśakālatayā
                        pratyakṣavadavyabhicāri ||22||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The <s>karma</s> previously performed that ripens as lifespan is of two kinds—<s>sopakrama</s> (with onset) and <s>nirupakrama</s> (without onset). Among these, <s>sopakrama</s> is that which operates together with its onset, with its cause-effect direction facing toward the production of fruit—just as wet cloth spread in a hot place dries very quickly. The opposite is <s>nirupakrama</s>—just as that same wet cloth, rolled up in a non-hot place, dries slowly. When one performs <s>saṃyama</s> on this twofold <s>karma</s>—'Is my <s>karma</s> quick-ripening or slow-ripening?'—thus, through the firmness of meditation, knowledge of death (<s>aparānta</s>) arises. <s>Aparānta</s> is the separation from the body; knowledge thereof: 'at such a time, in such a place, my separation from the body will occur'—one knows without doubt. 'Or from portents.' Portents (<s>ariṣṭas</s>) are threefold: <s>ādhyātmika</s> (pertaining to the self), <s>ādhibhautika</s> (pertaining to elements), and <s>ādhidaivika</s> (pertaining to the divine). Among these, <s>ādhyātmika</s>: one with closed senses does not hear the sound of the internal wind, and so forth. <s>Ādhibhautika</s>: the sudden vision of deformed persons, and so forth. <s>Ādhidaivika</s>: the sudden, unseasonable vision of things like heaven and other objects that cannot ordinarily be seen. From these, one knows the time of separation from the body. Although even for non-yogins, knowledge of death generally arises from portents, for them it is general in nature and doubtful; for yogins, however, it is specific as to place and time, unerring like direct perception. ||22||
In order to demonstrate the supernatural powers accomplished through preparatory practice, he says:
From [<s>saṃyama</s>] on <s>maitrī</s> (friendliness) and so forth, powers [arise]. ||Vibhūti 23||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- maitrīkaruṇāmuditopekṣāsu yo vihitasaṃyamastadbalāni tāsāṃ
                        maitryādīnāṃ sambandhīni prādurbhavanti| maitrīkaruṇāmuditopekṣāstathā+asya
                        prakarṣaṃ gacchanti yathā sarvasya mitratvādikamay+aṃ pratipadyate
                        ||23||
children.translated_text: Commentary: In <s>maitrī</s> (friendliness), <s>karuṇā</s> (compassion), <s>muditā</s> (joy), and <s>upekṣā</s> (equanimity)—for one who has performed <s>saṃyama</s> on these, the powers related to <s>maitrī</s> and the rest manifest. His <s>maitrī</s>, <s>karuṇā</s>, <s>muditā</s>, and <s>upekṣā</s> reach such excellence that everyone perceives friendliness and so forth toward him. ||23||
He states another supernatural power:
From [<s>saṃyama</s>] on strengths, the strength of an elephant and so forth [arises]. ||Vibhūti 24||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- hastyādisambandhiṣu baleṣu kṛtasaṃyamasya tadbalāni
                        hastyādibalānyāvirbhavanti| tadayamarthaḥ --- yasmin hastibale vāyuvege
                        siṃhavīrye vā tanmayībhāvenā+ayaṃ saṃyamaṃ karoti tattatsāmarthyayuktaṃ
                        sattvamasya

children.translated_text: manifests for him—this is the meaning. ||24||

Commentary: For one who has performed <s>saṃyama</s> on the strengths related to elephants and so forth, the strengths of elephants and such manifest. This is the meaning: when he performs <s>saṃyama</s> by identifying with elephant strength, wind speed, or lion courage, the power endowed with that respective capacity
He states another supernatural power:
From the projection of the light of higher perception, knowledge of the subtle, the hidden, and the distant [arises]. ||Vibhūti 25||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- pravṛttirviṣayavatī jyotiṣmatī ca prāguktā (1|35-36)| tasyā ya
                        ālokaḥ sāttvikaprakāśastasya nikhileṣu viṣayeṣu nyāsāt tadvāsitānāṃ
                        viṣayāṇāṃ bhāvanātaḥ santaḥkaraṇeṣu indriyeṣu ca prakṛṣṭaśaktimāpanneṣu
                        susūkṣmasya paramāṇvādervyavahitasya bhūmyantargatasya
                        nidhānāderviprakṛṣṭasya mervaparapārśvavartino rasāyanāderjñānamutpadyate
                        ||25||
children.translated_text: Commentary: <s>Pravṛtti</s> (activity)—that directed toward objects and the luminous one—has been previously stated (1.35-36). Its light (<s>āloka</s>), the <s>sāttvika</s> (lucid) illumination—from its projection upon all objects, from the meditation on objects pervaded by it—when the inner instruments and senses have attained supreme power—knowledge arises of the extremely subtle such as atoms, the hidden such as treasures buried under the earth, and the distant such as elixirs located on the far side of <s>Meru</s>. ||25||
He states another supernatural power of the same kind:
From <s>saṃyama</s> on the sun, knowledge of the worlds [arises]. ||Vibhūti 26||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- sūrye prakāśamaye yaḥ saṃyamaḥ karoti tasya saptasu
                        bhūrbhuvaḥsvaḥprabhṛtiṣu lokeṣu yāni bhuvanāni tattatsanniveśabhāñji purāṇi

teṣu yathāvadasya jñānamutpadyate| pūrvasmin
                        sūtre sāttvikaprakāśa ālambanatayoktaḥ| iha tu bhautika iti viśeṣaḥ
                        ||26||
children.translated_text: knowledge of those arises as they truly are. In the previous <s>sūtra</s>, <s>sāttvika</s> (lucid) light was stated as the support. Here, however, the distinction is that it is <s>bhautika</s> (physical). ||26||

Commentary: For one who performs <s>saṃyama</s> on the sun, which is full of light, in the seven worlds beginning with <s>Bhūḥ</s>, <s>Bhuvaḥ</s>, <s>Svaḥ</s>, and so forth, the regions (<s>bhuvanas</s>) that are cities endowed with their respective arrangements—
Through the medium of another physical light as support, he states another supernatural power:
From [<s>saṃyama</s>] on the moon, knowledge of the arrangement of the stars [arises]. ||Vibhūti 27||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tārāṇāṃ jyotiṣāṃ yo vyūho viśiṣṭaḥ sanniveśastasya candre
                        kṛtasaṃyamasya jñānamutpadyate| sūryaprakāśena hatatejaskatvāttārāṇāṃ
                        sūryasaṃyamāttajjñānaṃ na śakyaṃ bhavitumarhatīti pṛthagupāyo+abhihitaḥ
                        ||27||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The arrangement of the stars (<s>tārās</s>), the luminaries—that is, their particular spatial configuration—for one who has performed <s>saṃyama</s> on the moon, knowledge of that arises. Since the stars have their brilliance outshone by the sun's light, knowledge of them cannot come from <s>saṃyama</s> on the sun—therefore a separate means has been stated. ||27||
He states another supernatural power:
From [<s>saṃyama</s>] on the pole star, knowledge of their movements [arises]. ||Vibhūti 28||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- dhruve niścale jyotiṣāṃ pradhāne kṛtasaṃyamasya tāsāṃ tārāṇāṃ yā
                        gatiḥ pratyekaṃ niyatakālā niyatadeśā ca tasyā jñānamutpadyate --- iyaṃ
                        tārā+ayaṃ graha iyatā kālenā+amuṃ rāśimidaṃ nakṣatraṃ yāsyatīti sarvaṃ
                        jānāti| idaṃ kālajñānasya phalamityuktaṃ bhavati ||28||
children.translated_text: Commentary: On the pole star (<s>dhruva</s>), the unmoving chief among the luminaries—for one who has performed <s>saṃyama</s>—knowledge of the movement of those stars arises, each having a fixed time and fixed location: 'This star, this planet, will go to such a zodiac sign, to such a <s>nakṣatra</s> (lunar mansion), in such a time'—one knows everything. This is stated to be the fruit of knowledge of time. ||28||
Having described the external powers, he begins to describe the internal powers:
From [<s>saṃyama</s>] on the navel <s>cakra</s> (wheel/center), knowledge of the arrangement of the body [arises]. ||Vibhūti 29||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- śarīramadhyavarti nābhisaṃjñakaṃ yat ṣoḍaśāraṃ cakraṃ tasmin
                        kṛtasaṃyamasya yoginaḥ kāyagato yo+asau vyūho
                        viśiṣṭarasamaladhātunāḍyādīnāmavasthānaṃ tatra jñānamutpadyate| idamuktaṃ
                        bhavati --- nābhicakraṃ śarīramadhyavarti sarvataḥ prasṛtānāṃ nāḍyādīnāṃ
                        mūlabhūtam| atastatra kṛtāvadhānasya samagrasanniveśo yathāvadābhāti
                        ||29||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The sixteen-spoked <s>cakra</s> called the navel, situated in the center of the body—for the <s>yogin</s> who has performed <s>saṃyama</s> on that, knowledge arises of the arrangement within the body—the configuration of essences, wastes, bodily constituents (<s>dhātus</s>), <s>nāḍīs</s> (channels), and so forth. This amounts to saying: the navel <s>cakra</s>, situated in the center of the body, is the root of all the <s>nāḍīs</s> and such extending in all directions. Therefore, for one who has focused attention there, the entire configuration shines forth as it truly is. ||29||
He states another supernatural power:
From [<s>saṃyama</s>] on the throat-pit, cessation of hunger and thirst [results]. ||Vibhūti 30||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- kaṇṭhe gale kūpaḥ kaṇṭhakūpaḥ| jihvāmūle jihvātantoradhastāt kūpa
                        iva kūpo gartākārapradeśaḥ prāṇāderyatsamparkāt kṣutpipāsādayaḥ
                        prādurbhavanti tasmin kṛtasaṃyamasya yoginaḥ kṣutpipāsādayo nivartante|
                        ghaṇṭikādhastāt srotasā dhāryamāṇe tasmin bhāvite bhavatyevaṃvidhā siddhiḥ
                        ||30||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The pit in the throat (<s>kaṇṭhakūpa</s>)—the pit-like hollow region below the root of the tongue, below the palate—from whose contact with <s>prāṇa</s> and other vital airs, hunger, thirst, and the like arise—for the <s>yogin</s> who has performed <s>saṃyama</s> on that, hunger, thirst, and the like cease. When the current below the uvula (<s>ghaṇṭikā</s>) is held and meditated upon, such a supernatural power arises. ||30||
He states another supernatural power:
From [<s>saṃyama</s>] on the <s>kūrma-nāḍī</s> (tortoise channel), steadiness [arises]. ||Vibhūti 31||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- kaṇṭhakūpasyādhastādyā kūrmākhyā nāḍī tasyāṃ kṛtasaṃyamasya
                        cetasaḥ sthairyamutpadyate| tatsthānamanupraviṣṭasya cañcalatā na
                        bhavatītyarthaḥ| yadi vā kāyasya sthairyamutpadyate na kenacit spandayituṃ
                        śakyata ityarthaḥ ||31||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The <s>nāḍī</s> (channel) called <s>kūrma</s> (tortoise), located below the throat-pit—for one who has performed <s>saṃyama</s> on it, steadiness of mind arises. One who has entered that place does not experience restlessness—this is the meaning. Or alternatively, steadiness of the body arises—one cannot be made to tremble by anyone—this is the meaning. ||31||
He states another supernatural power:
From [<s>saṃyama</s>] on the light in the crown of the head, vision of the <s>Siddhas</s> (perfected beings) [arises]. ||Vibhūti 32||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- śiraḥkapāle brahmarandhrākhye chidre prakāśādhāratvājjyotiṣi|
                        yathā gṛhābhyantarasthasya maṇeḥ prasarantī prabhā kuñcitākāreva
                        sarvapradeśe saṃghaṭate tathā hṛdayasthaḥ sāttvikaḥ prakāśaḥ prasṛtastatra
                        sampiṇḍitatvaṃ bhajate| tatra kṛtasaṃyamasya ye
                        dyāvāpṛthivyorantarālavartinaḥ siddhā divyāḥ
                        puruṣāsteṣāmitaraprāṇibhiradṛśyānām tasya darśanaṃ bhavati| tān paśyati
                        taiśca sa sambhāṣata ityarthaḥ ||32||
children.translated_text: Commentary: In the skull, at the aperture called <s>brahmarandhra</s> (the opening of <s>Brahman</s>), which is the seat of light—just as the radiance of a jewel situated within a house, spreading out, converges in a curved form at every point, so the <s>sāttvika</s> (lucid) light situated in the heart, having spread, becomes concentrated there. For one who has performed <s>saṃyama</s> on that, the <s>Siddhas</s>—divine beings dwelling in the space between heaven and earth, invisible to other beings—he gains vision of them. He sees them and converses with them—this is the meaning. ||32||
He states the means to omniscience:
Or, from <s>prātibha</s> (intuitive knowledge), everything [is known]. ||Vibhūti 33||

children.text:
jñānaṃ pratibhā| tasyāṃ saṃyame
                        kriyamāṇe prātibhaṃ vivekakhyāteḥ pūrvabhāvi tārakaṃ jñānamudeti|
                        yathodeṣyataḥ savituḥ pūrvaṃ prabhā prādurbhavati tadvadvivekakhyāteḥ pūrvaṃ
                        tārakaṃ sarvaviṣayaṃ jñānamutpadyate| tasmin sati saṃyamāntarānapekṣaḥ
                        sarvaṃ jānātītyarthaḥ ||33||
