children.translated_text: that is <s>pratibhā</s> (intuition). When <s>saṃyama</s> is performed on it, intuitive knowledge arises—the <s>tāraka</s> (saving, liberating) knowledge that precedes <s>vivekakhyāti</s> (discriminative discernment). Just as light appears before the sun rises, so before <s>vivekakhyāti</s>, the <s>tāraka</s> knowledge arises, having all things as its objects. When that exists, one knows everything without recourse to any other <s>saṃyama</s>—this is the meaning. ||33||
Commentary: Knowledge that is spontaneous, born of mere mind, non-deceptive, arising instantly—
He states another supernatural power:
From [<s>saṃyama</s>] on the heart, knowledge of the mind [arises]. ||Vibhūti 34||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- hṛdayaṃ śarīrasya pradeśaviśeṣaḥ|
                        tasminnadhomukhasvalpapuṇḍarīkābhyantare+antaḥkaraṇasattvasya sthānam| tatra
                        kṛtasaṃyamasya svaparacittajñānamutpadyate| svacittagatāḥ sarvā vāsanāḥ
                        paracittagatāṃśca rāgādīñjānātītyarthaḥ ||34||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The heart (<s>hṛdaya</s>) is a particular region of the body. Within it, inside a small downward-facing lotus, is the seat of the <s>sattva</s> (lucidity) of the inner instrument (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>). For one who has performed <s>saṃyama</s> on that, knowledge of one's own and others' minds arises. One knows all the <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions) present in one's own mind, and the <s>rāga</s> (attachment) and other emotions present in others' minds—this is the meaning. ||34||
He states another supernatural power:

Experience (<s>bhoga</s>) is a cognition that does not distinguish between <s>sattva</s> (lucidity) and <s>Puruṣa</s> (the Self), which are utterly distinct. From <s>saṃyama</s> on what exists for its own sake, as opposed to what exists for another's sake, knowledge of <s>Puruṣa</s> [arises]. ||Vibhūti 35||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- sattvaṃ prakāśasukhātmakaḥ prādhānikaḥ pariṇāmaviśeṣaḥ| puruṣo
                        bhoktā+adhiṣṭhātṛrūpaḥ|
                        tayoratyantāsaṃkīrṇayorbhogyabhoktṛrūpatvādacetanacetanatvācca bhinnayoryaḥ
                        pratyayasyāviśeṣo bhedenāpratibhāsanaṃ tasmāt sattvasyaiva kartṛtāpratyayena
                        yā sukhaduḥkhasaṃvit sa bhogaḥ| sattvasya svārthanairapekṣyeṇa parārthaḥ
                        puruṣārthanimittaḥ| tasmādanyo yaḥ svārthaḥ puruṣasvarūpamātrālambanaḥ
                        parityaktāhaṃkārasattve yā cicchāyāsaṃkrāntistatra kṛtasaṃyamasya
                        puruṣaviṣayaṃ jñānamutpadyate| tatra tadevaṃ rūpaṃ svālambanaṃ jñānaṃ
                        sattvaniṣṭhaṃ purūṣo

jānātītyarthaḥ|
                        na punaḥ puruṣo jñātā jñānasya viṣayabhāvamāpadyate
                        jñeyatvāpatterjñātṛjñeyatvayoratyantavirodhāt ||35||
children.translated_text: this is the meaning. But <s>Puruṣa</s>, the knower, does not become an object of knowledge, for the attainment of being a knowable object would contradict the absolute opposition between knower and knowable. ||35||

Commentary: <s>Sattva</s> is the specific transformation of <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial nature) whose nature is luminosity and happiness. <s>Puruṣa</s> is the experiencer, of the nature of a presider. For these two, which are utterly unmixed, of the nature of enjoyed and enjoyer, of the nature of unconscious and conscious, and thus distinct—the non-distinction of cognition, the non-appearance as different—therefore, through the cognition of agency belonging to <s>sattva</s> alone, the experience of happiness and suffering constitutes enjoyment (<s>bhoga</s>). The 'for the sake of another' (<s>parārtha</s>) of <s>sattva</s> is its purpose for <s>Puruṣa</s>, without regard for its own interest. That which is other than this, 'for its own sake' (<s>svārtha</s>), has as its sole object the essential nature of <s>Puruṣa</s>; for one who has performed <s>saṃyama</s> (concentration) on the <s>sattva</s> in which ego has been relinquished and the reflection of consciousness has been transmitted—knowledge pertaining to <s>Puruṣa</s> arises. Therein, <s>Puruṣa</s> knows that very self-referential knowledge established in <s>sattva</s>,
He states the fruit of this very <s>saṃyama</s>:

From that arise the <s>prātibha</s> (intuitive), <s>śrāvaṇa</s> (auditory), <s>vedanā</s> (tactile), <s>ādarśa</s> (visual), <s>āsvāda</s> (gustatory), and <s>vārtā</s> (olfactory) [knowledges]. ||Vibhūti 36||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tataḥ puruṣasaṃyamādabhyasyamānādvyutthitasyāpi jñānāni jāyante|
                        tatra prātibhaṃ pūrvoktaṃ jñānaṃ tasyāvirbhavanāt sūkṣmādikamarthaṃ paśyati|
                        śrāvaṇaṃ śrotrendriyajaṃ jñānaṃ tasmācca prakṛṣṭaṃ divyaṃ śabdaṃ jānāti|
                        vedanā sparśendriyajaṃ jñānaṃ vedyate+anayeti kṛtvā tāntrikyā saṃjñayā
                        vyavahriyate| tasmāddivyasparśaviṣayaṃ jñānaṃ samupajāyate|
                        ādarśaścakṣurindriyajaṃ jñānam| ā samantāddṛśyate+anubhūyate rūpamaneneti
                        kṛtvā tasya prakarṣāddivyaṃ rūpajñānamutpadyate| āsvādo rasanendriyajaṃ
                        jñānam| āsvādyate+aneneti kṛtvā tasmin prakṛṣṭe divye rase saṃvidupajāyate|
                        vārtā gandhasaṃvit| vṛttiśabdena tāntrikyā paribhāṣayā ghrāṇendriyamucyate|
                        vartate gandhaviṣaye iti vṛtterghrāṇendriyājjātā vārtā gandhasaṃvit| tasyāṃ
                        prakṛṣyamānāyāṃ divyagandho+anubhūyate ||36||
children.translated_text: Commentary: From that <s>saṃyama</s> on <s>Puruṣa</s>, as it is practiced, knowledges arise even for one who has emerged [from <s>samādhi</s>]. Among these: <s>prātibha</s> is the knowledge previously described; from its manifestation, one perceives subtle and other objects. <s>Śrāvaṇa</s> is knowledge born of the auditory sense organ; from that, in its heightened state, one knows divine sounds. <s>Vedanā</s> is knowledge born of the tactile sense organ—it is so designated by the tantric terminology because 'by this one perceives.' From that arises knowledge pertaining to divine touch. <s>Ādarśa</s> is knowledge born of the visual sense organ—because 'form is completely seen and experienced by this'; from its intensification, knowledge of divine form arises. <s>Āsvāda</s> is knowledge born of the gustatory sense organ—because 'by this one tastes'; when that is intensified, awareness of divine taste arises. <s>Vārtā</s> is the perception of scent; by the tantric terminology, the word 'vṛtti' designates the olfactory sense organ—because 'it functions in the domain of scent.' Born from the olfactory organ, <s>vārtā</s> is the perception of scent; when that is intensified, divine scent is experienced. ||36||
He states the domain-distinction of these specific fruits:
These are obstacles in <s>samādhi</s>, but accomplishments in the outward-turned state. ||Vibhūti 37||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- te prākpratipāditāḥ phalaviśeṣāḥ samādheḥ prakarṣe gacchata
                        upasargā upadravā vighnāḥ| tatra harṣasmayādikaraṇena

samādhiḥ śithilībhavati| vyutthāne tu
                        punarvyavahāradaśāyāṃ viśiṣṭaphaladāyakatvāt siddhayo bhavanti ||37||
children.translated_text: <s>samādhi</s> becomes loosened. But in the outward-turned state, in the condition of ordinary activity, because they bestow distinguished fruits, they become <s>siddhis</s> (accomplishments). ||37||
Commentary: These previously described specific fruits are obstacles, hindrances, impediments when <s>samādhi</s> reaches its culmination. For by causing elation, pride, and the like,
He states another <s>siddhi</s>:
Through the loosening of the cause of bondage and through the knowledge of the channels of the mind, [one achieves] entering another's body. ||Vibhūti 38||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- vyāpakatvādātmacittayorniyatakarmavaśādeva śarīrāntargatayoreva
                        bhoktṛbhogyabhāvena yat saṃvedanamupajāyate sa eva śarīrabandha ityucyate|
                        tadyadā samādhivaśādbandhakāraṇaṃ dharmādharmākhyaṃ śithilaṃ bhavati
                        tānavamāpadyate| cittasya ca yo+asau pracāro hṛdayapraveśādindriyadvāreṇa
                        viṣayābhimukhyena prasarastasya saṃvedanaṃ jñānam --- iyaṃ cittavahā nāḍī|
                        anayā cittaṃ vahati| iyaṃ ca prāṇādivahābhyo

nāḍībhyo vilakṣaṇeti --- svaparaśarīrayoryadā saṃcāraṃ jānāti tadā
                        parakīyaṃ mṛtaṃ jīvaccharīraṃ vā cittasañcāradvāreṇa praviśati| cittaṃ ca
                        paraśarīre praviśadindriyāṇyapyanuvartante madhukararājamiva makṣikāḥ| atha
                        paraśarīrapraviṣṭo yogī svaśārīravat tena sarvaṃ vyavaharati| yato
                        vyāpakayościttapuruṣayorbhogasaṅkoce kāraṇaṃ karma taccet samādhinā kṣiptaṃ
                        tadā svātantryāt sarvatraiva bhoganiṣpattiḥ ||38||
children.translated_text: when one knows the course in both one's own and another's body, then one enters another's body, whether dead or living, through the channel of the mind's movement. And when the mind enters another's body, the senses also follow, like bees following their queen. Then the yogin who has entered another's body acts through it in all ways, just as with his own body. Since for the all-pervading mind and <s>Puruṣa</s>, <s>karma</s> is the cause that restricts enjoyment—if that is cast off through <s>samādhi</s>, then by one's own freedom, the accomplishment of enjoyment manifests everywhere. ||38||

Commentary: Because the self and the mind are pervading, it is only by the force of specific <s>karma</s> that they dwell within particular bodies; the experience that arises as enjoyer and enjoyed—that itself is called the bondage to the body. When, through the force of <s>samādhi</s>, the cause of bondage, known as merit and demerit, becomes loosened and attenuated; and when there is knowledge of the mind's channel—its movement through the entry point of the heart and through the doors of the senses toward objects, its course—'this is the channel that carries the mind; through this the mind moves; and this is different from the channels that carry <s>prāṇa</s> and the other [vital airs]'—
He states another <s>siddhi</s>:
Through mastery of <s>udāna</s>, non-contact with water, mud, thorns, and the like, and ascension. ||Vibhūti 39||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- samastānāmindriyāṇāṃ tuṣajvālāvadyā yugapadutthitā vṛttiḥ sā
                        jīvanaśabdavācyā| tasyāḥ kriyābhedāt prāṇāpānādisaṃjñābhirvyapadeśaḥ| tatra
                        hṛdayānmukhanāsikādvāreṇa vāyoḥ prāyaṇāt prāṇa ityucyate| nābhideśāt
                        pādāṅguṣṭhaparyantamapanayanādapānaḥ| nābhideśaṃ pariveṣṭya samantānnayanāt
                        samānaḥ| kṛkāṭikādeśādāśirovṛtterunnayanādudānaḥ| vyāpya nayanāt
                        sarvaśarīravyāpī vyānaḥ| tatrodānasya saṃyamadvāreṇa jayāditareṣāṃ vāyūnāṃ
                        rodhādūrdhvagatitvena jale mahānadyādau mahati vā kardame tīkṣṇeṣu kaṇṭakeṣu
                        vā na majjatyatilaghutvāt

children.translated_text: like a ball of cotton, even when plunged in water and the like, one rises up—this is the meaning. ||39||

Commentary: The activity that arises simultaneously in all the sense organs, like the flame of a husk—that is called by the term '<s>jīvana</s>' (vitality). Due to the distinction of its functions, it is designated by the names <s>prāṇa</s>, <s>apāna</s>, and the rest. Among these: because the wind moves from the heart through the mouth and nostrils, it is called <s>prāṇa</s>. Because it carries downward from the navel region to the tip of the great toe, it is <s>apāna</s>. Because it carries equally all around, encircling the navel region, it is <s>samāna</s>. Because it carries upward from the base of the neck to the crown of the head, it is <s>udāna</s>. Because it carries pervadingly throughout the entire body, it is <s>vyāna</s>. Among these, through <s>saṃyama</s> on <s>udāna</s> as the means of mastery, through the restraint of the other vital airs, due to the upward movement, one does not sink in water, great rivers, or great mud, or on sharp thorns, because of extreme lightness—
He states another <s>siddhi</s>:
Through mastery of <s>samāna</s>, effulgence. ||Vibhūti 40||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- agnimāveṣṭya vyavasthitasya samānākhyasya vāyorjayāt saṃyamena
                        vaśīkārānnirāvaraṇasyāgnerudbhūtattvāttejasā

children.translated_text: the yogin appears as if blazing with splendor. ||40|| He states another <s>siddhi</s>:

Commentary: Through mastery of the vital air called <s>samāna</s>, which is situated encircling the fire [of digestion], through <s>saṃyama</s> bringing it under control, the fire, being unveiled, blazing forth with radiance—
Through <s>saṃyama</s> on the relationship between the ear and space, divine hearing [is attained]. ||Vibhūti 41||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- śrotraṃ śabdagrāhakamāhaṃkārikamindriyam| ākāśaṃ vyoma
                        śabdatanmātrakāryam| tayoḥ sambandho deśadeśibhāvalakṣaṇastasmin
                        kṛtasaṃyamasya yogino divyaṃ śrotraṃ pravartate| yugapat
                        sūkṣmavyavahitaviprakṛṣṭaśabdagrahaṇasamarthaṃ bhavatītyarthaḥ ||41||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The ear is the <s>āhaṃkārika</s> (ego-derived) sense organ that grasps sound. Space (<s>ākāśa</s>) is the void, the effect of the sound-<s>tanmātra</s> (subtle element). Their relationship, characterized by the relation of place and that which occupies it—for the yogin who has performed <s>saṃyama</s> on that, divine hearing arises. It becomes capable of simultaneously grasping subtle, obstructed, and distant sounds—this is the meaning. ||41||
He states another <s>siddhi</s>:
Through <s>saṃyama</s> on the relationship between the body and space, and through <s>samāpatti</s> (absorption) on lightness like cotton, travel through space [is achieved]. ||Vibhūti 42||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- kāyaḥ pāñcabhautikaṃ śarīram| tasyākāśenāvakāśadāyakena yaḥ
                        sambandhastatra saṃyamaṃ vidhāya laghuni tūlādau samāpattiṃ
                        tanmayībhāvalakṣaṇāṃ vidhāya prāptātilaghubhāvo yogī prathamaṃ yathāruci
                        jale saṃcaraṇakrameṇorṇanābhatantujālena saṃcaramāṇa ādityaraśmibhiśca
                        viharan yatheṣṭamākāśena gacchati ||42||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The body is the physical body composed of the five elements. Its relationship with space, which provides room—having performed <s>saṃyama</s> on that, and having performed <s>samāpatti</s>, characterized by identification, on light things like cotton, having attained extreme lightness, the yogin first moves through water at will, then in sequence, moving along a spider's web of threads, and traveling on the rays of the sun, he goes through space as he wishes. ||42||
He states another <s>siddhi</s>:
The external non-imagined mental activity is the great disembodied state; from that, the destruction of the covering of light. ||Vibhūti 43||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- śarīrādbahiryā manasaḥ śarīranairapekṣyeṇa vṛttiḥ sā mahāvidehā
                        nāma vigatāhaṃkārakāryavegā

ucyate| tatastasyāṃ kṛtāt saṃyamāt prakāśāvaraṇakṣayaḥ sāttvikasya
                        cittasya yaḥ prakāśaḥ tasya yadāvaraṇaṃ kleśakarmādi tasya kṣayaḥ pravilayo
                        bhavati| ayamarthaḥ --- śarīrāhaṃkāre sati yā manaso bahirvṛttiḥ sā
                        kalpitetyucyate| yadā punaḥ śarīrādahaṃkārabhāvaṃ parityajya svātantryeṇa
                        manaso vṛttiḥ sā+akalpitā| tasyāṃ saṃyamādyoginaḥ sarve cittamalāḥ kṣīyante
                        ||43||
children.translated_text: From the <s>saṃyama</s> performed on that comes the destruction of the covering of light—the covering of the luminosity of the <s>sāttvika</s> (pure) mind, which consists of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), <s>karma</s>, and the like—its destruction, its dissolution, occurs. The meaning is: when there is ego regarding the body, the external activity of the mind is called 'imagined.' But when, having abandoned the sense of ego from the body, the mind's activity functions independently, that is 'non-imagined.' Through <s>saṃyama</s> on that, all mental impurities of the yogin are destroyed. ||43||
Commentary: The activity of the mind outside the body, independent of the body—that is called <s>mahāvidehā</s> (the great disembodied state), free from the momentum of ego-derived effects.

children.text:
tadevaṃ pūrvāntaviṣayāḥ parāntaviṣayā madhyabhāvāśca siddhīḥ
                        pratipādyā+anantaraṃ bhuvanajñānādirūpā bāhyāḥ kāyavyūhādirūpā ābhyantarāḥ
                        parikarmaniṣpannabhūtāśca maitryādiṣu balānītyevamādyāḥ
                        samādhyupayoginīścāntaḥkaraṇabahiḥkaraṇalakṣaṇendriyabhavāḥ
                        prāṇādivāyubhavāśca siddhīścittadārḍhyāya samādheścāśvāsotpattaye
                        pratipādyedānīṃ svadarśanopayogisabījanirbījasamādhisiddhaye
                        vividhopāyapradarśanāyāha ---
children.translated_text: Thus, having taught the <s>siddhis</s> pertaining to the past, the future, and intermediate states—and then those of external nature such as knowledge of worlds, those of internal nature such as the arrangement of the body, those accomplished through preparatory practices such as the powers in <s>maitrī</s> (friendliness) and the rest, those useful for <s>samādhi</s> arising from the senses characterized by the inner and outer instruments, and those arising from the vital airs beginning with <s>prāṇa</s>—all for the strengthening of the mind and for generating confidence in <s>samādhi</s>—now, to demonstrate various means for the accomplishment of seeded and seedless <s>samādhi</s> useful for one's own philosophical system, he says:
Through <s>saṃyama</s> on the gross, essential nature, subtle, inherent, and purposeful [aspects], mastery over the elements [is achieved]. ||Vibhūti 44||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- pañcānāṃ pṛthivyādīnāṃ bhūtānāṃ ye pañcā+avasthāviśeṣarūpā dharmāḥ
                        sthūlatvādayastatra kṛtasaṃyamasya bhūtajayo bhavati| bhūtānyasya vaśyāni
                        bhavantītyarthaḥ| tathā hi --- bhūtānāṃ paridṛśyamānaṃ viśiṣṭākāravat
                        sthūlarūpam| svarūpapañcaiṣāṃ yathākramaṃ kāryaṃ
                        gandhasnehoṣṇatāpreraṇāvakāśadānalakṣaṇam| sūkṣmaṃ ca yathākramaṃ bhūtānāṃ
                        kāraṇatvena vyavasthitāni gandhāditanmātrāṇi| anvayino guṇāḥ
                        prakāśapravṛttisthitirūpatayā sarvatraivā+anvayitvena samupalabhyante|
                        arthavattvaṃ teṣu eva guṇeṣu bhogāpavargasampādanākhyā śaktiḥ| tadevaṃ
                        bhūteṣu pañcasu uktadharmalakṣaṇāvasthābhinneṣu pratyavasthaṃ saṃyamaṃ
                        kurvan yogī bhūtajayī bhavati| tadyathā --- prathamaṃ sthūlarūpe saṃyamaṃ
                        vidhāya tadanu svarūpe ityevaṃ krameṇa tasya kṛtasaṃyamasya
                        saṃkalpānuvidhāyinyo vatsānusāriṇya iva gāvo bhūtaprakṛtayo bhavantītyarthaḥ
                        ||44||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Of the five elements beginning with earth, the five properties in the form of specific states—grossness and the rest—for one who has performed <s>saṃyama</s> on these, mastery over the elements occurs; the elements become obedient to him—this is the meaning. Thus: the gross form of the elements is the perceived form possessing specific configurations. Their essential nature (<s>svarūpa</s>) is, in order, the functions of smell, moisture, heat, propulsion, and providing space. The subtle (<s>sūkṣma</s>) are the <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements) beginning with smell, established as the causes of the elements in their respective order. The inherent (<s>anvaya</s>) are the <s>guṇas</s>, perceived everywhere as having the nature of luminosity, activity, and stability. Purposefulness (<s>arthavattva</s>) is the power in those very <s>guṇas</s> for accomplishing enjoyment and liberation. Thus, performing <s>saṃyama</s> on the five elements distinguished by these states of the described properties, stage by stage, the yogin becomes a master of the elements. That is: first performing <s>saṃyama</s> on the gross form, then on the essential nature—in this order, for one who has performed <s>saṃyama</s>, the elemental natures become obedient to his will, like cows following their calves—this is the meaning. ||44||
He states the fruit of this very mastery over the elements:
From that arises the manifestation of <s>aṇimā</s> (minuteness) and the other [powers], perfection of the body, and non-obstruction of its properties. ||Vibhūti 45||
1. <s>Aṇimā</s> (minuteness): attaining the form of an atom.
2. <s>Mahimā</s> (greatness): attaining immensity.
3. <s>Laghimā</s> (lightness): attaining lightness like a ball of cotton.
4. <s>Garimā</s> (heaviness): attaining heaviness.
5. <s>Prāpti</s> (reach): the power to touch the moon and such with the tip of one's finger.
6. <s>Prākāmya</s> (irresistible will): non-obstruction of one's desires.
7. <s>Īśitva</s> (lordship): sovereignty over the body and inner faculties.

children.text:
8| sarvatra prabhaviṣṇutā vaśitvam| sarvāṇyeva
                                bhūtānyanugāmitvāttaduktaṃ nātikrāmanti|
children.translated_text: 8. <s>Vaśitva</s> (mastery): the power to prevail everywhere; all elements indeed, because they follow him, do not transgress his command.

children.text:
9| yatrakāmāvasāyo yasmin viṣaye+asya kāmaḥ svecchā bhavati
                                tasmin viṣaye yogino+adhyavasāyo bhavati| taṃ viṣayaṃ
                                svīkāradvāreṇābhilāṣasamāptiparyantaṃ nayatītyarthaḥ|
children.translated_text: 9. <s>Yatrakāmāvasāyitva</s> (fulfillment of desire): in whatever object the yogin has desire, his own wish, in that object the yogin's determination prevails; he brings that object, through acceptance, to the completion of his wish—this is the meaning.

children.text:
ta ete+aṇimādyāḥ samādhyupayogino bhūtajayādyoginaḥ prādurbhavanti|
                        yathā paramāṇutvaṃ prāpto vajrādīnāmapyantaḥ praviśati| evaṃ sarvatra
                        yojyam| ete+aṇimādayo+aṣṭau guṇā mahāsiddhaya ucyante| kāyasampadvakṣyamāṇā
                        (3|46) tāṃ prāpnoti| taddharmā+anabhighātaśca tasya kāyasya ye dharmā
                        rūpādayasteṣāmanabhighāto nāśo na kutaścidbhavati nāsya rūpamagnirdahati na
                        vāyuḥ śoṣayatītyādi yojyam ||45||
children.translated_text: These supernatural powers beginning with <s>aṇimā</s> (becoming minute) arise for the yogin who conquers the elements through the aid of <s>samādhi</s>. For instance, one who has attained the state of an atom can enter even within diamonds and the like. In the same way, this should be applied everywhere. These eight qualities beginning with <s>aṇimā</s> are called the great <s>siddhis</s> (supernatural powers). He attains the perfection of the body (<s>kāyasampat</s>) that will be described [in 3.46]. And the non-destruction of its properties—the properties of that body such as form and the like are not destroyed from any cause. Fire does not burn his form, wind does not dry it—and so on should be applied. || 45 ||
Commentary:
He states the perfection of the body:
Beauty, grace, strength, and adamantine firmness constitute perfection of the body. || <s>Vibhūti</s> 46 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- rūpalāvaṇyabalāni prasiddhāni| vajrasaṃhananatvaṃ vajravat kaṭhinā
                        saṃhatirasya śarīre bhavatītyarthaḥ| iti kāyasya āvirbhūtaguṇasampat
                        ||46||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Beauty, grace, and strength are well-known. Adamantine firmness (<s>vajrasaṃhanana</s>) means that a compactness hard like a <s>vajra</s> (diamond/thunderbolt) exists in his body—this is the meaning. Thus is the perfection of the body in its manifested qualities. || 46 ||
Having thus stated the conquest of the elements, he states the conquest of the senses for one who has attained a particular stage:
From <s>saṃyama</s> on the process of grasping, own-nature, <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness), inherence, and purposefulness, [comes] mastery over the senses. || <s>Vibhūti</s> 47 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- grahaṇamindriyāṇāṃ viṣayābhimukhī vṛttiḥ| svarūpaṃ sāmānyena
                        prakāśakatvam| asmitā ahaṃkārānugamaḥ| anvayārthavattve pūrvavat (3|44)|
                        eteṣāṃ indriyāṇāmavasthāpañcake pūrvavat saṃyamaṃ kṛtvendriyajayī bhavati
                        ||47||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Grasping (<s>grahaṇa</s>) is the modification of the senses directed toward objects. Own-nature (<s>svarūpa</s>) is, in general, the quality of illumination. <s>Asmitā</s> is the following of the ego-sense. Inherence and purposefulness are as before [explained in 3.44]. Having performed <s>saṃyama</s> on these five states of the senses, as before, one becomes a conqueror of the senses. || 47 ||
He states its fruit:
Thence [comes] speed of mind, the state of being independent of instruments, and conquest of <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter). || <s>Vibhūti</s> 48 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- śarīrasya manovadanuttamagatilābho manojavitvam|
                        kāyanirapekṣāṇāmindriyāṇāṃ vṛttilābho vikaraṇabhāvaḥ| sarvavaśitvaṃ
                        pradhānajayaḥ| etāḥ siddhyayo jitendriyasya prādurbhavanti| tāścāsmin śāstre
                        madhupratīkā ityucyante| yathā madhuna ekadeśo+api svadata evaṃ
                        pratyekametāḥ siddhayaḥ svadanta iti madhupratīkāḥ ||48||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Speed of mind (<s>manojavitva</s>) is the body's attainment of unsurpassed movement like the mind. The state of being independent of instruments (<s>vikaraṇabhāva</s>) is the senses' attainment of functioning independently of the body. Conquest of <s>Pradhāna</s> is complete mastery over all. These <s>siddhis</s> manifest for one who has conquered the senses. And in this teaching (<s>śāstra</s>), these are called <s>madhupratīkā</s> (honey-faced). Just as even a portion of honey is sweet, so each of these <s>siddhis</s> individually is sweet—hence they are called <s>madhupratīkā</s>. || 48 ||
Having stated mastery over the senses, he states mastery over the inner instrument (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>):

For one who has merely the discernment (<s>khyāti</s>) of the difference between <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, [there comes] sovereignty over all states of existence and omniscience. || <s>Vibhūti</s> 49 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tasmin buddheḥ sāttvike pariṇāme kṛtasaṃyamasya yā
                        sattvapuruṣayorutpadyate vivekakhyātirguṇānāṃ
                        kartṛtvābhimānaśithilībhāvarūpā tanmāhātmyāt tatraiva sthitasya yoginaḥ
                        sarvādhiṣṭhātṛtvaṃ sarvajñātṛtvaṃ ca samādherbhavati| sarveṣāṃ
                        guṇapariṇāmānāṃ bhāvānāṃ svāmivadākramaṇaṃ sarvabhāvādhiṣṭhātṛtvam| teṣāmeva
                        ca śāntoditāvyapadeśyadharmitvenāvasthitānāṃ yathāvadvivekajñānaṃ
                        sarvajñātṛtvam| eṣāṃ cāsmiñchāstre parasyāṃ vaśīkārasaṃjñāyāṃ prāptāyāṃ
                        viśokā nāma siddhirityucyate ||49||
children.translated_text: Commentary: When one has performed <s>saṃyama</s> on the <s>sāttvika</s> transformation of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), the discriminative discernment (<s>vivekakhyāti</s>) that arises between <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>—which is of the nature of the loosening of the sense of doership regarding the <s>guṇas</s>—through its greatness, for the yogin established therein, sovereignty over all states of existence and omniscience arise from <s>samādhi</s>. Sovereignty over all states of existence (<s>sarvabhāvādhiṣṭhātṛtva</s>) is the mastery, like a lord's, over all states that are transformations of the <s>guṇas</s>. And omniscience (<s>sarvajñātṛtva</s>) is the knowledge as it truly is of those very [states], established in the condition of having qualities that are quiescent, arisen, and indeterminate. When, in this teaching, the supreme stage called <s>vaśīkāra</s> (mastery) is reached, the <s>siddhi</s> called <s>viśokā</s> (free from sorrow) is said [to arise]. || 49 ||
He states the next stage in sequence:
From <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion) even toward that, through the destruction of the seed of defects, [comes] <s>kaivalya</s> (liberation). || <s>Vibhūti</s> 50 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tasyāmapi viśokāyāṃ siddhau yadā vairāgyamutpadyate yoginastadā
                        tasmāddoṣāṇāṃ rāgādīnāṃ yadbījamavidyādayastasya kṣaye nirmūlane
                        kaivalyamātyantikī duḥkhanivṛttiḥ puruṣasya guṇānāmadhikāraparisamāptau
                        svarūpapratiṣṭhatvam
children.translated_text: Commentary: When <s>vairāgya</s> arises in the yogin even toward that <s>viśokā</s> <s>siddhi</s>, then from that, through the destruction—the uprooting—of the seed of defects such as <s>rāga</s> (attachment) and the like, namely <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) and the rest, <s>kaivalya</s> arises: the absolute cessation of suffering; the establishment of <s>Puruṣa</s> in its own nature when the function of the <s>guṇas</s> has been completed.
He states the means of abiding in that very <s>samādhi</s>:
When invited by the celestial rulers, one should avoid attachment and pride, because of the possibility of renewed undesirable connection. || <s>Vibhūti</s> 51 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- catvāro yogino bhavanti| tatrābhyāsavān pravṛttamātrajyotiḥ
                        prathamaḥ| ṛtambharaprajño dvitīyaḥ| bhūtendriyajayī tṛtīyaḥ|
                        atikrāntabhāvanīyaścaturthaḥ| tatra caturthasya samādheḥ
                        prāptasaptavidhabhūmiprāntaprajño bhavati| ṛtambharaprajñasya dvitīyāṃ
                        madhumatīsaṃjñāṃ bhūmikāṃ sākṣātkurvataḥ svāmino devā upanimantrayitāro
                        bhavanti| divyastrīrasāyanādikam

upaḍhaukayantīti tasminnupanimantraṇe nā+anena saṅgaḥ kartavyo nāpi smayaḥ|
                        saṅgatikaraṇe punarviṣayabhoge patati smayakaraṇe kṛtakṛtyamātmānaṃ
                        manyamāno na samādhāvutsahate| ataḥ saṅgasmayayostena varjanaṃ kartavyam
                        ||51||
children.translated_text: therefore, at such an invitation, one should not form attachment nor pride. If one makes attachment, one falls back into the enjoyment of sense-objects; if one yields to pride, thinking 'I have accomplished my purpose,' one does not strive for <s>samādhi</s>. Therefore, one must avoid both attachment and pride. || 51 ||

Commentary: There are four kinds of yogins. Among these: the first is the practitioner (<s>abhyāsavān</s>), who has merely the light of incipient activity. The second is one of truth-bearing wisdom (<s>ṛtambharaprajña</s>). The third is the conqueror of elements and senses. The fourth is one who has transcended [all] that is to be cultivated. Among these, the fourth, in <s>samādhi</s>, possesses the wisdom of the final seventh stage. For the second—one of truth-bearing wisdom—as he directly realizes the second stage called <s>Madhumatī</s> (honey-stage), celestial rulers (<s>svāmins</s>) become inviters. Offering divine women, elixirs, and the like—
He states another means, distinct from the previously stated <s>saṃyama</s>, for this very discriminative discernment (<s>vivekakhyāti</s>) which is its fruit:
From <s>saṃyama</s> on the moment and its succession, knowledge born of discrimination [arises]. || <s>Vibhūti</s> 52 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- kṣaṇaḥ sarvāntyaḥ kālāvayavo yasya kalāḥ prabhavituṃ na śakyante|
                        tathāvidhānāṃ kālakṣaṇānāṃ yaḥ kramaḥ paurvāparyeṇa pariṇāmastatra saṃyamāt
                        prāguktaṃ vivekajaṃ jñānamutpadyate| ayamarthaḥ --- ayaṃ kālakṣaṇo+amuṣmāt
                        kālakṣaṇāduttaro+ayamasmāt pūrva ityevaṃvidhe krame
                        kṛtasaṃyamasyātyantasūkṣme+api kṣaṇakrame yadā bhavati
                        sākṣātkārastadā+anyadapi sūkṣmaṃ mahadādi sākṣātkarotīti vivekajñānotpattiḥ
                        ||52||
children.translated_text: Commentary: A moment (<s>kṣaṇa</s>) is the ultimate, most minute unit of time, whose subdivisions cannot be produced. The succession (<s>krama</s>) of such temporal moments is their transformation in sequence of before and after. From <s>saṃyama</s> on that, the previously stated knowledge born of discrimination arises. The meaning is this: 'This temporal moment is after that temporal moment; this one is before that'—when one who has performed <s>saṃyama</s> on such a succession achieves direct realization even of the most extremely subtle succession of moments, then one also directly realizes other subtle [realities] such as <s>mahat</s> (the great principle) and so forth—thus discriminative knowledge arises. || 52 ||
To introduce the domain of discriminative knowledge for this very <s>saṃyama</s>, he says:
Therefrom [arises] discernment of two things that are alike, when the distinction by class, characteristic, and position is not the [basis of] differentiation. || <s>Vibhūti</s> 53 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- padārthānāṃ bhedahetavo jātilakṣaṇadeśā bhavanti|
                        kvacidbhedaheturjātiḥ| yathā gauriyaṃ mahiṣīyamiti| jātyā tulyayorlakṣaṇaṃ
                        bhedahetuḥ| iyaṃ karbureyamaruṇeti| jātyā lakṣaṇenābhinnayorbhedaheturdeśo
                        drṛṣṭaḥ| yathā tulyapramāṇayorāmalakayorbhinnadeśasthitayoḥ| yatra
                        punarbhedo+avadhārayituṃ na śakyate yathā ekadeśasthitayoḥ śuklayoḥ
                        pārthivayoḥ paramāṇvostathāvidhe viṣaye bhedāya kṛtasaṃyamasya bhedena
                        jñānamutpadyate tadā tadabhyāsāt sūkṣmāṇyapi tattvāni bhedena pratipadyate|
                        etaduktaṃ bhavati --- yatra kenacidupāyena bhedo nāvadhārayituṃ śakyastatra
                        saṃyamādbhavatyeva bhedapratipattiḥ ||53||
children.translated_text: Commentary: The causes of differentiation among objects are class, characteristic, and position. Sometimes the cause of differentiation is class (<s>jāti</s>)—as in 'this is a cow, that is a buffalo.' When class is the same, the characteristic (<s>lakṣaṇa</s>) is the cause of differentiation—as in 'this one is spotted, that one is tawny.' When both class and characteristic are identical, the observed cause of differentiation is position (<s>deśa</s>)—as with two <s>āmalaka</s> fruits of equal size situated in different places. But where differentiation cannot be ascertained—as with two white, earthy atoms situated in the same place—in such a domain, for one who has performed <s>saṃyama</s> for the purpose of differentiation, knowledge arises through differentiation. Then, through the practice of that, one discerns even subtle realities with differentiation. What is stated is this: where differentiation cannot be ascertained by any means, there, through <s>saṃyama</s>, the discernment of differentiation indeed arises. || 53 ||
To explain the designation, scope, and essential nature of the knowledge born of discrimination regarding subtle realities as stated, he says:

children.text:
tārakaṃ sarvaviṣayaṃ sarvathāviṣayamakramaṃ ceti vivekajaṃ jñānam ||vibhūti
                        54||
children.translated_text: The knowledge born of discrimination is <s>tāraka</s> (liberating), has all objects [as its scope], has all conditions [as its scope], and is non-sequential. || <s>Vibhūti</s> 54 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- uktasaṃyamabalādevā+antyāyāṃ bhūmikāyāmutpannaṃ jñānaṃ tārakamiti
                        tārayatyagādhāt saṃsārasāgarādyoginamityānvarthikyā saṃjñayā
                        tārakamityucyate| asya viṣayamāha --- sarvaviṣayamiti| sarvāṇi tattvāni
                        mahadādīni viṣayo+asyeti sarvaviṣayam| svabhāvaścāsya sarvathāviṣayatvam|
                        sarvābhiravasthābhiḥ sthūlasūkṣmādibhedena taistaiḥ pariṇāmaiḥ sarveṇa
                        prakāreṇā+avasthitāni tattvāni viṣayo+asyeti sarvathāviṣayam|
                        svabhāvāntaramāha --- akramaṃ ceti|
                        niḥśeṣanānāvasthāpariṇatasyātmakabhāvagrahaṇenāsya

kramo
                        vidyata ityakramam| sarvaṃ karatalāmalakavadyugapat paśyatītyarthaḥ
                        ||54||
children.translated_text: because it grasps the entirety of all [realities] transformed into countless states, there is no sequence in it—hence non-sequential. It sees everything simultaneously, like an <s>āmalaka</s> fruit on one's palm—this is the meaning. || 54 ||

Commentary: The knowledge arisen at the final stage through the power of the aforementioned <s>saṃyama</s> is called <s>tāraka</s>—by an etymologically meaningful designation, because it 'carries across' (<s>tārayati</s>) the yogin from the fathomless ocean of <s>saṃsāra</s> (cyclical existence). He states its scope: 'having all objects'—all the <s>tattvas</s> (principles of reality) such as <s>mahat</s> and the rest are its objects, hence it has all objects. Its essential nature is 'having all conditions as its scope'—the <s>tattvas</s> in all their conditions, in all their forms of transformation, in the distinction of gross and subtle and so forth, in every manner, are its objects, hence it has all conditions as its scope. He states another essential nature: 'and non-sequential'—
And what results from this discriminative, liberating (<s>tāraka</s>) knowledge? He says:
When there is equality of purity between <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, [there is] <s>kaivalya</s> (liberation). || <s>Vibhūti</s> 55 ||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- sattvapuruṣāvuktalakṣaṇau (2|6, 2|18, 2|20)| tayoḥ śuddhisāmye
                        kaivalyam| sattvasya sarvakartṛtvābhimānanivṛtyā svakāraṇānupraveśaḥ
                        śuddhiḥ| puruṣasya śuddhirupacaritabhogābhāva iti dvayoḥ samānāyāṃ śuddhau
                        puruṣasya kaivalyamutpadyate| mokṣo bhavatītyarthaḥ ||55||
children.translated_text: Commentary: <s>Sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s> are as previously defined [in 2.6, 2.18, 2.20]. When there is equality of purity between them, <s>kaivalya</s> [arises]. The purity of <s>sattva</s> is its re-entry into its own cause through the cessation of all sense of doership. The purity of <s>Puruṣa</s> is the absence of superimposed experience. When the purity of both is equal, <s>kaivalya</s> of <s>Puruṣa</s> arises—<s>mokṣa</s> (liberation) occurs, this is the meaning. || 55 ||

children.text:
tadevamantaraṅgaṃ yogāṅgatrayamabhidhāya tasya ca saṃyamasaṃjñāṃ kṛtvā
                        saṃyamasya viṣayapradarśanārthaṃ pariṇāmatrayamupapādya
                        saṃyamabalotpadyamānāḥ pūrvāntaparāntamadhyabhavāḥ siddhīrupadarśya
                        samādhyabhyāsopapattaye

bāhyā
                        bhuvanajñānādirūpā ābhyantarāśca kāyavyūhajñānādirūpāḥ pradarśya
                        samādhyupayogāyendriyaprāṇajayādipūrvikāḥ paramapuruṣārthasiddhaye
                        yathākramamavasthāsahitabhūtajayendriyasattvajayodbhavāśca vyākhyāya
                        vivekajñānopapattaye tāṃstānupāyānupanyasya tārakasya
                        sarvasamādhyavasthāparyantabhavasya svarūpamabhidhāya tatsamāpatteḥ
                        kṛtādhikārasya cittasattvasya svakāraṇānupraveśāt kaivalyamutpadyata
                        ityabhihitamiti nirṇīto vibhūtipādastṛtīyaḥ|
children.translated_text: having shown the external [powers] such as knowledge of the worlds and the internal [powers] such as knowledge of the bodily arrangement, and for the utility of <s>samādhi</s> having presented the conquest of senses and <s>prāṇa</s> and so forth as prerequisites, and for the accomplishment of the supreme goal of human existence (<s>puruṣārtha</s>) having explained in sequence the conquests of elements, senses, and <s>sattva</s> together with their respective stages, and for the purpose of establishing discriminative knowledge having presented the various means, and having described the essential nature of the liberating [knowledge] (<s>tāraka</s>) that exists up to the final state of all <s>samādhis</s>, it has been stated that <s>kaivalya</s> arises from the re-entry of the mind-<s>sattva</s>, whose qualifications are fulfilled, into its own cause. Thus the third chapter, the <s>Vibhūti Pāda</s>, is concluded.

Thus, having described the three inner limbs of <s>yoga</s>, having given them the designation <s>saṃyama</s>, and having established the three kinds of transformation for the purpose of demonstrating the objects of <s>saṃyama</s>, having shown the <s>siddhis</s> (powers) that arise through the power of <s>saṃyama</s>—those pertaining to the past, future, and intermediate states—and for the purpose of establishing the practice of <s>samādhi</s>,

children.text:
iti dhāreśvarabhojadevaviracitāyāṃ rājamārtaṇḍābhidhāyāṃ pātañjalavṛttau
                    vibhūtipādastṛtīyaḥ| iti vibhūtipādaḥ|
children.translated_text: Thus ends the third chapter, the <s>Vibhūti Pāda</s>, in the <s>Rājamārtaṇḍa</s>, the commentary on the <s>Pātañjala</s> [Yogasūtras], composed by <s>Dhāreśvara Bhojadeva</s>. Thus ends the <s>Vibhūti Pāda</s>.
<s>Kaivalya Pāda</s> (Chapter on Liberation)

children.text:
atha kaivalyapādaḥ yadājñayaiva kaivalyaṃ vinopāyaiḥ prajāyate|
                    tamekamajamīśānaṃ cidānandamayaṃ stumaḥ||
children.translated_text: Now the <s>Kaivalya Pāda</s>. We praise that One—unborn, sovereign, full of consciousness and bliss—through whose mere will <s>kaivalya</s> (liberation) arises without [other] means.

children.text:
kaivalyapādo+ayamārabhyate| tatra yāḥ pūrvamuktāḥ
                    siddhayastāsāṃ nānāvidhajanmādikāraṇapratipādanadvāreṇaivaṃ bodhayati --- madīyā
                    yā etāḥ siddhayastāḥ sarvāḥ
                    pūrvajanmābhyastasamādhibalājjanmādinimittamātratvenā+a+aśritya pravartante|
                    tataścānekabhavasādhyasya samādherna kṣatirastītyāśvāsotpādanāya
                    samādhisiddheśca prādhānyakhyāpanārthaṃ kaivalyopayogārthaṃ cāha ---
children.translated_text: this <s>Kaivalya Pāda</s> is commenced. Therein, regarding the <s>siddhis</s> (powers) previously mentioned, through the door of demonstrating the various causes such as birth and the like, he teaches thus: all those <s>siddhis</s> of mine operate by depending merely on the occasion of birth and the like, through the power of <s>samādhi</s> practiced in previous lives. Therefore, there is no loss for <s>samādhi</s> that is accomplished over many lives—for the purpose of inspiring confidence and for declaring the pre-eminence of <s>samādhi</s> as the means to <s>kaivalya</s>, he says:
The <s>siddhis</s> (supernatural powers) arise from birth, herbs, <s>mantras</s>, austerity (<s>tapas</s>), and <s>samādhi</s>.
|| <s>Kaivalya</s> 1 ||
Now, for the purpose of revealing the true nature of <s>kaivalya</s> through reasoning, by removing the confusion arising from conflicting views,

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- kāścana janmanimittā eva siddhayo yathā
                        pakṣyādīnāmākāśagamanādayaḥ| yathā vā kapilamaharṣiprabhṛtīnāṃ
                        janmasamanantaramevopajāyamānā jñānādayaḥ sāṃsiddhikā guṇāḥ| oṣadhisiddhayo
                        yathā pāradādirasāyanādyupayogāt| mantrasiddhiryathā mantrajapāt
                        keṣāṃcidākāśagamanādiḥ| tapaḥsiddhiryathā viśvāmitrādīnām| samādhisiddhiḥ
                        prākpratipāditā| etāḥ siddhayaḥ pūrvajanmakṣayitakleśānāmevopajāyante|
                        tasmāt samādhisiddhāvivā+anyāsāṃ siddhīnāṃ samādhireva janmāntarābhyastaḥ
                        kāraṇm| mantrādīni nimittamātrāṇi ||1||
children.translated_text: Commentary — Certain <s>siddhis</s> (attainments) arise from birth alone, such as the power of flying through the sky and the like possessed by birds and similar creatures. Or, as in the case of the great sage <s>Kapila</s> and others, innate qualities such as knowledge and the like that arise immediately upon birth are natural (<s>sāṃsiddhika</s>) attributes. The <s>siddhis</s> arising from herbs are like those obtained through the use of <s>rasāyana</s> (elixirs) such as mercury and the like. The <s>siddhi</s> arising from <s>mantras</s> is like the power of flying through the sky and so forth that some attain through the recitation of <s>mantras</s>. The <s>siddhi</s> arising from austerity (<s>tapas</s>) is like that of <s>Viśvāmitra</s> and others. The <s>siddhi</s> arising from <s>samādhi</s> has been previously explained. These <s>siddhis</s> arise only for those whose <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) have been exhausted in previous births. Therefore, just as in the case of the <s>siddhi</s> born of <s>samādhi</s>, for all the other <s>siddhis</s> too, it is <s>samādhi</s> practiced in previous births that is the cause. <s>Mantras</s> and the like are merely instrumental occasions. ||1||

children.text:
nanu nandīśvarādikānāṃ jātyādipariṇāmo+asminneva janmani dṛśyate| tat kathaṃ
                        janmāntarābhyastasya samādheḥ kāraṇatvamucyata ityāśaṅkyāha ---
children.translated_text: Now, the transformation of class and the like of <s>Nandīśvara</s> and others is observed in this very birth. How then can <s>samādhi</s> practiced in a previous birth be said to be the cause? — anticipating this, he says —
The transformation into another class of existence (<s>jātyantarapariṇāma</s>) [occurs] through the filling in (<s>āpūra</s>) of <s>prakṛti</s> (nature). ||<s>Kaivalya</s> 2||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- yo+ayamihaiva janmani nandīśvarādīnāṃ jātyādipariṇāmaḥ sa
                        prakṛtyāpūrāt| pāścāttyā eva hi prakṛtayo+amuṣmiñjanmani vikārānāpūrayanti
                        jātyantarākāreṇa pariṇamanti ||2||
children.translated_text: Commentary — This transformation of class and the like of <s>Nandīśvara</s> and others that occurs in this very birth — that is from the filling in of <s>prakṛti</s>. For the subsequent <s>prakṛtis</s> (natural potencies) fill up their modifications in that [new] birth, transforming in the form of another class of existence. ||2||

children.text:
nanu dharmādharmādayastatra kriyamānā upalabhyante| tat kathaṃ
                        prakṛtīnāmāpūrakatvam ityāha ---
children.translated_text: Now, <s>dharma</s> (merit), <s>adharma</s> (demerit), and the like are observed being performed there. How then can the <s>prakṛtis</s> be said to be the fillers? — to this he says —
The incidental cause (<s>nimitta</s>) is not the impeller of the <s>prakṛtis</s>; but from that, the breaking of the barrier — like a farmer. ||<s>Kaivalya</s> 3||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- nimittaṃ dharmādi| tat prakṛtīnāmarthāntarapariṇāme na prayojakam|
                        na hi kāryeṇa kāraṇaṃ pravartate| kutra tarhi tasya dharmādervyāpāra ityāha
                        --- varaṇabhedastu tataḥ kṣetrikavat|
                        tatastasmādanuṣṭhīyamānāddharmādvaraṇamāvaraṇakamadharmādi tasyaiva
                        virodhitvādbhedaḥ kṣayaḥ kriyate| tasmin pratibandhake kṣīṇe prakṛtayaḥ
                        svayamabhimatakāryāya prabhavanti| dṛṣṭāntamāha --- kṣetrikavat| yathā
                        kṣetrikaḥ kṛṣībalaḥ kedārāt kedārāntaraṃ jalaṃ
                        ninīṣurjalapratibandhakāvaraṇabhedamātraṃ karoti| tasmin bhinne jalaṃ
                        svayameva prasaradrūpaṃ pariṇāmaṃ gṛhṇāti na tu jalaprasaraṇe tasya kaścit
                        prayatnaḥ| evaṃ dharmāderboddhavyam ||3||
children.translated_text: Commentary — The incidental cause is <s>dharma</s> and the like. That is not the impeller for the transformation of the <s>prakṛtis</s> into something else. For an effect does not set a cause into motion. Where then is the function of <s>dharma</s> and the like? — to this he says — 'but from that, the breaking of the barrier — like a farmer.' From that — from the <s>dharma</s> being practiced — the barrier (<s>varaṇa</s>), meaning the obstruction, which is <s>adharma</s> and the like, being its very opposite, is broken, meaning destroyed. When that obstruction is destroyed, the <s>prakṛtis</s> by themselves become capable of [producing] their desired effect. He gives an illustration — 'like a farmer.' Just as a farmer (<s>kṣetrika</s>), a cultivator, wishing to lead water from one field to another, merely breaks the barrier obstructing the water. When that is broken, the water by itself assumes the form of flowing — he makes no effort for the water's flowing. The same should be understood regarding <s>dharma</s> and the like. ||3||

children.text:
yadā sākṣātkṛtatattvasya yogino yugapat
                        karmaphalabhogāyā+a+atmīyaniratiśayavibhūtyanubhavād
                        yugapadanekaśarīranirmitsā jāyate tadā kutastāni cittāni prabhavantītyāha
                        ---
children.translated_text: When a <s>yogin</s> who has directly realized the truth needs simultaneously to enjoy the fruits of <s>karma</s> and to experience his own unsurpassed powers, and when the simultaneous creation of many bodies arises — then, from where do those minds originate? — to this he says —
The created minds (<s>nirmāṇacittāni</s>) [arise] from the sense of pure I-am-ness (<s>asmitāmātra</s>) alone. ||<s>Kaivalya</s> 4||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- yoginaḥ svayaṃ nirmiteṣu kāyeṣu yāni cittāni tāni
                        mūlakāraṇādasmitāmātrādeva tadicchayā prasaranti| agnervisphuliṅgā iva
                        yugapat pariṇamanti ||4||
children.translated_text: Commentary — The minds in the bodies created by the <s>yogin</s> himself — those spread forth from the root cause, the mere sense of I-am-ness (<s>asmitāmātra</s>) alone, by his will. Like sparks from fire, they transform simultaneously. ||4||
Now, since the many minds have different intentions, they cannot be agents of a single purpose — to this he says —
In the differentiation of activities, one mind is the director of the many. ||<s>Kaivalya</s> 5||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- teṣāmanekeṣāṃ cetasāṃ pravṛttibhede vyāpāranānātva eakaṃ
                        yoginaścittaṃ prayojakaṃ prerakamadhiṣṭhātṛtvena| tena na bhinnamatatvam|
                        ayamarthaḥ --- yathātmīyaśarīre manaścakṣuḥpāṇyādīni yathecchaṃ
                        prerayatyadhiṣṭhātṛtvenaievaṃ kāyāntareṣvapīti ||5||
children.translated_text: Commentary — Among those many minds, in the differentiation of activities — meaning in the variety of functions — the one mind of the <s>yogin</s> is the director, the impeller, through its governing authority. Therefore, there is no divergence of views. The meaning is this: just as in one's own body, the mind directs the eyes, hands, and other [organs] as it wishes through its governing authority, so too in the other bodies. ||5||

children.text:
janmādiprabhavatvāt siddhīnāṃ cittamapi tatprabhavaṃ pañcavidhameva| ato
                        janmādiprabhavāccittāt samādhiprabhavasya cittasya vailakṣaṇyamāha ---
children.translated_text: Since the <s>siddhis</s> arise from birth and the like, the mind too, being born from those, is of five kinds only. Therefore, he states the distinction of the mind born from <s>samādhi</s> from the mind born from birth and the like —
Among those, the one born of meditation (<s>dhyānaja</s>) is without residual impressions (<s>anāśaya</s>). ||<s>Kaivalya</s> 6||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- dhyānajaṃ samādhijaṃ yaccittaṃ tat pañcasu madhye+anāśayaṃ
                        karmavāsanārahitamityarthaḥ ||6||
children.translated_text: Commentary — The mind born of meditation, born of <s>samādhi</s> — that, among the five, is without residual store (<s>anāśaya</s>), meaning free from <s>karma</s>-impressions (<s>karmavāsanā</s>). ||6||

children.text:
yathetaracittebhyo yoginaścittaṃ vilakṣaṇaṃ kleśādirahitaṃ tathā karmāpi
                        vilakṣaṇamityāha ---
children.translated_text: Just as the <s>yogin</s>'s mind is distinct from other minds in being free from <s>kleśas</s> and the like, so too his <s>karma</s> is distinct — thus he says —
<s>Karma</s> is neither white nor black for the <s>yogin</s>; for others it is threefold. ||<s>Kaivalya</s> 7||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- śubhaphaladaṃ karma yāgādi śuklam| aśubhaphaladaṃ brahmahatyādi
                        kṛṣṇam| ubhayasaṃkīrṇaṃ śuklakṛṣṇam| tatra śuklaṃ karma vicakṣaṇānāṃ
                        dānatapaḥsvādhyāyādimatāṃ puruṣāṇām| kṛṣṇaṃ karma dānavānām

| śuklakṛṣṇaṃ manuṣyāṇām| yogināntu saṃnyāsavatāṃ
                        trividhakarmaviparītaṃ yat phalatyāgānusandhānenaivānuṣṭhānānna kiñcit
                        phalamārabhate ||7||
children.translated_text: White-black <s>karma</s> belongs to humans. But for <s>yogins</s> who have adopted renunciation (<s>saṃnyāsa</s>), that which is the opposite of the threefold <s>karma</s> — since their practice is performed solely with the intention of renouncing results — does not initiate any fruit whatsoever. ||7||

Commentary — <s>Karma</s> that yields auspicious results, such as sacrificial rites and the like, is white. That which yields inauspicious results, such as <s>brahmahatyā</s> (killing a Brahmin) and the like, is black. That which is a mixture of both is white-black. Among these, white <s>karma</s> belongs to discerning persons who engage in charity, austerity, self-study (<s>svādhyāya</s>), and the like. Black <s>karma</s> belongs to <s>dānavas</s> (demons).
He states the result of this very <s>karma</s> —
From that, the manifestation of only those <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions) that correspond to that ripening. ||<s>Kaivalya</s> 8||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- iha hi dvividhā karmavāsanāḥ smṛtimātraphalā
                        jātyāyurbhogaphalāśca| tatra jātyāyurbhogaphalā ekānekajanmabhavā ityanena
                        pūrvameva (2|12--13) kṛtanirṇayāḥ| yāstu smṛtimātraphalāstāstataḥ karmaṇo
                        yena karmaṇā yādṛk śarīramārabdhaṃ devamanuṣyatiryagādibhedena tasya
                        vipākasyā+anuguṇā anurūpā yā vāsanāstāsāmeva tasmādabhivyaktirvāsanānāṃ
                        bhavati| ayamarthaḥ --- yena karmaṇā pūrvaṃ devatādiśarīramārabdhaṃ
                        jātyantaraśatavyavadhānena punastathāvidhasyaiva śarīrasyārambhe tadanurūpā
                        eva smṛtiphalā vāsanāḥ prakaṭībhavanti| lokāntareṣvevārtheṣu tasya
                        smṛtyādayo jāyante| itarāstu satyo+api avyaktasaṃjñāstiṣṭhanti na tasyāṃ
                        daśāyāṃ nārakādiśarīrodbhavā vāsanā vyaktimāyānti ||8||
children.translated_text: Commentary — Here, <s>karma</s>-impressions are of two kinds: those whose fruit is mere memory, and those whose fruit is class of birth (<s>jāti</s>), lifespan (<s>āyus</s>), and experience (<s>bhoga</s>). Among these, those whose fruit is class, lifespan, and experience — whether arising from one or many births — have already been determined by this [earlier discussion] (2.12-13). But those whose fruit is mere memory — from that <s>karma</s>, by whatever <s>karma</s> whatever body has been initiated, whether divine, human, animal, or otherwise — the <s>vāsanās</s> that correspond to, that is, are conformable to the ripening of that [<s>karma</s>] — only those <s>vāsanās</s> manifest. The meaning is this: by whatever <s>karma</s> a divine body and the like was previously initiated, upon the initiation of a similar body again even after the interval of hundreds of other births, only the memory-fruiting <s>vāsanās</s> conformable to that [body] become manifest. His memories and so forth arise regarding things of those [corresponding] worlds. But the others, though real, remain in the state designated as 'unmanifest' — in that condition, the <s>vāsanās</s> arising from infernal and other bodies do not come to manifestation. ||8||
Anticipating the impossibility of the cause-effect relationship of these very <s>vāsanās</s>, he sets out to justify it —
Even for those separated by class, place, and time, there is uninterruptedness, because memory and <s>saṃskāras</s> (impressions) are of one form. ||<s>Kaivalya</s> 9||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- iha nānāyoniṣu bhramatāṃ saṃsāriṇāṃ kāṃcidyonimanubhūya yadā
                        yonyantarasahasravyavadhānena punastāmeva yoniṃ pratipadyate tadā tasyāṃ
                        pūrvānubhūtāyāṃ yonau tathāvidhaśarīrādivyañjakāpekṣayā vāsanā yāḥ
                        prakaṭībhūtā āsaṃstāstathāvidhavyañjakābhāvāttirohitāḥ
                        punastathāvidhavyañjakaśarīrādilābhe prakaṭībhavanti|
                        jātideśakālavyavadhāne+api tāsāṃ svānurūpasmṛtyādiphalasādhana ānantaryaṃ
                        nairantaryam| kutaḥ| smṛtisaṃskārayorekarūpatvāt| tathāhi --- anuṣṭhīyamānāt
                        karmaṇaścittasattve vāsanārūpaḥ saṃskāraḥ samutpadyate| sa ca
                        svarganarakādīnāṃ phalānāṃ cāṅkurībhāvaḥ karmaṇāṃ vā yāgādīnāṃ
                        śaktirūpatayā+avasthānam| karturvā tathāvidhabhogyabhoktṛtvarūpaṃ
                        sāmarthyam| saṃskārāt smṛtiḥ smṛteśca sukhaduḥkhopabhogastadanubhavācca
                        punarapi saṃskārasmṛtyādayaḥ| evaṃ ca yasya smṛtisaṃskārādayo
                        bhinnāstasyā+a+anantaryābhāve durlabhaḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ| asmākaṃ tu
                        yadānubhava eva saṃskārībhavati saṃskāraśca smṛtirūpatayā pariṇamate
                        tadaikasyaiva cittasyānusandhātṛtvena sthitatvānna kāryakāraṇabhāvo
                        durghaṭaḥ ||9||
children.translated_text: Commentary — Here, for beings wandering in various wombs (<s>yonis</s>), when one has experienced a certain <s>yoni</s> and then, after the interval of thousands of other <s>yonis</s>, attains that very same <s>yoni</s> again — then in that previously experienced <s>yoni</s>, the <s>vāsanās</s> that had become manifest due to the need for an appropriate manifesting agent such as that kind of body and the like — those [<s>vāsanās</s>], having become concealed due to the absence of such a manifesting agent, become manifest again upon obtaining a manifesting body and the like of that kind. Even though there is separation by class, place, and time, there is uninterruptedness (<s>ānantarya</s>), meaning continuity, for those [<s>vāsanās</s>] in producing their appropriate fruits of memory and the like. Why? Because memory and <s>saṃskāras</s> are of one form. Thus — from the <s>karma</s> being performed, a <s>saṃskāra</s> in the form of a <s>vāsanā</s> arises in the mind-substance (<s>cittasattva</s>). And that is the germination of fruits such as heaven, hell, and the like, or the existence in the form of potency of ritual acts such as sacrifices, or the capacity of the agent in the form of being an experiencer of such objects. From the <s>saṃskāra</s> arises memory; from memory, the experience of pleasure and pain; and from that experience, again <s>saṃskāras</s>, memory, and so forth. Thus, for one whose memory, <s>saṃskāras</s>, and the rest are different, in the absence of uninterruptedness, the cause-effect relationship is difficult to obtain. But for us, since the very experience becomes a <s>saṃskāra</s>, and the <s>saṃskāra</s> transforms into the form of memory — since a single mind remains as the connecting thread — the cause-effect relationship is not difficult to establish. ||9||

children.text:
bhavatvānantaryaṃ kāryakāraṇabhāvaśca vāsanānām yadā tu prathamamevānubhavaḥ
                        pravartate tadā kiṃ vāsanānimitta uta nirnimitta iti śaṅkāṃ vyapanetumāha
                        ---
children.translated_text: Granted there is uninterruptedness and cause-effect relationship of the <s>vāsanās</s>; but when the very first experience arises, is it caused by a <s>vāsanā</s> or is it causeless? — to remove this doubt he says —
And those [<s>vāsanās</s>] are beginningless, because the desire [to live] is eternal. ||<s>Kaivalya</s> 10||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tāsāṃ vāsanānāmanāditvam| na vidyata ādiryasya tasya bhāvastattvaṃ
                        tāsāmādirnāstītyarthaḥ| kuta iti| āśiṣo nityatvāt| yeyamāśīrmahāmoharūpā
                        sadaiva sukhasādhanāni me bhūyāsurmā kadācana tairme viyogo bhūditi yaḥ
                        saṃkalpaviśeṣo vāsanānāṃ kāraṇaṃ tasya nityatvādanāditvamityarthaḥ|
                        etaduktaṃ bhavati --- kāraṇasya sannihitatvādanubhavasaṃskārādīnāṃ kāryāṇāṃ
                        pravṛttiḥ kena vāryate| anubhavasaṃskārānubiddhaṃ saṃkocavikāśadharmi cittaṃ
                        tattadabhivyañjakavipākalābhāt tattatphalarūpatayā pariṇamata ityarthaḥ
                        ||10||
children.translated_text: Commentary — Those <s>vāsanās</s> are beginningless (<s>anādi</s>). That which has no beginning — such is their nature, meaning their beginning does not exist. Why? Because the desire (<s>āśis</s>) is eternal. This desire, whose nature is great delusion — the particular mental resolve 'May the means of happiness always be mine! May I never be separated from them!' — which is the cause of the <s>vāsanās</s>, because of its eternality, [the <s>vāsanās</s>] are beginningless. What has been said amounts to this: since the cause is ever-present, what prevents the operation of the effects — experience, <s>saṃskāras</s>, and the rest? The mind, permeated by experience and <s>saṃskāras</s>, possessing the property of contraction and expansion, transforms into the form of various fruits upon obtaining the appropriate manifesting ripening. ||10||
Since they are endless, how can their cessation come about? — anticipating this, he states the means of cessation —
Because they are held together by cause, fruit, substratum, and object — in the absence of these, there is the absence of those [<s>vāsanās</s>]. ||<s>Kaivalya</s> 11||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- vāsanānāmanantarānubhavo hetustasyāpyanubhavasya
                        rāgādayasteṣāmavidyeti sākṣāt pāramparyeṇa hetuḥ| phalaṃ śarīrādi smṛtyādi
                        ca| āśrayo buddhisattvam| ālambanaṃ yadevānubhavasya tadeva vāsanānām|
                        atastairhetuphalāśrayālambanairanantānāmapi vāsanānāṃ saṃgṛhītatvāt| eṣāṃ
                        hetvādīnāmabhāve jñānayogābhyāṃ dagdhabījakalpatve vihite nirmūlatvānna
                        vāsanāḥ prarohanti na kāryamārabhanta iti tāsāmabhāvaḥ ||11||
children.translated_text: Commentary — The immediately preceding experience is the cause of the <s>vāsanās</s>; the cause of that experience is attachment (<s>rāga</s>) and the like; their [cause] is <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) — thus, directly and indirectly, the cause. The fruit is the body and the like, as well as memory and the like. The substratum (<s>āśraya</s>) is the <s>buddhi</s>-substance (intellect). The object (<s>ālambana</s>) — whatever is the object of experience is also the object of the <s>vāsanās</s>. Therefore, since even innumerable <s>vāsanās</s> are held together by cause, fruit, substratum, and object — in the absence of these — that is, when through knowledge-yoga the state of burnt seeds is effected — being rootless, the <s>vāsanās</s> do not sprout, do not initiate any effect — thus there is their absence. ||11||

children.text:
nanu pratikṣaṇaṃ cittasya naśvaratvopalabdhervāsanānāṃ tatphalānāṃ ca
                        kāryakāraṇabhāvena yugapadabhāvitvādbhede
                        kathamekatvamityāśaṅkyaikatvasamarthanāyāha ---
children.translated_text: Now, since the mind is observed to be perishable at every moment, and since the <s>vāsanās</s> and their fruits, by being in a cause-effect relationship, cannot exist simultaneously — how can there be unity in difference? — anticipating this, he sets out to establish their unity —
The past and the future exist in their own nature, because of the difference of paths (<s>adhvan</s>) of the <s>dharmas</s>. ||<s>Kaivalya</s> 12||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ ---ihātyantamasatāṃ bhāvānāmutpattirna yuktimatī teṣāṃ
                        sattvasambandhāyogāt| na hi śaśaviṣāṇādīnāṃ kvacidapi sattvasambandho
                        dṛṣṭaḥ| nirupākhye ca kārye kimuddiśya kāraṇāni pravarteran| na hyasantaṃ
                        viṣayamālocya kaścit pravartate| satāmapi virodhānnābhāvasambandho+asti| yat
                        svarūpaṃ labdhasattākaṃ tat kathaṃ nirupākhyatāmabhāvarūpatāṃ vā bhajate na
                        viruddhaṃ rūpaṃ svīkarotītyarthaḥ| tasmāt satāmabhāvāsambhavādasatāṃ
                        cotpattyasambhavāt taistairdharmairvipariṇamamāno dharmī sadaikarūpa
                        evāvatiṣṭhate| dharmāstu tryadhvakatvena

traikālikatvena tatra vyavasthitāḥ svasmin svasminnadhvani vyavasthitāḥ na
                        svarūpaṃ tyajanti| vartamāne+adhvani vyavasthitāḥ kevalaṃ bhogyatāṃ
                        bhajante| tasmāddharmāṇāmevātītānāgatādyadhvabhedāt tenaiva rūpeṇa
                        kāryakāraṇabhāvo+asmin darśane pratipadyate| tasmādapavargaparyantamekameva
                        cittaṃ dharmitayā+anuvartamānaṃ na nihnotuṃ pāryate ||12||
children.translated_text: being established in the three times, are established each in their own time-path and do not abandon their essential nature. Those established in the present time-path merely assume the state of being experienced. Therefore, because of the difference of time-paths—past, future, and so forth—of the properties alone, the cause-effect relation is understood in this philosophical system as having that very form. Therefore, from [the beginning] to the end of liberation (<s>apavarga</s>), the one and same mind, continuing as the substance, cannot be denied. ||12||

Commentary: Here, the origination of utterly non-existent entities is not reasonable, because of the impossibility of their connection with existence. For the horns of a hare and such are never seen to have any connection with existence. And with regard to a non-existent effect, for what purpose would causes operate? For no one acts having contemplated a non-existent object. Nor is there a connection with non-existence for existent things, because of contradiction. How can that which has attained being, whose nature is what it is, assume non-existence or the nature of absence? It does not take on a contradictory form—this is the meaning. Therefore, since non-existence is impossible for the existent and origination is impossible for the non-existent, the substance (<s>dharmin</s>), transforming through various properties (<s>dharmas</s>), always remains of one single nature. But the properties, through their being in three time-paths,
He asks: of what nature are these properties and their substance?
They are manifest and subtle, having the <s>guṇas</s> (constituents of nature) as their nature. ||Kaivalya 13||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- ya ete dharmadharmiṇaḥ proktāste vyaktasūkṣmabhedena vyavasthitāḥ
                        guṇāḥ sattvarajastamorūpāstadātmānastatsvabhāvāstatpariṇāmarūpā ityarthaḥ|
                        yataḥ sattvarajastamobhiḥ sukhaduḥkhamoharūpaiḥ sarvāsāṃ
                        bāhyābhyantarabhedabhinnānāṃ bhāvavyaktīnāmanvayānugamo dṛśyate|
                        yadyadanvayi tattat pariṇāmarūpaṃ dṛṣṭam| yathā ghaṭādayo mṛdanvitā
                        mṛtpariṇāmarūpāḥ ||13||
children.translated_text: Commentary: These properties (<s>dharmas</s>) and substance (<s>dharmin</s>) that have been described are established with the distinction of manifest and subtle. The <s>guṇas</s>—<s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s> in form—they have those as their nature, their essential character, being of the form of their transformation—this is the meaning. For in all manifestations of entities, both external and internal, the constant accompaniment of <s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s>—whose forms are pleasure, pain, and delusion—is observed. Whatever accompanies something is seen to be of the form of its transformation. Just as pots and such, being accompanied by clay, are transformations of clay. ||13||

children.text:
yadyete trayo guṇāḥ sarvatra mūlakāraṇaṃ kathameko dharmīti vyapadeśa
                        ityāśaṅkyāha ---
children.translated_text: If these three <s>guṇas</s> are everywhere the root cause, how is there the designation of one substance?—anticipating this doubt, he says:
The reality of the object is [established] because of the unity of transformation. ||Kaivalya 14||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- yadyapi trayo guṇāstathāpi teṣāmaṅgāṅgibhāvagamanalakṣaṇo yaḥ
                        pariṇāmaḥ kvacit sattvamaṅgi kvacidrajaḥ kvacicca tama
                        ityevaṃrūpastasyaikatvādvastunastattvamekamucyate| yathā --- iyaṃ pṛthivī|
                        ayaṃ vāyurityevamādi ||14||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Although there are three <s>guṇas</s>, nevertheless, the transformation characterized by the mutual interplay of principal and subordinate roles—sometimes <s>sattva</s> is principal, sometimes <s>rajas</s>, sometimes <s>tamas</s>—because of the unity of that [transformation], the reality of the object is said to be one. Just as 'this is earth,' 'this is wind'—and so forth. ||14||

children.text:
nanu jñānavyatirikte satyarthe vastvekamanekaṃ vā vaktuṃ yujyate| yadā ca
                        vijñānameva vāsanāvaśāt kāryakāraṇabhāvenāvasthitaṃ tathā tathā pratibhāti
                        tadā kathametacchakyate vaktumityāśaṅkyāha ---
children.translated_text: Objection: When an object exists independently of cognition, it is reasonable to speak of the object as one or many. But when cognition itself, by the power of <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions), is established as cause and effect and appears in various ways, how can this be said?—anticipating this doubt, he says:
The object being the same, due to the difference of minds, the paths of the two are distinct. ||Kaivalya 15||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tayorjñānārthayorviviktaḥ panthā vivikto mārgo deśa iti yāvat|
                        katham| vastusāmye cittabhedāt| samāne vastuni stryādāvupalabhyamāne
                        nānāpramātṝṇāṃ cittasya bhedaḥ sukhaduḥkhamoharūpatayā samupalabhyate|
                        tathāhi ekasyāṃ rūpalāvaṇyavatyāṃ yoṣiti upalabhyamānāyāṃ sarāgasya
                        sukhamutpadyate sapatnyāstu dveṣaḥ parivrājakāderghṛṇetyekasmin vastuni
                        nānāvidhacittodayāt kathaṃ cittakāryatvaṃ vastuna ekacittakāryatve
                        vastvekarūpatayaivā+avabhāseta| kiñca cittakāryatve vastuno yadīyasya
                        cittasya tadvastu kāryaṃ tasminnarthāntaravyāsakte tadvastu na kiñcit syāt|
                        bhavatviti cenna| tadeva kathamanyairbahubhirupalabhyeta| upalabhyate ca
                        tasmānna cittakāryam| atha yugapadbahubhiḥ so+arthaḥ kriyate tadā
                        bahunirmitasyārthasyaikanirmitādvailakṣaṇyaṃ syāt| yadā tu vailakṣaṇyaṃ
                        neṣyate tadā kāraṇabhede sati kāryabhedasyābhāve nirhetukamekarūpaṃ vā jagat
                        syāt| etaduktaṃ bhavati --- satyapi bhinne kāraṇe yadi kāryasyābhedastadā
                        samagraṃ jagannānāvidhakāraṇajanyamekarūpaṃ syāt| kāraṇabhedānanugamāt
                        svātantryeṇa nirhetukaṃ vā syāt| yadyevaṃ kathaṃ tena triguṇātmanā
                        cittenaikasyaiva pramātuḥ sukhaduḥkhamohamayāni jñānāni janyante

pā0
                            kathaṃ tena triguṇātmanā+arthe naikasyaiva pramātuḥ
                            sukhaduḥkhamohabhayāni jñānāni na janyante

| maivam|
                        yathā+arthastriguṇastathā cittamapi triguṇam| tasyārthapratibhāsotpattau
                        dharmādayaḥ sahakārikāraṇam| tadudbhavābhibhavavaśāt kadāciccittasya tena
                        tena rūpeṇābhivyaktiḥ| tathā ca --- kāmukasya sannihitāyāṃ yoṣiti
                        dharmasahakṛtaṃ cittaṃ sattvasyāṅgitayā pariṇamamānaṃ sukhamayaṃ bhavati|
                        tadevā+adharmasahakāri rajaso+aṅgitayā duḥkharūpaṃ sapatnīmātrasya bhavati|
                        tīvrādharmasahakāritayā pariṇamamānaṃ tamaso+aṅgitvena kopanāyāḥ sapatnyā
                        mohamayaṃ bhavati| tasmādvijñānavyatirekeṇāsti grāhyārthaḥ
children.translated_text: Not so. Just as the object has three <s>guṇas</s>, so the mind too has three <s>guṇas</s>. In the arising of the mind's reflection of the object, <s>dharma</s> (merit) and the rest serve as cooperative causes. Through their emergence and suppression, the mind is sometimes manifested in one form and sometimes in another. And thus: for the lustful person, when a woman is nearby, the mind, cooperating with <s>dharma</s>, transforming with <s>sattva</s> as principal, becomes blissful. That same mind, cooperating with <s>adharma</s> (demerit), with <s>rajas</s> as principal, becomes painful for the mere co-wife. Transforming through cooperation with intense <s>adharma</s>, with <s>tamas</s> as principal, it becomes delusory for the angry co-wife. Therefore, the graspable object exists independently of cognition.

children.text:
| tadevaṃ vijñānārthayostādātmyavirodhānna
                        kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ| kāraṇābhede satyapi kāryabhedaprasaṅgāditi
                        jñānādvyatiriktatvamarthasya vyavasthitam ||15||
children.translated_text: Thus, because of the contradiction of identity between cognition and object, there is no cause-effect relation [between them]. Since, even without non-difference of cause, there is the unwanted consequence of difference of effect, the existence of the object as independent from knowledge is established. ||15||

Commentary: Of the two—knowledge and object—the path is distinct, the course is separate, the realm [is distinct]—this is the extent. How? 'The object being the same, due to the difference of minds.' When the same object such as a woman is being perceived, the difference of minds of various perceivers is observed in the form of pleasure, pain, and delusion. For instance: when one beautiful woman is perceived, for one with desire, pleasure arises; for a co-wife, aversion; for a renunciant and such, disgust—thus, from the arising of various kinds of mental states regarding one object, how can the object be the product of mind? If the object were the product of one mind, it would appear as having only one form. Moreover, if the object were the product of mind, then for the mind to which that object is a product, when that mind is occupied with something else, that object would not exist at all. 'Let it be so'—but no! How would it then be perceived by many others? And it is perceived [by others]. Therefore, it is not a product of mind. If, simultaneously, many [minds] create that object, then the object created by many would differ from one created by a single [mind]. But when no difference is intended, then, given difference of cause but absence of difference of effect, the world would be either causeless or of one uniform nature. This amounts to saying: even though the cause differs, if there is non-difference of effect, then the entire world, produced by various causes, would be of one uniform nature. Or, because the variety of causes would have no bearing, it would be causeless by its own independence. If this is so, how are cognitions consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion produced for one single perceiver by that very mind whose nature is the three <s>guṇas</s>?

children.text:
yadyevaṃ jñānaṃ cet prakāśakatvādgrahaṇasvabhāvamarthaśca
                        prakāśyatvādgrāhyasvabhāvastadā yugapat sarvānarthān kathaṃ na gṛhṇāti| na
                        smarati cetyāśaṅkāṃ parihartumāha ---
children.translated_text: If knowledge is illuminating by nature and thus of the nature of grasping, and the object is illuminable by nature and thus of the nature of being grasped, then why does [the mind] not grasp all objects simultaneously? And why does it not remember?—to remove this doubt, he says:
An object is known or unknown to the mind, depending on the mind's coloring by it. ||Kaivalya 16||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- tasyārthasyoparāgādākārasamarpaṇāccitte bāhyaṃ vastu jñātamajñātaṃ
                        ca bhavati| ayamarthaḥ --- sarvaḥ padārtha ātmalābhe cittaṃ
                        sāmagrīmapekṣate| nīlādijñānaṃ copajāyamānamindriyapraṇālikayā
                        samāgatamarthoparāgaṃ sahakārikāraṇatvenāpekṣate| vyatiriktasyārthasya
                        sambandhābhāvādgrahītumaśakyatvāt| tataśca yenaivārthenāsya svarūpoparāgaḥ
                        kṛtastamevārthaṃ tajjñānaṃ vyavahārayogyatāṃ nayati| tataḥ so+artho jñāta
                        ucyate| yena cā+a+akāro na samarpitaḥ sa na jñātatvena vyavahriyate|
                        yasmiṃścānubhūte+arthe sādṛśyādirarthaḥ saṃskāramudbodhayan sahakāritāṃ
                        pratipadyate tasminnevārthe smṛtirupajāyata iti na sarvatra jñānaṃ nāpi
                        smṛtiriti na kaścidvirodhaḥ ||16||
children.translated_text: Commentary: Through the coloring by that object, through the imparting of its form to the mind, an external object becomes known or unknown. This is the meaning: every object, in being apprehended by the self, depends on the mind as its instrument. And cognition of blue and such, arising through the channel of the senses, depends on the coloring by the object that has arrived as a cooperative cause. Since an object unrelated [to the mind] cannot be grasped. Therefore, only the object by which the mind has been colored in its own form—that object alone is brought to functional awareness by that cognition. Therefore, that object is said to be 'known.' And that by which the form has not been imparted—that is not functionally recognized as known. And when, regarding an experienced object, an object of similarity and such, awakening the <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression), serves as a cooperative cause—memory arises regarding that very object. Thus there is neither knowledge of everything nor memory of everything—so there is no contradiction. ||16||

children.text:
yadyevaṃ pramātāpi puruṣo yasmin kāle nīlaṃ vedayate na tasmin kāle
                        pītādimataścittasattvasyāpi kadācit grahītṛrūpatvādākāragrahaṇe pariṇāmitvaṃ
                        prāptamityāśaṅkāṃ parihartumāha ---
children.translated_text: If the cognizer too, <s>Puruṣa</s>, at the time when he cognizes blue, does not [cognize] yellow and the rest—then since even the <s>sattva</s> of the mind sometimes has the nature of a grasper, in its grasping of form, transformation has been arrived at—to remove this doubt, he says:
The modifications of the mind are always known, because of the unchangingness of their lord, <s>Puruṣa</s>. ||Kaivalya 17||

children.text:
vṛttiḥ --- yā etāścittasya pramāṇaviparyayādirūpā vṛttayaḥ,
                        tāstatprabhościttasya grahītuḥ puruṣasya sadā sarvakālameva jñātāḥ

| tasya cidrūpatayā+apariṇāmitvāt
                        pariṇāmitvābhāvādityarthaḥ| yadyasau pariṇāmī syāt tadā pariṇāmasya
                        kādācitkatvāt tāsāṃ cittavṛttīnāṃ sadā jñātatvaṃ nopapadyeta| ayamarthaḥ ---
                        puruṣasya cidrūpasya sadaivādhiṣṭhātṛtvena vyavasthitasya yadantaraṅgaṃ
                        nirmalaṃ sattvam tasyāpi sadaivāvasthitatvādyenārthenoparaktaṃ bhavati
                        tathāvidhasyārthasya sadaiva cicchāyāsaṃkrāntisadbhāvastasyāṃ satyāṃ siddhaṃ
                        jñātṛtvamiti na kadācit kācit pariṇāmitvāśaṅkā ||17||
children.translated_text: because of his unchangingness—his being of the nature of consciousness (<s>cit</s>)—the absence of transformation—this is the meaning. If he were subject to transformation, then because transformation is occasional, the mind's modifications would not always be known—this would not be tenable.
